uni-cse-dsa.title: Data Structures (B.Tech CSE)
uni-cse-dsa.description: Unit-by-unit Data Structures for B.Tech/B.E. CSE: complexity, linked lists, stacks and queues, trees and AVL, heaps and hashing, graphs, and sorting — with runnable C, C++ and Java code activities and GATE-style unit exams.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Complexity, Arrays and Linked Lists
courses.summary: Abstract data types, asymptotic notation, array storage and address calculation, and singly, doubly and circular linked lists with all standard operations. Covers topics commonly taught in second-year B.Tech data structures courses.
outcomes: Learners can state Big-O, Omega and Theta and find the complexity of simple loops
Learners can compute row-major and column-major addresses
Learners can insert, delete, search and reverse a singly linked list
Learners can compare arrays, singly, doubly and circular lists for a task

scenes.text: Isha's shopping app searches 10 lakh products one by one. It feels slow during a sale.
Her mentor sorts the list once and uses binary search: about 20 comparisons instead of up to 10 lakh. The idea of growth rate clicks.

steps.title: ADT vs data structure
steps.body:
An **abstract data type** (ADT) says *what* operations exist (e.g. Stack: push, pop, top, isEmpty) without saying *how*. A **data structure** is a concrete implementation (array-based stack, linked stack).

We judge implementations by **time** and **space** as the input size n grows.

steps.title: Asymptotic notations
steps.body:
- **O(g)**: f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n0 (upper bound).
- **Ω(g)**: f(n) ≥ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n0 (lower bound).
- **Θ(g)**: both — tight bound.
- **o, ω**: strict versions (f grows strictly slower / faster).

Order: 1 < log n < √n < n < n log n < n² < n³ < 2ⁿ < n! < nⁿ.

steps.title: Solved example: count the work
steps.body:
Q1: `for(i=1;i<=n;i++) for(j=1;j<=i;j++) x++;`
- Step 1: inner loop runs i times.
- Step 2: total = 1+2+…+n = n(n+1)/2.
- Step 3: Θ(n²).

Q2: `for(i=1;i<n;i=i*2) x++;`
- Step 1: i takes 1,2,4,…,2^k < n.
- Step 2: k ≈ log₂n iterations → Θ(log n).

Q3: Is 3n²+5n+7 = O(n²)? Take c = 15, n0 = 1: 3n²+5n+7 ≤ 15n² for n ≥ 1. Yes.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying Big-O means 'worst case'. O is a bound on a function; worst/best/average are separate cases you can bound with any notation.
- Adding nested loop counts instead of multiplying them.
- Forgetting that log base does not matter asymptotically (log₂n = Θ(log₁₀n)).

steps.title: GATE tip
steps.body: To compare f and g, take logs or limits: if lim f/g = 0 then f = o(g). Example: n^100 vs 2^n → log gives 100 log n vs n, so 2^n wins.

activity.prompt: Read n and print how many times `x++` runs in the doubly nested loop where j goes from 1 to i (i from 1 to n). Print just the count.
activity.hint: The answer should equal n(n+1)/2.

quiz.q: Which is the tightest bound for f(n)=5n log n + 2n?
quiz.why: For large n, n log n grows faster than n, so the 2n term is absorbed. The constant 5 is ignored, so f(n) = Θ(n log n).
i is halved every iteration (n, n/2, n/4, ...) until it reaches 0. This takes about log₂ n steps.

options: f grows at most as fast as g, up to a constant
quiz.why: f(n) = O(g(n)) means that for large n, f is bounded above by a constant multiple of g. It is an asymptotic upper bound, not equality.
Exponential functions such as 2ⁿ eventually outgrow every polynomial, including n¹⁰, and n log n is slower still.
An abstract data type defines what operations exist and how they behave, not how they are stored. The implementation is hidden.

scenes.text: A cinema stores seats as a 2-D array. Ravi must find the memory address of seat [7][12] for a debug report.
With base address, element size and the row-major formula, he gets it in one line.

steps.title: 1-D arrays
steps.body:
Elements are contiguous. With base address B, element size w and lower bound LB:

**Addr(A[i]) = B + (i − LB)·w**

Access is O(1) (random access). Insertion/deletion in the middle is O(n) because elements must shift.

steps.title: 2-D arrays
steps.body:
For A[LR..UR][LC..UC] with N = UC − LC + 1 columns and M = UR − LR + 1 rows:

- **Row-major** (C, C++, Java): Addr = B + [(i−LR)·N + (j−LC)]·w
- **Column-major** (Fortran, MATLAB): Addr = B + [(j−LC)·M + (i−LR)]·w

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the number of rows in the row-major formula (it needs columns).
- Forgetting to subtract the lower bound when arrays start at 1.
- Thinking C checks bounds — out-of-range access is undefined behaviour.

steps.title: Sparse matrices
steps.body: If most entries are zero, store only (row, col, value) triplets. A 1000×1000 matrix with 3000 non-zeros needs 9000 numbers instead of 10⁶.

activity.prompt: Read B, w, LR, LC, number of columns N, and i j. Print the row-major address of A[i][j].
activity.hint: B + ((i-LR)*N + (j-LC))*w

quiz.q: Accessing a[i] in an array takes
quiz.why: The address of a[i] is base + i·size, a single calculation. So access takes constant time, O(1).
C stores 2-D arrays row by row, so each row sits next to the next in memory. This is row-major order.

quiz.q: int a[10] at base 500, w=4. Address of a[7]?
quiz.why: Address = base + index·width = 500 + 7·4 = 528.

quiz.q: Inserting at the front of an array of n elements costs
quiz.why: To insert at the front, all n existing elements must shift one place right. That takes O(n) time.

quiz.q: Sparse matrices are best stored as
quiz.why: A sparse matrix has mostly zeros. Storing only the non-zero entries as (row, column, value) triplets saves a lot of space.

scenes.text: A railway yard adds and removes coaches anywhere in a train without moving the others — just re-coupling links.
Neha realises that a linked list is the same: each node holds data and a pointer to the next coach.

steps.title: Node and head
steps.body:
`struct Node { int data; struct Node *next; };` A list is accessed through a **head** pointer; the last node's next is NULL.

- Insert at head: O(1)
- Insert at tail: O(n) (O(1) with a tail pointer)
- Search / access k-th: O(n)
- Delete after a known node: O(1)

steps.title: Solved example: insert at head
Solved example: reverse in place
steps.body:
Keep prev = NULL, cur = head.
- Step 1: next = cur->next
- Step 2: cur->next = prev
- Step 3: prev = cur; cur = next
- Repeat until cur is NULL; prev is the new head. Time O(n), space O(1).

Trace 1→2→3: after pass 1: 1→NULL; pass 2: 2→1; pass 3: 3→2→1.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Losing the rest of the list by overwriting `cur->next` before saving it.
- Not handling empty list or single node.
- Forgetting to `free` deleted nodes (memory leak).
- Dereferencing NULL at the tail (`p->next->data` when p->next is NULL).

steps.title: Floyd's cycle check
steps.body: Move slow by 1 and fast by 2. If they meet, a cycle exists. The same idea finds the middle node: when fast reaches the end, slow is at the middle.

activity.prompt: Read n then n integers. Insert each at the HEAD of a linked list, then print the list from head, space separated.
activity.hint: New node's next = head; head = new node.

quiz.q: Inserting at the head of a singly linked list costs
quiz.why: To insert at the head, create a node, point its next to the old head, and update head. That is only two pointer changes, O(1).

quiz.q: Finding the k-th element of a linked list costs
quiz.why: A linked list has no direct indexing, so you must follow k links from the head. That costs O(k).
Floyd's tortoise-and-hare moves one pointer by 1 and another by 2. If there is a cycle they must eventually meet, so it detects cycles.

quiz.q: Reversing a list iteratively needs extra space
quiz.why: An iterative reversal only needs prev, current and next pointers, whatever the list length. So extra space is O(1).

quiz.q: The last node of a singly linked list has next equal to
quiz.why: In a normal (non-circular) singly linked list, the last node's next pointer is NULL. This marks the end.

scenes.text: Kabir's browser lets him press Back and Forward through pages. He wonders what structure supports moving both ways.
A music app's 'repeat all' playlist loops forever. One is a doubly linked list, the other circular.

steps.title: Doubly linked list
steps.body:
Each node has `prev` and `next`. Deleting a node given only its pointer is O(1):

`p->prev->next = p->next; p->next->prev = p->prev; free(p);` (check for NULL at the ends).

Cost: one extra pointer per node.

steps.title: Circular lists
steps.body: Last node points back to the first. Keeping a pointer to the **last** node gives O(1) insertion at both front and end. Used for round-robin scheduling and multiplayer turns.

steps.title: Solved example: Josephus with a circular list
steps.body:
n = 5 people, every 2nd is removed, starting at 1.
- Step 1: 1→2→3→4→5→(1). Remove 2.
- Step 2: from 3, remove 4. Step 3: from 5, remove 1. Step 4: from 3, remove 5.
- Survivor: **3**. Recurrence J(1)=0, J(n)=(J(n−1)+k) mod n (0-based) gives 2 → person 3.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Updating only one direction in a doubly linked list.
- Infinite loops in circular lists: stop when you come back to the start, not at NULL.
- Forgetting to update head when deleting the first node.

steps.title: Where they are used
steps.body:
- LRU caches: doubly linked list + hash map.
- OS ready queue (round robin): circular list.
- Text editors' undo/redo: doubly linked lists or two stacks.

activity.prompt: Josephus: read n and k. People 1..n stand in a circle; counting from person 1, every k-th person is removed. Print the survivor.

quiz.q: Deleting a given node in a doubly linked list costs
quiz.why: A doubly linked node knows both prev and next. So you can unlink it directly in O(1) without walking the list.

quiz.q: In a circular list, traversal stops when
options: we return to the start node
quiz.why: A circular list has no NULL pointer, so you stop when you return to the starting node. Otherwise the loop would never end.
The hash map gives O(1) lookup of an entry, and the doubly linked list lets you move it to the front or evict the tail in O(1). Together they give a fast LRU cache.

quiz.q: Extra space per node in a doubly linked list compared with singly
quiz.why: A doubly linked node adds one extra pointer (prev) beyond the data and the next pointer.
With n = 5 and every 2nd person removed, the removal order is 2, 4, 1, 5. The last remaining person, 3, survives.

questions.q: Big-Θ of 4n³ + 100n²
questions.why: In 4n³ + 100n² the n³ term dominates for large n, and constants are dropped. So it is Θ(n³).

questions.q: Which statement is TRUE?
questions.why: 2^(n+1) = 2·2ⁿ, which is a constant multiple of 2ⁿ, so it is O(2ⁿ). n! outgrows 2ⁿ, 2^(2n) = 4ⁿ outgrows 2ⁿ, and n² is not O(n).

questions.q: Loop: for(i=1;i*i<=n;i++) runs
questions.why: The loop continues while i² ≤ n, so i runs up to √n. That gives Θ(√n) iterations.

questions.q: A[0..4][0..9], w=2, B=100, row-major. Address of A[2][3]?
questions.why: Row-major: address = B + (row·columns + col)·w = 100 + (2·10 + 3)·2 = 100 + 46 = 146.

questions.q: Same array, column-major (5 rows). Address of A[2][3]?
questions.why: Column-major: address = B + (col·rows + row)·w = 100 + (3·5 + 2)·2 = 100 + 34 = 134.

questions.q: Inserting at the end of a singly linked list WITHOUT a tail pointer
questions.why: Without a tail pointer you must walk from the head to the last node before linking the new one. That takes O(n).

questions.q: Assertion: binary search cannot be done efficiently on a linked list. Reason: linked lists lack random access.
options: Both true, reason does not explain
questions.why: Binary search needs to jump to the middle, but a linked list has no random access. Finding the middle costs O(n), so the reason explains why the assertion is true.

questions.q: Which detects the middle of a list in one pass?
questions.why: Move one pointer by 1 step and another by 2 steps. When the fast one reaches the end, the slow one is at the middle, in one pass.

questions.q: Time for T(n): for(i=1;i<=n;i++) for(j=1;j<=n;j*=2)
questions.why: The inner loop doubles j, so it runs about log n times. It is repeated for each of n outer iterations: Θ(n log n).

questions.q: Case: a music app needs 'next', 'previous' and wrap-around. Best structure?
questions.why: You need to move both forward and backward, and wrap around from the last song to the first. A circular doubly linked list does all of these.

questions.q: Which is NOT an advantage of linked lists over arrays?
questions.why: Arrays store items contiguously, so they are more cache-friendly for sequential access. Linked list nodes are scattered, which is a disadvantage, not an advantage.

questions.q: f(n)=n^(log n), g(n)=2^n. Then
questions.why: Take logs: log f = (log n)² while log g = n. Since (log n)² < n for large n, f grows slower than g, so f = O(g).

questions.q: Number of NULL pointers in a doubly linked list of n ≥ 1 nodes (non-circular)
questions.why: Only head→prev and tail→next are NULL; every other pointer links to a node. So there are exactly 2 NULL pointers.

questions.q: Reversing a singly linked list recursively uses stack space
questions.why: A recursive reversal makes one call per node before returning. Each call keeps a stack frame, so stack space is O(n).

questions.q: Josephus n=7, k=3 survivor
questions.why: Josephus recurrence: J(1) = 0, J(n) = (J(n−1) + 3) mod n. This gives J(7) = 3 in 0-based numbering, so the survivor is position 4.

questions.q: Sum 1 + 2 + 4 + … + 2^k where 2^k ≤ n is
questions.why: The sum 1 + 2 + 4 + … + 2^k is a geometric series equal to 2^(k+1) − 1. Since 2^k ≤ n, it is less than 2n, so Θ(n).

questions.q: Which notation is used for a lower bound?
questions.why: Ω (Omega) gives an asymptotic lower bound. O is an upper bound and Θ is both.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Stacks and Queues
courses.summary: Stack and queue ADTs with array and linked implementations, expression conversion and evaluation, circular queues, deques and priority queues, and recursion as an implicit stack.
outcomes: Learners can implement stacks and queues with arrays and linked lists
Learners can convert infix to postfix and evaluate postfix
Learners can implement a circular queue and detect full/empty correctly
Learners can explain how recursion uses the call stack

scenes.text: At the hostel mess, the last plate washed is the first one picked up.
Ananya notices her editor's Undo works the same way: the most recent change is undone first.

steps.title: LIFO
steps.body:
A **stack** is Last-In-First-Out. Operations: push(x), pop(), top()/peek(), isEmpty(). All O(1).

- Array version: `top` index starts at −1; push does `a[++top]=x`; pop returns `a[top--]`.
- **Overflow**: push when top == MAX−1. **Underflow**: pop when top == −1.

steps.title: Solved example: trace
steps.body:
push 5, push 8, pop, push 3, push 9, pop, top?
- Step 1: [5] → [5,8] → pop 8 → [5]
- Step 2: [5,3] → [5,3,9] → pop 9 → [5,3]
- Step 3: top = **3**.

Linked stack: push = insert at head, pop = delete head, both O(1), no overflow until memory runs out.

steps.title: Solved example: balanced brackets
steps.body:
Check `{[()]}(`:
- Push on every opener; on a closer, the top must be the matching opener.
- `{[()]}` matches fully; the final `(` stays on the stack → **unbalanced**.

Rule: balanced iff every closer matched and the stack is empty at the end.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Popping without checking empty (underflow).
- Returning the wrong verdict when the string ends with unmatched openers.
- Using `top = 0` initially and then mixing pre/post increment.

steps.title: Applications
steps.body: Function calls, undo, browser back, expression evaluation, DFS, backtracking (mazes), syntax parsing.

activity.prompt: Read a bracket string (only ()[]{}). Print YES if balanced, else NO.
activity.hint: At the end the stack must be empty.

quiz.why: A stack removes the most recently added item first. That is last-in, first-out (LIFO).

quiz.q: Array stack with MAX=5 and top=4 (0-based). A push causes
quiz.why: With 0-based indices, top = 4 means all 5 slots are used. Another push would overflow the stack.

quiz.q: push 1, push 2, pop, push 3, pop, pop returns in order
quiz.why: Trace: push 1, push 2, pop gives 2, push 3, pop gives 3, pop gives 1. So the output is 2, 3, 1.
The head of the list acts as the top. Push is insertion at the head, which takes O(1).
A closing ] must match the most recent opening [. Here the ] meets a ( on the stack, so the string is unbalanced.

scenes.text: A cheap calculator chip cannot handle brackets directly. Engineers convert the user's expression to postfix first.
Postfix needs no brackets and no precedence rules — just one stack.

steps.title: Three notations
steps.body:
- Infix: A + B * C
- Prefix (Polish): + A * B C
- Postfix (Reverse Polish): A B C * +

Precedence: ^ (right-assoc) > * / (left) > + − (left).

steps.title: Shunting-yard (infix → postfix)
steps.body:
Scan left to right:
- Operand → output.
- `(` → push. `)` → pop to output until `(`; discard both.
- Operator op → pop while top has **higher** precedence, or **equal** precedence and op is left-associative; then push op.
- End → pop everything.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
Convert A+B*(C-D)/E.
- A → out: A
- + → push
- B → out: AB
- * → top + lower → push
- ( → push; C → ABC; - → push; D → ABCD; ) → pop - → ABCD-
- / → top * equal, left-assoc → pop * → ABCD-*; push /
- E → ABCD-*E; end → pop / then + → **ABCD-*E/+**

steps.title: Solved example: evaluate postfix
steps.body:
Evaluate 6 2 3 + - 3 8 2 / + * :
- 6,2,3 → + gives 5 → 6,5 → − gives 1
- 3,8,2 → / gives 4 → 3,4 → + gives 7
- 1,7 → * gives **7**.

For `a b -` pop b first, then a, compute a − b.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reversing operand order for − and / when evaluating.
- Treating ^ as left-associative: 2^3^2 = 2^9 = 512, postfix 2 3 2 ^ ^.
- Forgetting to pop remaining operators at the end.

activity.prompt: Read a postfix expression of single-digit operands and + - * / (integer division), all without spaces, e.g. 23*5+. Print its value.
activity.hint: Pop y first, then x; compute x op y.

quiz.why: The brackets force A+B to be done first, then multiplied by C. In postfix this is AB+ followed by C and *, giving AB+C*.
Postfix 5 3 − means 5 − 3 = 2. Then 2 2 * — here the last operand is 2, so the result is (5 − 3)·2 = 4.
Exponentiation groups from the right: a^b^c means a^(b^c). So ^ is right-associative.
Multiplication binds tighter, so A*B is first and then + C. In prefix this is + (* A B) C = +*ABC.

quiz.q: Data structure used to evaluate postfix
quiz.why: Postfix evaluation pushes operands onto a stack. An operator pops the top two, applies itself, and pushes the result back.

scenes.text: The department printer prints jobs in the order they arrive. Nobody wants the newest job to jump the line.
Rahul's array-based queue says 'full' even though the front is empty. A circular queue fixes it.

steps.title: FIFO
steps.body:
Queue: enqueue at **rear**, dequeue from **front**. All O(1).

A linear array queue wastes slots: after dequeues, front moves right and cannot reuse space.

steps.title: Circular queue
steps.body:
Use indices modulo N:
- enqueue: `rear = (rear+1) % N; a[rear]=x`
- dequeue: `front = (front+1) % N`
- Common convention keeps one slot empty: **empty** when front == rear, **full** when (rear+1)%N == front. Capacity N−1.
- Or keep a `count` variable to use all N slots.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
N = 5, front = rear = 0 (one-slot-empty). Enqueue 10,20,30,40:
- rear becomes 1,2,3,4. (4+1)%5 = 0 = front → **full** with 4 items.
- Dequeue twice → front = 2. Enqueue 50 → rear = 0. Enqueue 60 → rear = 1. Now (1+1)%5 = 2 = front → full again.

steps.title: Deque and priority queue
steps.body:
- **Deque**: insert/delete at both ends. Input-restricted and output-restricted variants.
- **Priority queue**: remove the highest (or lowest) priority first; efficient with a binary heap (O(log n) insert/delete).
- Queue with two stacks: amortised O(1) per operation.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using front == rear for both full and empty without a count.
- Forgetting `% N` on one of the indices.
- Calling a priority queue 'FIFO' — ties may be FIFO, but order is by priority.

activity.prompt: Simulate a circular queue of size N (with a count variable, so capacity N). Input: N, then q commands: `E x` (enqueue; print FULL if full) or `D` (dequeue and print the value, or EMPTY). Print each output on its own line.
activity.hint: Track count; wrap indices with % N.

quiz.why: A queue serves the oldest item first, which is first-in, first-out (FIFO).

quiz.q: Circular queue, N=6, one slot kept empty. Full when
quiz.why: With one slot kept empty to tell full from empty, the queue is full when the slot after rear is front: (rear + 1) % 6 == front.
A deque (double-ended queue) allows insertion and deletion at both the front and the rear.

quiz.q: Best structure for a priority queue
quiz.why: A binary heap gives insert and extract-max (or min) in O(log n). An unsorted list makes one of the operations O(n).

quiz.q: Queue using two stacks gives amortised cost per op
quiz.why: Enqueue pushes onto an input stack; dequeue pops from an output stack, refilling it from the input stack when empty. Each element moves at most once, so the amortised cost is O(1).

story.title: Tower of Hanoi at the fest

scenes.text: A tech-fest stall challenges students to move 6 discs. Most give up after 20 moves.
Sahil writes a three-line recursive function that prints all 63 moves.

steps.title: How recursion runs
steps.body:
Each call pushes an **activation record** (parameters, locals, return address) on the call stack. A base case stops the recursion; without it the stack overflows.

Any recursion can be converted to iteration with an explicit stack.

steps.title: Solved example: Tower of Hanoi
steps.body:
hanoi(n, A, C, B): move n−1 from A to B, move disc n from A to C, move n−1 from B to C.
- T(n) = 2T(n−1) + 1, T(1) = 1
- Unroll: T(n) = 2ⁿ − 1. For n = 6 → 63 moves.
- n = 2 moves: A→B, A→C, B→C.

steps.title: Solved example: call count of naive Fibonacci
steps.body:
fib(n) = fib(n−1) + fib(n−2). Calls C(n) = C(n−1) + C(n−2) + 1, C(0)=C(1)=1.
- C(2)=3, C(3)=5, C(4)=9, C(5)=15.
- Growth is exponential (about 1.618ⁿ); memoisation makes it O(n).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Missing or unreachable base case.
- Thinking recursion is always slower — tail recursion may be optimised, and many tree algorithms are cleanest recursively.
- Forgetting the stack depth: recursion on a 10⁶-node list can overflow.

steps.title: Tail recursion
steps.body: If the recursive call is the last action (`return f(n-1, acc*n)`), compilers may reuse the frame. C/C++ compilers often do this at -O2; Java does not guarantee it.

activity.prompt: Read n and print the moves of Tower of Hanoi from A to C using B, one per line as `A->C`, then a final line `Total: <moves>`.
activity.hint: Move n-1 to the spare peg first.

quiz.q: Moves for Tower of Hanoi with 5 discs
quiz.why: Hanoi needs T(n) = 2T(n−1) + 1 moves, which solves to 2ⁿ − 1. For 5 discs that is 31.

quiz.q: Each recursive call stores its data in
quiz.why: Every function call gets an activation record on the call stack that holds its parameters, locals and return address.

quiz.q: Recursion without a base case leads to
quiz.why: Without a base case, calls never stop and the call stack fills up. The result is a stack overflow.
Naive fib(n) = fib(n−1) + fib(n−2) recomputes the same subproblems again and again. The number of calls grows exponentially.
To move n discs, move n−1 discs aside, move the largest one, then move n−1 discs again: T(n) = 2T(n−1) + 1.

questions.q: Which operation sequence leaves the stack empty? (start empty)
questions.why: Each pop needs a matching earlier push. push, pop, push, pop pushes and removes twice, ending empty. Others either pop an empty stack or leave elements.

questions.q: Postfix of A*(B+C)/D
questions.why: Brackets first: B+C becomes BC+. Then A*(…) gives ABC+*, and /D gives ABC+*D/.

questions.q: Value of postfix 2 3 1 * + 9 -
questions.why: Evaluate: 3 1 * = 3, then 2 3 + = 5, then 5 9 − = −4.

questions.q: Postfix of 2^3^2 and its value
questions.why: ^ is right-associative, so 2^3^2 = 2^(3^2) = 2^9 = 512. Its postfix is 2 3 2 ^ ^.

questions.q: Circular queue N=8 (one slot empty), front=5, rear=2. Number of elements?
questions.why: Number of elements = (rear − front + N) mod N = (2 − 5 + 8) mod 8 = 5.

questions.q: Assertion: a queue can be built from two stacks. Reason: reversing a reversed order restores the original order.
options: Both true, reason does not explain
questions.why: The input stack reverses the arrival order, and moving everything into the output stack reverses it again. This restores first-in, first-out order, so the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Minimum stack size needed to evaluate postfix 1 2 + 3 4 + *
questions.why: Push 1, 2, then + leaves 3. Pushing 3 and 4 makes the stack hold 3, 3, 4, i.e. size 3 at the peak. Then + and * reduce it.

questions.q: BFS uses which structure?
questions.why: BFS visits vertices level by level in first-in, first-out order, which is exactly a queue.

questions.q: Number of calls by naive fib(5) counting all calls (fib(0),fib(1) base)
questions.why: The call count C(n) = 1 + C(n−1) + C(n−2) with C(0) = C(1) = 1. This gives C(2)=3, C(3)=5, C(4)=9, C(5)=15.

questions.q: Case: a ticket system must serve senior citizens before others regardless of arrival. Use
questions.why: Seniors must be served first regardless of arrival time. A priority queue serves the highest-priority item first, and a plain queue would use arrival order.

questions.q: Output-restricted deque allows deletion at
questions.why: An output-restricted deque lets you insert at both ends but delete from one end only.

questions.q: Sequence 1,2,3 pushed in order (pops allowed anytime). Which output is IMPOSSIBLE?
questions.why: To output 3 first, push 1, 2, 3 and pop 3; the top is now 2, so 2 must come out next, not 1. So 3, 1, 2 is impossible.

questions.q: Number of valid pop sequences for 3 pushed elements
questions.why: The number of valid stack output permutations of n items is the Catalan number Cₙ. For n = 3 that is 5.

questions.q: Converting infix to postfix needs a stack of
questions.why: Operands go straight to the output. Operators wait on a stack until precedence rules say to output them.

questions.q: Hanoi with n discs: minimum moves of the largest disc
questions.why: The largest disc can only move once, from the source to the target, after all smaller discs have moved aside.

questions.q: Space complexity of recursive factorial(n)
questions.why: factorial(n) calls factorial(n−1) and so on down to 1. That is n frames on the call stack, so O(n) space.

questions.q: Prefix expression * + 2 3 - 7 4 equals

courses.title: Unit 3 · Trees, Binary Search Trees and AVL Trees
courses.summary: Tree terminology and properties, binary tree traversals, building a tree from traversals, BST search/insert/delete, and height-balanced AVL trees with rotations.
outcomes: Learners can apply the counting properties of binary trees
Learners can perform and reconstruct from inorder, preorder and postorder traversals
Learners can insert into and delete from a BST
Learners can perform LL, RR, LR and RL rotations in AVL trees

scenes.text: Meera draws her family tree for a school project: grandparents at the top, cousins as leaves.
Her brother points out that the folders on his laptop form the same shape — one root, many branches.

steps.title: Words you must know
steps.body:
Root, parent, child, sibling, leaf (no children), internal node, **depth** (edges from root), **height** (edges on the longest path to a leaf), degree, subtree, level.

A tree with n nodes has exactly **n − 1 edges**.

steps.title: Binary tree facts
steps.body:
- Max nodes at level i (root level 0): 2^i.
- Max nodes in a tree of height h: 2^(h+1) − 1.
- Min height with n nodes: ⌈log₂(n+1)⌉ − 1.
- **n₀ = n₂ + 1** (leaves = nodes with two children + 1).
- Full (every node 0 or 2 children), complete (all levels full except last, filled left to right), perfect (all levels full).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
Q1: A binary tree has 20 nodes with two children. How many leaves? → n₀ = 20 + 1 = **21**.

Q2: Max nodes of height 4? → 2⁵ − 1 = **31**.

Q3: Number of distinct binary tree *shapes* with 3 nodes? → Catalan C₃ = (1/4)·C(6,3) = **5**.

steps.title: Representations
steps.body:
- Linked: node with left, right pointers.
- Array (good for complete trees): root at index 1, children of i at 2i and 2i+1, parent at ⌊i/2⌋ (0-based: 2i+1, 2i+2, ⌊(i−1)/2⌋).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing height counted in edges vs nodes — always state the convention.
- Applying n₀ = n₂ + 1 to non-binary trees.
- Calling every complete tree 'full'.

activity.prompt: Read h (height in edges). Print the maximum number of nodes in a binary tree of height h, and the maximum number of leaves, separated by a space.
activity.hint: Use shifts: 1LL<<k is 2^k.

quiz.q: A tree with 15 nodes has how many edges?
quiz.why: A tree with n nodes always has n − 1 edges. With 15 nodes, that is 14.

quiz.q: Binary tree with 10 leaves has how many nodes of degree 2?
quiz.why: In a binary tree, the number of nodes with two children is one fewer than the number of leaves: n₂ = n₀ − 1. So 10 leaves gives 9.

quiz.q: In a 1-based array heap, children of index 5 are
quiz.why: In a 1-based array heap, the children of node i are at 2i and 2i+1. For i = 5 these are 10 and 11.

quiz.q: Number of binary tree shapes with 3 nodes
quiz.why: The number of distinct binary tree shapes with n nodes is the Catalan number Cₙ. For n = 3 this is 5.

quiz.q: A perfect binary tree of height 3 has how many leaves?
quiz.why: A perfect binary tree of height h has 2ʰ leaves. For height 3 that is 8.

scenes.text: HR wants the org chart printed so that every manager appears before their team. Finance wants totals computed bottom-up.
Preorder serves HR, postorder serves Finance, and level order prints floor by floor.

steps.title: Depth-first traversals
steps.body:
- **Preorder**: Node, Left, Right (copying a tree, prefix expressions)
- **Inorder**: Left, Node, Right (gives sorted order in a BST)
- **Postorder**: Left, Right, Node (deleting a tree, postfix expressions)
- **Level order**: BFS using a queue.

Each visits every node once → O(n).

steps.title: Solved example: traverse
steps.body:
Tree: root A; A.left = B, A.right = C; B.left = D, B.right = E; C.right = F.
- Preorder: A B D E C F
- Inorder: D B E A C F
- Postorder: D E B F C A
- Level: A B C D E F

steps.title: Solved example: rebuild from preorder + inorder
steps.body:
Pre: A B D E C F, In: D B E A C F.
- Step 1: first of preorder, A, is the root. In inorder, left of A = {D,B,E}, right = {C,F}.
- Step 2: next in preorder is B → root of left part; in inorder D is left of B, E right.
- Step 3: C is root of right part; F is right of C.
- Unique tree recovered. Preorder + postorder alone is NOT enough for a unique binary tree (unless full).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing level order when asked for preorder.
- Assuming inorder alone determines the tree.
- Forgetting that the last element of postorder is the root.

steps.title: Expression trees
steps.body: For (a+b)*c, inorder (with brackets) gives infix, preorder gives prefix * + a b c, postorder gives postfix a b + c *.

activity.prompt: Insert the given n keys (in order) into an empty BST, then print the preorder, inorder and postorder traversals on three lines (space separated).
activity.hint: Inorder of a BST is sorted — use that to check.

quiz.q: Inorder traversal of a BST gives
quiz.why: In a BST every left key is smaller and every right key is larger than the node. So inorder (left, node, right) gives keys in sorted order.

quiz.q: Root of a tree from its postorder is
quiz.why: Postorder visits the left subtree, then the right subtree, then the node. So the root comes last.
Level-order traversal visits nodes level by level using a first-in, first-out queue, the same idea as BFS.

quiz.q: Which pair uniquely determines a binary tree?
quiz.why: Preorder gives the root and inorder shows which nodes lie left or right of it. Together they rebuild the tree uniquely. Preorder and postorder alone can be ambiguous.
Postorder visits left, right, then root. The tree has + with children a and b, under * with c, so the postorder is ab+c*.

lessons.title: Binary search trees: search, insert, delete

scenes.text: A college stores 5,000 student roll numbers. Linear search is too slow at admission rush.
A BST answers each lookup by going left or right at each node — about 13 steps when balanced.

steps.title: BST property
steps.body:
For every node: all keys in the left subtree < key < all keys in the right subtree.

Search, insert, delete: O(h). Balanced → O(log n); skewed (sorted insertions) → O(n).

steps.title: Deletion — three cases
steps.body:
- **Leaf**: remove it.
- **One child**: link the parent directly to the child.
- **Two children**: replace the key with its **inorder successor** (minimum of right subtree) or predecessor (maximum of left), then delete that node (which has at most one child).

steps.title: Solved example: delete 50
steps.body:
BST from 50, 30, 70, 60, 80, 65.
- 50 has two children. Successor = min of right subtree {70, 60, 80, 65} = 60.
- Copy 60 into the root; delete 60 from the right subtree. 60 had right child 65 → 70.left = 65.
- Result: root 60; left 30; right 70 with children 65 and 80. Inorder: 30 60 65 70 80 ✔

steps.title: Solved example: count BSTs
steps.body:
How many distinct BSTs on keys {1,2,3}? → Catalan C₃ = **5**. With 4 keys → C₄ = 14.

Formula: Cₙ = C(2n, n)/(n+1).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the successor from the *left* subtree.
- Forgetting to update the parent pointer after deletion.
- Claiming BST operations are always O(log n).

activity.prompt: Read n keys and insert into a BST, then read a key k. Print FOUND d where d is its depth (root depth 0), or NOT FOUND.
activity.hint: Walk down from the root counting steps.

quiz.q: Worst-case search in a BST of n nodes
quiz.why: If the BST is skewed like a chain, a search may need to visit all n nodes. The worst case is O(n).

quiz.q: Inorder successor of a node with a right child is
quiz.why: With a right child, the next larger key is the smallest key in the right subtree, found by going right once and then left as far as possible.

quiz.q: Inserting 1,2,3,4,5 in order gives a tree of height
quiz.why: Inserting sorted keys 1 to 5 makes each new key the right child of the last. This is a right chain of 5 nodes, with 4 edges, so height 4.
The number of distinct BSTs on n keys is the Catalan number Cₙ. For n = 4, C₄ = 14.

quiz.q: Deleting a leaf from a BST requires
quiz.why: A leaf has no children to reattach. So you simply set its parent's pointer to NULL.

scenes.text: A logging system inserts timestamps in increasing order. Its BST turns into a long chain and lookups crawl.
Switching to an AVL tree keeps height near 1.44 log n with a few rotations per insert.

steps.title: Balance factor
steps.body:
BF(node) = height(left) − height(right). AVL requires BF ∈ {−1, 0, +1} at every node.

Height of an AVL tree with n nodes is O(log n) (at most about 1.44 log₂ n). Min nodes N(h) = N(h−1) + N(h−2) + 1, N(0)=1, N(1)=2.

steps.title: Four rotation cases
steps.body:
Let z be the first unbalanced node on the way up from the inserted node.
- **LL** (insert in left of left): single right rotation at z.
- **RR**: single left rotation at z.
- **LR**: left rotate z.left, then right rotate z.
- **RL**: right rotate z.right, then left rotate z.

Insertion needs at most one (single or double) rotation; deletion may need O(log n).

steps.title: Solved example: insert 10, 20, 30
steps.body:
- 10 → 20 (right) → 30 (right of right). BF(10) = −2 → **RR case**.
- Left rotate at 10: 20 becomes root, 10 left, 30 right.

Insert 30, 10, 20: 20 goes left-right of 30 → **LR**: rotate 10 left (20 above 10), then rotate 30 right → root 20.

steps.title: Solved example: minimum nodes
steps.body:
Min nodes in an AVL tree of height 3?
- N(0)=1, N(1)=2, N(2)=N(1)+N(0)+1=4, N(3)=N(2)+N(1)+1=**7**.
- So with 7 nodes the height can be as large as 3.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Rotating at the root instead of the lowest unbalanced ancestor.
- Confusing LR with RL — name the path from z towards the new node.
- Forgetting to update heights after a rotation (update the lower node first).

steps.title: Other balanced trees
steps.body: Red-black trees (used in C++ std::map and Java TreeMap) allow slightly more imbalance with fewer rotations. B-trees and B+ trees are used by databases and file systems.

activity.prompt: Read h and print the minimum number of nodes in an AVL tree of height h (height in edges, N(0)=1, N(1)=2).

quiz.q: Allowed balance factors in AVL trees
quiz.why: An AVL tree keeps each node's balance factor (height of left minus right) at −1, 0, or 1. Anything outside this range triggers a rotation.

quiz.q: Inserting 3, 2, 1 into an empty AVL tree triggers
quiz.why: Inserting 3, 2, 1 makes a left-left chain, so the root 3 has balance factor +2 with a left-heavy left child. That needs a single LL (right) rotation.

quiz.q: Rotations needed per AVL insertion at most
quiz.why: After an insertion, fixing the lowest unbalanced node with one single or one double rotation restores the subtree's original height. So no more rotations are needed.

quiz.q: Minimum nodes in an AVL tree of height 2
quiz.why: The minimum nodes N(h) = N(h−1) + N(h−2) + 1 with N(0)=1 and N(1)=2. So N(2) = 2 + 1 + 1 = 4.

quiz.q: C++ std::map is usually implemented as
quiz.why: C++ std::map is commonly implemented as a red-black tree, which keeps keys ordered and balanced with O(log n) operations.

questions.q: Edges in a tree of 25 nodes
questions.why: A tree with n nodes has n − 1 edges. For 25 nodes that is 24.

questions.q: Maximum nodes in a binary tree of height 5 (edges)
questions.why: A binary tree of height h (edges) has at most 2^(h+1) − 1 nodes. For h = 5 that is 2⁶ − 1 = 63.

questions.q: Inorder: D B E A F C G; Preorder: A B D E C F G. Postorder?
options: D B E F C G A
D E B F G C A
D E F B G C A
E D B G F C A
questions.why: Preorder gives root A; inorder splits into left D B E and right F C G. Rebuilding gives B with children D, E, and C with children F, G. Postorder is D E B F G C A.

questions.q: A binary tree has 7 leaves. Nodes with two children
questions.why: For a binary tree, nodes with two children = leaves − 1. With 7 leaves, that is 6.

questions.q: Keys 40, 20, 60, 10, 30, 50, 70 inserted into a BST. Height?
questions.why: Inserting 40, 20, 60, 10, 30, 50, 70 fills every level, forming a perfect tree. It has three levels, so the height is 2 edges.

questions.q: Delete 20 (two children 10, 30) from the BST above using successor. New key at that position
questions.why: The inorder successor of 20 is the smallest key in its right subtree, which is 30. Replace 20's key with 30 and delete the old 30 leaf.

questions.q: Number of distinct BSTs with 5 keys
questions.why: The number of distinct BSTs with n keys is Cₙ. C₅ = 42.

questions.q: Assertion: inorder of an AVL tree is sorted. Reason: every AVL tree is a BST.
options: Both true, reason does not explain
questions.why: An AVL tree is a BST that is kept balanced, so its inorder traversal is sorted. The reason is true and it explains the assertion.

questions.q: Inserting 30, 10, 20 into an empty AVL tree requires
questions.why: 30 becomes the root, 10 its left child, and 20 the right child of 10. That is a left-right case, fixed by a double (LR) rotation, making 20 the new root.

questions.q: Min nodes in AVL tree of height 4
Maximum height of an AVL tree with 7 nodes
questions.why: The smallest AVL tree of height 3 has 7 nodes, and height 4 needs at least 12. So 7 nodes can reach at most height 3.

questions.q: Array representation, 0-based. Parent of index 9
questions.why: In a 0-based array tree, the parent of index i is ⌊(i − 1)/2⌋. For 9, that is ⌊8/2⌋ = 4.

questions.q: Case: a dictionary app inserts words already in alphabetical order into a plain BST. Expected effect
options: degenerates to a chain, O(n) lookups
questions.why: Words in sorted order always go to the right, so the plain BST becomes a chain. Lookups then take O(n), not O(log n).

questions.q: Which traversal is used to delete all nodes safely?
questions.why: Postorder visits the children before their parent. So you can free both children before freeing the node itself.

questions.q: Preorder of a BST is 30 20 10 25 40 35 50. Its postorder
questions.why: Preorder root 30, then smaller keys 20, 10, 25 form the left subtree and 40, 35, 50 the right. Postorder (left, right, root) is 10 25 20 35 50 40 30.

questions.q: Time to build a BST by inserting n sorted keys
questions.why: Sorted input makes a chain. Insert number i needs about i comparisons, so the total is 1 + 2 + … + n = Θ(n²).

questions.q: A complete binary tree with 100 nodes has how many leaves?
questions.why: In a complete binary tree with n nodes, the internal nodes are ⌊n/2⌋. So leaves = 100 − 50 = 50.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Heaps, Priority Queues and Hashing
courses.summary: Binary heaps and heap operations, building a heap in linear time, priority queues, hash functions, collision resolution by chaining and open addressing, and load factor analysis. Also introduces B-trees and tries at overview level.
outcomes: Learners can insert into and delete from a binary max/min heap
Learners can explain why build-heap is O(n)
Learners can resolve collisions with chaining, linear and quadratic probing and double hashing
Learners can reason about load factor and expected probes

scenes.text: In a hospital emergency ward, the most critical patient is seen first, not the earliest arrival.
The triage software keeps patients in a max-heap keyed by severity, so finding the most critical is O(1).

steps.title: Heap property
steps.body:
A binary heap is a **complete** binary tree stored in an array where every parent ≥ children (max-heap) or ≤ children (min-heap).

- getMax: O(1)
- insert: put at end, **sift up** — O(log n)
- extractMax: move last to root, **sift down** (swap with larger child) — O(log n)

steps.title: Solved example: insert
steps.body:
Max-heap [50, 30, 40, 10, 20]. Insert 45.
- Step 1: place at index 5 (0-based): [50,30,40,10,20,45]. Parent index 2 holds 40.
- Step 2: 45 > 40 → swap: [50,30,45,10,20,40]. Parent index 0 holds 50.
- Step 3: 45 < 50 → stop. Final: **[50,30,45,10,20,40]**.

steps.title: Solved example: extract max
steps.body:
From [50,30,45,10,20,40]:
- Step 1: remove 50, move 40 to root: [40,30,45,10,20].
- Step 2: children 30, 45 → larger 45 > 40 → swap: [45,30,40,10,20].
- Step 3: 40 has no children at indices 5,6 → stop.

steps.title: Build-heap in O(n)
steps.body:
Call sift-down on nodes from index ⌊n/2⌋−1 down to 0. Most nodes are near the bottom and move little: Σ (n/2^(h+1))·h = O(n).

Heapsort: build-heap, then repeatedly swap root with the last element and sift down → O(n log n), in place, not stable.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Swapping with the *smaller* child in a max-heap sift-down.
- Thinking a heap is sorted — only the root is guaranteed to be max.
- Saying build-heap is O(n log n) (that's the naive repeated-insert bound).

activity.prompt: Read n integers, insert them one by one into a MAX-heap stored in an array (sift up), then print the array (space separated).
activity.hint: Parent of c is (c-1)/2.

quiz.q: In a max-heap the maximum is at
quiz.why: The max-heap property says each parent is at least as large as its children, so the largest key sits at the root.

quiz.q: Time to build a heap from n elements bottom-up
quiz.why: Bottom-up heap building sifts nodes down. Most nodes are near the bottom and move little, so the total work sums to O(n).
Check parents: 10 ≥ 8, 9; 8 ≥ 7, 3; 9 ≥ 2. All hold, so it is a max-heap.
Heapsort builds a heap in the array and repeatedly swaps the max to the end. It runs in O(n log n) with O(1) extra space, but it is not stable.

quiz.q: In a min-heap of n distinct keys, the maximum is located in
quiz.why: In a min-heap every internal node is smaller than at least one child. So the maximum cannot be internal, and must be a leaf.

scenes.text: A gym assigns lockers by the last two digits of your phone number. Two members with ...42 fight over locker 42.
The manager adds hooks so each locker can hold a small chain of bags. That is separate chaining.

steps.title: Hashing
steps.body:
A hash function maps a key to an index in a table of size m. Goal: O(1) average search/insert/delete.

- **Division**: h(k) = k mod m (choose m prime, not near a power of 2).
- **Multiplication**: h(k) = ⌊m·(kA mod 1)⌋, A ≈ 0.618.
- **Mid-square, folding** for some keys. Strings: polynomial rolling hash.

steps.title: Separate chaining
steps.body:
Each slot holds a linked list. **Load factor α = n/m** can exceed 1.

Under simple uniform hashing: unsuccessful search ≈ 1 + α probes, successful ≈ 1 + α/2.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Choosing m = 100 for decimal keys: only the last two digits matter.
- Forgetting that worst-case search is O(n) when all keys collide.
- Mixing up α for chaining (can be > 1) and open addressing (must be < 1).

steps.title: Real use
steps.body: Java HashMap uses chaining and converts long chains to balanced trees; Python dict uses open addressing. Both resize when α passes a threshold (Java default 0.75).

activity.prompt: Read m and n keys. Using h(k)=k mod m with separate chaining, print the length of the longest chain.
activity.hint: You only need counts, not actual lists.

quiz.why: The load factor α = n/m is the number of stored keys per table slot.
An unsuccessful search hashes to a slot (constant time) and scans that whole chain, whose average length is α. So Θ(1 + α).

quiz.q: Good choice of m for division hashing
options: a prime not near a power of 2
quiz.why: For division hashing h(k) = k mod m, a prime m far from a power of 2 spreads keys evenly. A power of 2 uses only the low bits of the key.

quiz.q: h(k)=k mod 11, key 47 goes to slot
Worst-case search in a hash table with chaining
quiz.why: In the worst case all n keys hash to the same slot, giving one long chain. A search then walks it, costing O(n).

lessons.title: Open addressing: probing and double hashing

scenes.text: At a mall, if your favourite slot is taken, you drive to the next free slot.
Soon cars bunch up in one corner. Engineers try jumping by squares or by a second hash to spread them.

steps.title: Probe sequences
steps.body:
All keys live in the table (α < 1). For attempt i = 0,1,2,…
- **Linear**: (h(k) + i) mod m — suffers *primary clustering*.
- **Quadratic**: (h(k) + c₁i + c₂i²) mod m — *secondary clustering*.
- **Double hashing**: (h₁(k) + i·h₂(k)) mod m — h₂(k) must never be 0 and should be coprime to m.

steps.title: Solved example: double hashing
steps.body:
m = 7, h₁ = k mod 7, h₂ = 5 − (k mod 5). Insert 10, 17.
- 10 → 3.
- 17 → h₁ = 3 (taken). h₂ = 5 − 2 = 3. Next (3 + 3) mod 7 = **6**.

Expected probes (uniform hashing): unsuccessful ≤ 1/(1−α); successful ≈ (1/α) ln(1/(1−α)).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Deleting by emptying a slot — breaks later searches. Use a **tombstone** (DELETED marker).
- Letting α approach 1: expected probes explode (α = 0.9 → up to 10 probes for misses).
- Using quadratic probing with a non-prime m and α > 0.5 — it may fail to find a free slot.

steps.title: Beyond hashing: B-trees and tries
steps.body:
- **B-tree of order m**: every node has ≤ m children, non-root nodes ≥ ⌈m/2⌉; all leaves at the same depth; used by databases for disk-friendly search.
- **Trie**: tree of characters; search a word of length L in O(L), great for autocomplete.

activity.prompt: Read m and n keys. Insert using linear probing with h(k)=k mod m. Print the final table, using -1 for empty slots, space separated.
activity.hint: Advance p=(p+1)%m while occupied.

quiz.q: Primary clustering is a problem of
quiz.why: In linear probing, keys fill consecutive slots, forming long occupied runs that grow even longer. This is primary clustering.

quiz.q: In open addressing, α must be
quiz.why: In open addressing, all keys sit in the table itself, so n ≤ m and therefore α < 1 in practice (the table must not be full).

options: keep probe chains intact after deletion
quiz.why: If a deleted slot were marked empty, a search would stop there and miss keys placed beyond it. A tombstone tells the search to keep probing.

quiz.q: Expected probes for unsuccessful search at α=0.5 (bound)
quiz.why: The expected probes for an unsuccessful search are at most 1/(1 − α) = 1/(1 − 0.5) = 2.

quiz.q: Searching a word of length L in a trie costs
quiz.why: In a trie you follow one edge per character. So a search for a word of length L takes O(L), independent of the number of words.

scenes.text: A news app must show the top 3 trending tags out of millions of events every minute.
Instead of sorting everything, Arjun keeps a min-heap of size 3 and replaces its root when a bigger count arrives.

steps.title: Top-K with a min-heap
steps.body:
Keep a min-heap of the K largest seen so far. For each new x: if size < K push; else if x > top, pop and push.

Time O(n log K), space O(K) — much better than sorting (O(n log n)) when K ≪ n.

steps.title: Solved example: merge k sorted lists
steps.body:
Push the first element of each list into a min-heap with (value, list id). Pop min, output it, push the next from that list.
- k lists, N total elements → O(N log k).
- Lists [1,4], [2,5], [3]: pops 1,2,3,4,5.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using a max-heap for top-K largest (you need fast access to the *smallest* of the kept K).
- In C++, `priority_queue<int>` is a **max**-heap; use `greater<int>` for min.
- In Java, `PriorityQueue` is a **min**-heap by default.

steps.title: Other uses
steps.body: Dijkstra's and Prim's algorithms, event simulation, CPU scheduling, Huffman coding, median maintenance with two heaps.

activity.prompt: Read n, k and n integers. Print the k largest in decreasing order, space separated, using a min-heap of size k.
activity.hint: Popping a min-heap gives ascending order; print in reverse.

quiz.q: Top-K largest of n items with a heap of size K costs
quiz.why: Keep a min-heap of size K. Each of the n items costs at most O(log K) to push or replace, so the total is O(n log K).
The default C++ std::priority_queue puts the largest element on top, so it is a max-heap.
Java's PriorityQueue orders by natural ordering and removes the smallest first, so by default it is a min-heap.

quiz.q: Merging k sorted lists of total N items with a heap
quiz.why: Keep one pointer per list in a heap of size k. Each of the N items needs one O(log k) heap operation, giving O(N log k).
Keep the lower half in a max-heap and the upper half in a min-heap. The median is at one or between the two tops, found in O(1).

questions.q: Insert 35 into max-heap [40, 30, 20, 10]. Result
questions.why: Add 35 at the end, index 4. Its parent at index 1 is 30 < 35, so swap: [40, 35, 20, 10, 30]. Its parent 40 is larger, so it stops.

questions.q: Extract max from [9, 7, 8, 3, 5]. Result
questions.why: Remove 9, move the last element 5 to the root, giving [5, 7, 8, 3]. Swap 5 with the larger child 8, giving [8, 7, 5, 3].

questions.q: Height of a heap with 100 elements (edges)
questions.why: A heap is a complete tree, so its height is ⌊log₂ n⌋. For 100 elements, ⌊log₂ 100⌋ = 6.

questions.q: Is [1, 3, 2, 7, 4, 5] a valid min-heap?
questions.why: Check parents: 1 ≤ 3, 2; 3 ≤ 7, 4; 2 ≤ 5. Every parent is at most its children, so it is a valid min-heap.

questions.q: Bottom-up build-heap time
questions.why: Building a heap bottom-up costs the sum of node heights, which is O(n). This is a classic result.

questions.q: h(k)=k mod 13. Slot of key 100
Chaining, m=10, n=25. Load factor
questions.why: Load factor α = n/m = 25/10 = 2.5, meaning an average of 2.5 keys per chain.

questions.q: Linear probing m=7, h=k mod 7, insert 14, 21, 7. Slot of 7?
questions.why: 14, 21 and 7 all hash to slot 0. 14 takes slot 0, 21 probes to slot 1, and 7 probes to slot 2.

questions.q: Double hashing requires h₂(k)
questions.why: The step h₂(k) must never be 0 and must be coprime to the table size m. Then the probe sequence can reach every slot.

questions.q: Assertion: deletion in open addressing uses a marker. Reason: an empty slot would stop a search too early.
questions.why: A deleted slot is marked (tombstone) because making it empty would end later searches too early. Both statements are true and the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Expected probes for unsuccessful search, open addressing, α=0.75 (bound 1/(1−α))
questions.why: The expected number of probes is at most 1/(1 − α) = 1/(1 − 0.75) = 1/0.25 = 4.

questions.q: Case: an autocomplete box must suggest words with a typed prefix. Best structure
questions.why: A trie lets you walk down the typed prefix and then list the words beneath it. A prefix search costs O(L), which suits autocomplete.

questions.q: Minimum number of keys in a B-tree of order 5 non-root node
questions.why: A B-tree of order 5 allows at most 5 children. A non-root node needs at least ⌈5/2⌉ = 3 children, i.e. at least 2 keys.

questions.q: k-th smallest of n elements using a min-heap built in O(n) then k extracts
questions.why: Building the heap costs O(n). Each of the k extract-mins costs O(log n), so the total is O(n + k log n).

questions.q: In a max-heap with distinct keys, the second largest is
questions.why: In a max-heap each node is larger than its children, so anything other than the root is below it. The second largest must be directly under the root, one of its children.

questions.q: Which is NOT a valid use of a priority queue?
questions.why: Dijkstra, Huffman coding and event simulation all repeatedly need the smallest item. Checking balanced brackets uses a stack instead.

questions.q: Number of comparisons to find max in a min-heap of n elements (worst)
questions.why: The maximum in a min-heap must be a leaf, and there are about n/2 leaves. So you need to scan them all, roughly n/2 comparisons.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Graphs: Representation and Traversal
courses.summary: Graph terminology, adjacency matrix and list, BFS and DFS with their properties, connected components, cycle detection, topological sort, and an introduction to shortest paths and spanning trees (treated fully in the Algorithms pack).
outcomes: Learners can choose between adjacency matrix and list
Learners can run BFS and DFS by hand and in code
Learners can detect cycles and count connected components
Learners can produce a topological order of a DAG with Kahn's algorithm

scenes.text: Delhi's metro map has stations as dots and lines between them. Priya wants the app to find routes.
Her first task is to choose how to store the map in memory.

steps.title: Terminology
steps.body:
G = (V, E). Directed / undirected, weighted / unweighted, degree (in/out), path, cycle, connected, complete graph Kₙ (n(n−1)/2 edges), tree (connected, acyclic, n−1 edges), DAG.

**Handshake lemma**: Σ deg(v) = 2|E| in an undirected graph, so the number of odd-degree vertices is even.

steps.title: Matrix vs list
steps.body:
- **Adjacency matrix**: V×V; edge check O(1); space O(V²); iterating neighbours O(V). Good for dense graphs.
- **Adjacency list**: each vertex keeps its neighbours; space O(V+E); neighbours in O(deg). Good for sparse graphs (most real graphs).
- Edge list: list of (u, v, w), used by Kruskal.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
Q1: Undirected graph with degrees 3, 3, 2, 2, 2. Edges? → (3+3+2+2+2)/2 = **6**.

Q2: Can a graph have degrees 3, 3, 3? → Sum 9 is odd → **impossible**.

Q3: Space for a matrix of 10⁵ vertices → 10¹⁰ cells — infeasible; use a list.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding an undirected edge only once in an adjacency list (add u→v and v→u).
- Saying matrix BFS is O(V+E) — it is O(V²).
- Confusing a simple graph with a multigraph (parallel edges, loops).

steps.title: Graphs everywhere
steps.body: Road networks, social networks, web links, course prerequisites, package dependencies, circuit nets, molecule structures.

activity.prompt: Read n (vertices), m (edges) and m undirected edges u v (0-based). Print the degree of each vertex, space separated.
activity.hint: Each edge adds 1 to both ends.

quiz.why: A complete graph on n vertices has n(n−1)/2 edges. For K₆ that is 6·5/2 = 15.
An adjacency list stores one list per vertex and one entry per edge (two for undirected). So the space is O(V + E).

quiz.q: Sum of degrees in an undirected graph with 9 edges
quiz.why: Each edge adds 1 to the degree of each of its two ends. So the sum of degrees is 2|E| = 2·9 = 18.
An adjacency matrix lets you check matrix[u][v] directly in O(1). A list must scan the neighbours.

quiz.q: Number of vertices with odd degree is always
quiz.why: By the handshake lemma, the degree sum equals 2|E|, which is even. Odd degrees can only total an even number if there is an even count of odd-degree vertices.

scenes.text: A social app wants to show 'friends of friends' and how many hops away anyone is.
BFS spreads like a ripple: first all friends, then their friends, level by level.

steps.title: Algorithm
steps.body:
```
mark s visited; dist[s]=0; enqueue s
while queue not empty:
  u = dequeue
  for each neighbour v of u:
    if not visited: visited, dist[v]=dist[u]+1, parent[v]=u, enqueue v
```
Time O(V+E) with lists. Gives **shortest paths in unweighted graphs**.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
Edges: 0-1, 0-2, 1-3, 2-3, 3-4. BFS from 0 (neighbours in increasing order).
- Queue: [0] → visit 1, 2 → [1,2]
- From 1: 3 → [2,3]; from 2: 3 already seen; from 3: 4 → [4]
- Order **0 1 2 3 4**; dist: 0,1,1,2,3.

steps.title: Solved example: bipartite check
steps.body:
Colour s with 0; each neighbour gets the opposite colour. If an edge joins two same-coloured vertices, the graph is **not bipartite** (it contains an odd cycle).
- A 4-cycle is bipartite; a triangle is not.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Marking visited when *dequeuing* instead of when *enqueuing* — causes duplicates in the queue.
- Using BFS for shortest paths in weighted graphs (use Dijkstra).
- Forgetting to restart BFS from unvisited vertices in a disconnected graph.

steps.title: BFS tree
steps.body: In an undirected BFS tree, non-tree edges join vertices whose levels differ by at most 1.

activity.prompt: Read n, m, m undirected edges and a source s. Run BFS (visit neighbours in increasing order) and print the visit order, space separated.
activity.hint: Mark visited when you push.

quiz.why: BFS visits vertices in the order they were discovered, level by level, which needs a first-in, first-out queue.
BFS dequeues each vertex once and scans each edge's adjacency entry once, so the cost is O(V + E).
BFS reaches nodes in order of the number of edges, which is the shortest path when all edges count the same, i.e. unweighted graphs.

quiz.q: A graph with an odd cycle is
quiz.why: A graph is bipartite only if it has no odd cycles. An odd cycle cannot be coloured with two colours, so the graph is not bipartite.

quiz.q: When should a vertex be marked visited in BFS?
quiz.why: Mark a vertex as visited when it is enqueued, not when dequeued. Otherwise the same vertex could be added to the queue several times.

scenes.text: In a hedge maze, Karan keeps one hand on the wall and goes as deep as possible before turning back.
That 'go deep, then backtrack' strategy is DFS, and it can also tell him if paths loop.

steps.title: Algorithm
steps.body:
```
DFS(u): visited[u]=true; for v in adj[u]: if !visited[v]: DFS(v)
```
Time O(V+E). Record discovery/finish times to classify edges: tree, back, forward, cross (directed).

steps.title: Uses of DFS
steps.body:
- **Connected components**: run DFS from every unvisited vertex; count the runs.
- **Cycle detection (undirected)**: a visited neighbour that is not the parent → cycle.
- **Cycle detection (directed)**: an edge to a vertex currently on the recursion stack (grey) → back edge → cycle.
- Topological sort, articulation points, bridges, strongly connected components.

steps.title: Solved example: components
steps.body:
n = 6, edges 0-1, 1-2, 3-4. DFS from 0 visits {0,1,2}; from 3 visits {3,4}; from 5 visits {5}.
- **3 components**.

Directed 0→1→2→0: while at 2 (stack 0,1,2) we see 0 which is grey → **cycle**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the undirected 'parent' rule on a directed graph.
- Deep recursion overflow on huge graphs — use an explicit stack.
- Forgetting that DFS order depends on neighbour order (many valid answers).

steps.title: Parenthesis theorem
steps.body: For any two vertices, their DFS intervals [d, f] are either disjoint or nested — a favourite GATE question.

activity.prompt: Read n, m and m undirected edges. Print the number of connected components.
activity.hint: Each DFS started from an unvisited vertex is one component.

quiz.why: DFS goes as deep as possible and then backtracks, which is last-in, first-out. So it uses a stack or recursion.

quiz.q: A back edge in a directed DFS implies
quiz.why: A back edge in a directed graph points to an ancestor still on the DFS stack. Following the tree path back to it forms a cycle.

quiz.q: Graph with 10 vertices, 0 edges has components
quiz.why: With no edges, no vertex is connected to another. So each vertex forms its own component, giving 10.

quiz.q: Undirected cycle check: a visited neighbour that is not the parent means
quiz.why: If a DFS meets an already visited neighbour that is not the parent, there is a second route between the two vertices. That forms a cycle.
With an adjacency matrix, finding the neighbours of each vertex means scanning a full row of V entries. Over V vertices that is O(V²).

lessons.title: Topological sort and a preview of shortest paths

scenes.text: Data Structures needs C; Algorithms needs Data Structures and Discrete Maths. In what order should Riya take courses?
A topological order of the prerequisite graph gives a valid plan.

steps.title: Topological order
steps.body:
A linear order of a DAG's vertices with u before v for every edge u→v. Exists **iff** the graph has no directed cycle.

**Kahn's algorithm**: queue all in-degree-0 vertices; repeatedly remove one, output it, decrement its neighbours' in-degree, enqueue new zeros. If fewer than V are output → cycle.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
Edges: 5→2, 5→0, 4→0, 4→1, 2→3, 3→1. In-degrees: 0:2, 1:2, 2:1, 3:1, 4:0, 5:0.
- Using a min-priority choice: 4 → (0:1, 1:1); 5 → (2:0, 0:0); pick 0, then 2 → 3:0; 3 → 1:0; 1.
- Order: **4 5 0 2 3 1**.

DFS method: output vertices in decreasing finish time.

steps.title: Preview: weighted shortest paths
steps.body:
- Dijkstra (non-negative weights): O((V+E) log V) with a heap.
- Bellman–Ford (negative edges allowed, detects negative cycles): O(VE).
- Floyd–Warshall (all pairs): O(V³).
- Shortest paths in a DAG: relax in topological order, O(V+E).
Full treatment: Algorithms pack, Unit 3.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Claiming topological order is unique — usually there are many.
- Running topological sort on an undirected graph.
- Forgetting the cycle check (output count < V).

activity.prompt: Read n, m and m directed edges. Print a topological order using Kahn's algorithm, always choosing the SMALLEST available vertex (min-heap). If a cycle exists print CYCLE.
activity.hint: If fewer than n vertices come out, there is a cycle.

quiz.q: Topological sort exists iff the graph is
quiz.why: A topological order exists only when there are no directed cycles, i.e. the graph is a DAG. With a cycle, some vertex would have to come before itself.

quiz.q: Kahn's algorithm starts with vertices of
quiz.why: Kahn's algorithm begins with vertices with in-degree 0, i.e. no prerequisites. It then removes them and updates the in-degrees.
Each vertex is enqueued once, and each edge reduces one in-degree once. So the time is O(V + E).

quiz.q: Which algorithm handles negative edge weights?
quiz.why: Bellman–Ford relaxes all edges V − 1 times, so it handles negative weights (and can detect negative cycles). Dijkstra and Prim assume non-negative weights.

quiz.q: Number of topological orders of a DAG with 3 vertices and no edges
quiz.why: With no edges, there are no constraints, so any ordering of the 3 vertices is valid. That is 3! = 6.

questions.q: Max edges in a simple undirected graph of 8 vertices
questions.why: The most edges in a simple undirected graph is 8·7/2 = 28, one for every pair of vertices.

questions.q: Max edges in a simple directed graph of 8 vertices
questions.why: In a simple directed graph each ordered pair (u, v) with u ≠ v can have an edge, so 8·7 = 56.

questions.q: Degrees 4,3,3,2,2 — number of edges
questions.why: The degree sum is 4 + 3 + 3 + 2 + 2 = 14, and it equals 2E. So E = 7.

questions.q: BFS from A on edges A-B, A-C, B-D, C-D, D-E (alphabetical). Distance to E
questions.why: The shortest route is A→B→D→E, with 3 edges. A→C→D→E also has length 3.

questions.q: Which is true of DFS on an undirected graph?
questions.why: In an undirected DFS every non-tree edge joins a vertex to its ancestor or descendant (a back edge). Cross edges cannot occur.

questions.q: Assertion: BFS gives shortest paths in unweighted graphs. Reason: BFS visits vertices in non-decreasing distance order.
questions.why: BFS explores vertices in non-decreasing distance order, level by level. So the first time it reaches a vertex is by a shortest path, and the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: A connected graph with V vertices and V−1 edges is
questions.why: A connected graph with V − 1 edges has no cycle (one more edge would create it), so it is a tree.

questions.q: Valid topological order for edges a→b, a→c, b→d, c→d
questions.why: a must come first and d last, and b, c can be in either order. a c b d respects all edges.

questions.q: Number of topological orders for edges a→b, a→c, b→d, c→d
questions.why: a must be first and d must be last. The middle b and c can appear in either order, giving 2 orders.

questions.q: Space of adjacency matrix for 1000 vertices storing 1 bit per entry
questions.why: The matrix has V × V = 1000² = 10⁶ entries, so at 1 bit each that is 10⁶ bits.

questions.q: Case: a build tool must order 500 tasks with dependencies and report circular dependencies. Use
questions.why: Tasks with dependencies form a directed graph. Kahn's algorithm gives a topological order and reports a cycle if some tasks can never reach in-degree 0.

questions.q: Minimum colours needed for a cycle with 7 vertices
questions.why: An odd cycle is not bipartite, so 2 colours fail. Three colours are enough for any cycle, so 3.

questions.q: In a DFS of a directed graph, edge (u,v) with d[u] < d[v] < f[v] < f[u] that is not a tree edge is a
questions.why: The interval of v is nested inside u's, so v is a descendant of u. An edge from u to a non-child descendant is a forward edge.

questions.q: Number of connected components of a forest with 20 vertices and 15 edges
questions.why: A forest has V − E components, since each tree has one more vertex than edge. So 20 − 15 = 5.

questions.q: Which graph is bipartite?
questions.why: A tree has no cycles, so no odd cycles, so it is bipartite. K₃, K₄ and a 5-cycle each contain an odd cycle (a triangle or 5-cycle).

questions.q: BFS on a complete graph Kₙ with adjacency list takes
questions.why: K_n has n(n−1)/2 = Θ(n²) edges, and BFS costs O(V + E). So the time is Θ(n²).

questions.q: A DAG has at least one vertex with
questions.why: Every DAG has a source. If each vertex had an incoming edge, following edges backward forever would eventually repeat a vertex, forming a cycle.

courses.title: Unit 6 · Searching and Sorting
courses.summary: Linear and binary search, elementary sorts (bubble, selection, insertion), divide-and-conquer sorts (merge, quick), heapsort recap, non-comparison sorts (counting, radix), stability and the Ω(n log n) lower bound.
outcomes: Learners can write a bug-free binary search including lower bound
Learners can trace bubble, selection and insertion sort and count swaps
Learners can implement merge sort and quicksort and state their complexities
Learners can choose a sort using stability, memory and input properties

scenes.text: Outside the exam hall, 900 roll numbers are pinned in sorted order. Students scan line by line and crowd the board.
Tanvi opens the list near the middle, decides which half her number is in, and finds it in seconds.

steps.title: Two searches
steps.body:
- **Linear search**: O(n), works on any list.
- **Binary search**: sorted array; compare with the middle and discard half. O(log n). At most ⌊log₂n⌋+1 comparisons.

Use `mid = lo + (hi − lo)/2` to avoid integer overflow.

steps.title: Solved example: trace
steps.body:
A = [3, 8, 15, 21, 34, 47, 52], find 34.
- lo=0, hi=6, mid=3 → 21 < 34 → lo=4
- mid=5 → 47 > 34 → hi=4
- mid=4 → 34 found at index **4** after 3 comparisons.

steps.title: Solved example: lower bound
steps.body:
First index with A[i] ≥ x. Search on [lo, hi) with hi = n:
- while lo < hi: mid; if A[mid] < x: lo = mid+1 else hi = mid.
- A = [1,2,2,2,5], x = 2 → returns **1**. x = 3 → returns 4. Count of 2s = upper − lower = 4 − 1 = 3.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Infinite loop from `lo = mid` with `while(lo < hi)`.
- Running binary search on unsorted data.
- Off-by-one with `hi = n` vs `hi = n − 1` — pick one convention and keep it.

steps.title: Binary search on the answer
steps.body: If a predicate is monotonic (false…false true…true), binary search finds the first true — e.g. the minimum capacity to ship packages in D days.

activity.prompt: Read n, a sorted array of n integers, then x. Print the index of x using binary search, or -1 if absent.
activity.hint: while(lo<=hi) with hi=n-1.

quiz.why: Binary search halves the range using the middle element, so the data must be sorted and you must be able to jump to the middle in O(1).

quiz.q: Maximum comparisons for binary search in 1000 elements
quiz.why: Each comparison halves the range, so at most ⌊log₂ 1000⌋ + 1 = 9 + 1 = 10 comparisons are needed.
lo + (hi − lo)/2 gives the same midpoint as (lo + hi)/2 but avoids integer overflow when lo + hi is huge.
If the target is equally likely to be at any position 1..n, the average number of comparisons is (1 + 2 + … + n)/n = (n + 1)/2.
The lower bound is the first position whose value is ≥ 3. In [1,2,2,2,5] this is the 5 at index 4.

scenes.text: A teacher sorts 40 answer sheets by roll number. She picks up one sheet at a time and slides it into place — insertion sort.
Card players do the same with their hand. For nearly sorted piles, it is surprisingly fast.

steps.title: Three O(n²) sorts
steps.body:
- **Bubble**: swap adjacent out-of-order pairs; after pass k, the k largest are in place. Best O(n) with an early-exit flag. Stable.
- **Selection**: select the minimum of the unsorted part and swap into place. Always Θ(n²) comparisons, at most n−1 swaps. Not stable.
- **Insertion**: insert A[i] into the sorted prefix by shifting. Best O(n), worst O(n²). Stable, adaptive, online.

steps.title: Solved example: bubble passes
steps.body:
[4, 3, 2, 1]
- Pass 1: [3,2,1,4] (3 swaps)
- Pass 2: [2,1,3,4] (2 swaps)
- Pass 3: [1,2,3,4] (1 swap)
Total swaps 6 = inversions = n(n−1)/2 for reverse order.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling selection sort stable.
- Forgetting the early-exit flag when claiming bubble sort's best case O(n).
- Counting comparisons and swaps as the same thing.

steps.title: Inversions
steps.body: An inversion is a pair i < j with A[i] > A[j]. Bubble swaps and insertion shifts both equal the inversion count. Merge sort can count inversions in O(n log n).

activity.prompt: Read n integers and sort them with insertion sort. Print the sorted array on line 1 and the number of shifts (element moves to the right) on line 2.
activity.hint: Count each a[j+1]=a[j].

quiz.why: If the array is already sorted, each element is compared once with its predecessor and no shifts are needed. So it takes O(n).

quiz.q: Which makes the fewest swaps in the worst case?
quiz.why: Selection sort swaps once per pass, so at most n − 1 swaps. Bubble and insertion sort can make Θ(n²) swaps or shifts.
An inversion is a pair out of order. In [3,1,2] the pairs (3,1) and (3,2) are inverted, while (1,2) is fine. So 2.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT stable in its usual form?
quiz.why: Selection sort swaps the minimum with a faraway position, which can jump past equal keys and change their order. Merge, insertion and bubble sorts are stable.

quiz.q: After 1 bubble pass on [5,1,4,2], array is
quiz.why: One bubble pass compares neighbours and swaps: 5,1 → 1,5; 5,4 → 4,5; 5,2 → 2,5. The result is [1,4,2,5], with the largest at the end.

scenes.text: A university merges sorted mark lists from 8 departments: merging sorted halves is fast and predictable.
Its search engine uses quicksort-style partitioning because, on average, it is the fastest in memory.

steps.title: Merge sort
steps.body: Split in half, sort both recursively, merge. T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Θ(n) = **Θ(n log n)** in every case. Stable. Needs Θ(n) extra space for arrays (linked lists can be merged in place).

steps.title: Quicksort
steps.body:
Choose a pivot, **partition** so smaller elements are left and larger right, recurse.
- Best/average: Θ(n log n). Worst (already sorted with first/last pivot): T(n) = T(n−1) + Θ(n) = Θ(n²).
- In place (O(log n) stack on average), not stable.
- Randomised pivot or median-of-three makes the worst case unlikely.

steps.title: Solved example: merge
steps.body:
Merge [1, 4, 9] and [2, 3, 10]:
- 1 vs 2 → 1; 4 vs 2 → 2; 4 vs 3 → 3; 4 vs 10 → 4; 9 vs 10 → 9; append 10.
- Result [1,2,3,4,9,10] with 5 comparisons (worst case m + n − 1).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying quicksort is always O(n log n).
- Writing `<` instead of `<=` in the merge step and breaking stability.
- Recursing on the pivot itself in quicksort (infinite recursion).

steps.title: Lower bound
steps.body: Any comparison sort needs Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case: a decision tree with n! leaves has height ≥ log₂(n!) = Θ(n log n).

activity.prompt: Read n integers and sort them with your own merge sort (no std::sort). Print them space separated.
activity.hint: Use <= when merging to keep it stable.

quiz.why: Merge sort always splits in half and merges in linear time. So the worst case is also Θ(n log n).

quiz.q: Quicksort worst case occurs with last-element pivot on
quiz.why: With the last element as pivot, sorted input puts the pivot at the extreme end each time. Partitions are 0 and n−1, so the time is Θ(n²).
Merge sort is stable if equal keys are taken from the left half first (using <=). Selection sort, heapsort and quicksort are not stable in their usual forms.
Merge sort sorts two halves of size n/2 and then merges in linear time: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n.
A decision tree for n items has n! leaves, so its height is at least log₂(n!) = Ω(n log n). So any comparison sort needs that many comparisons.

lessons.title: Counting sort, radix sort and choosing a sort

scenes.text: A board must sort 10 lakh students by marks out of 100. Comparison sorts take time.
Because marks are integers 0–100, counting sort does it in one linear sweep.

steps.title: Counting sort
steps.body: For integer keys in [0, k]: count occurrences, take prefix sums, place elements from right to left (keeps it **stable**). Time Θ(n + k), space Θ(n + k). Great when k = O(n).

steps.title: Radix sort
steps.body:
Sort by each digit from least significant to most, using a stable sort (counting sort) per digit. d digits in base b: Θ(d(n + b)).

Example: 32-bit integers with base 2⁸ → 4 passes.

steps.title: Solved example: pick the sort
steps.body:
- Nearly sorted 10⁵ items → **insertion sort** (or TimSort).
- Need stable, guaranteed n log n → **merge sort**.
- In-place, fast average, memory tight → **quicksort / introsort**.
- Integers in small range → **counting sort**.
- Guaranteed O(n log n) and O(1) extra → **heapsort**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using counting sort when k is huge (e.g. keys up to 10⁹).
- Radix sort with an unstable per-digit sort — gives wrong results.
- Forgetting negative numbers in counting sort (shift by the minimum).

activity.prompt: Read n marks (0–100) and print them in non-decreasing order using counting sort.
activity.hint: c[v] counts how many times v appears.

quiz.q: Counting sort time for n keys in [0,k]
quiz.why: Counting sort counts each key (O(n)) and then places items using a count array of size k + 1 (O(k)). The time is Θ(n + k).

quiz.q: Radix sort needs the per-digit sort to be
quiz.why: Radix sort sorts digit by digit. The per-digit sort must be stable, or the order from earlier passes would be lost.

quiz.q: Best choice for nearly sorted data
quiz.why: Insertion sort takes time proportional to the number of inversions. Nearly sorted data has few, so it runs close to O(n).

quiz.q: Which sort is in-place with guaranteed O(n log n)?
quiz.why: Heapsort rearranges the array into a heap in place and has O(n log n) worst case. Merge sort needs extra space and quicksort can be Θ(n²).

quiz.q: Counting sort is a comparison sort.
quiz.why: Counting sort never compares two keys; it uses key values as array indices. So it is not a comparison sort and can beat n log n.

questions.q: Binary search on 64 sorted elements, max comparisons
questions.why: Max comparisons = ⌊log₂ 64⌋ + 1 = 6 + 1 = 7.

questions.q: Number of inversions in [2, 4, 1, 3, 5]
questions.why: Count pairs with the earlier element larger: (2,1), (4,1), (4,3). That makes 3 inversions.

questions.q: Selection sort comparisons on n elements
questions.why: Selection sort scans the whole remaining part to find the minimum on every pass. So it makes (n−1) + (n−2) + … + 1 = n(n−1)/2 comparisons, whatever the input.

questions.q: Quicksort with median pivot every time has recurrence
questions.why: With the median as pivot, the array splits into two halves of n/2 and partitioning costs n: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n.

questions.q: Partition always splits 1:9. Quicksort time
questions.why: A fixed 1:9 split still makes the recursion depth O(log n), and each level costs O(n). So it is Θ(n log n), just with a larger constant.

questions.q: Assertion: merge sort is preferred for sorting linked lists. Reason: merging lists needs no random access and no extra array.
questions.why: Merging linked lists only relinks nodes and needs no random access or extra array. Merge sort therefore suits linked lists, so the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Which sort's running time does NOT depend on input order?
questions.why: Merge sort always splits and merges the same way, so it is Θ(n log n) for any order. Quicksort and insertion sort vary a lot with input order.

questions.q: Minimum comparisons to merge two sorted lists of sizes m and n (worst case)
questions.why: In the worst case, each comparison outputs one element, and the last element needs no comparison. So m + n − 1 comparisons.

questions.q: Case: sort 10⁷ phone numbers (10 digits) as fast as possible. Best
