- **Semi-supervised**: few labels, many unlabelled.
- **Reinforcement learning**: an agent takes actions and learns from rewards.
- **Self-supervised**: labels created from the data itself (e.g. predict the next word).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1. Classify the task.** Predict house price → supervised regression. Group customers by behaviour → unsupervised clustering. Detect fraud yes/no → supervised classification. A robot learning to walk → reinforcement learning.

**Example 2. Features and label.** For loan default: features = income, existing EMIs, credit history length; label = defaulted (yes/no).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling any if-else program 'AI/ML'.
- Confusing regression (numeric output) with logistic regression (a classifier).
- Using ML when a simple rule works reliably.
- Forgetting that models learn **bias present in the data** too.

activity.prompt: Which kind of learning fits each task?

items.text: Predict tomorrow's temperature from past data
Group news articles by topic without labels

quiz.why: Regression predicts a continuous number such as a price. Classification predicts a category.
Clustering finds groups without labels, so it is unsupervised learning.

quiz.q: In Mitchell's definition, P stands for…
quiz.why: In Mitchell's definition, a program learns from experience E on task T with performance measure P, which shows how success is judged.
Despite its name, logistic regression outputs probabilities for classes, so it is used for classification.

quiz.q: An agent learning from rewards is…
quiz.why: An agent that learns by acting and receiving rewards or penalties is doing reinforcement learning.

scenes.text: A hospital asks: can we predict which patients will miss appointments?
The team defines the goal, collects data, builds a baseline, iterates, deploys and keeps monitoring.

steps.title: Steps
steps.body:
- Define the problem and success metric (and the cost of errors).
- Collect and understand data (EDA).
- Clean and prepare features.
- Split into train / validation / test.
- Train a **baseline**, then better models.
- Tune hyperparameters on validation data.
- Evaluate once on the test set.
- Deploy, monitor for **drift**, retrain.

steps.title: Parameters vs hyperparameters
steps.body:
- **Parameters** are learned from data (weights of a linear model, split thresholds of a tree).
- **Hyperparameters** are set before training (learning rate, k in kNN, tree depth, regularisation strength) and tuned using validation data.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1. Baseline.** 90% of patients attend. A model that always predicts 'attends' has 90% accuracy — any real model must beat this and must be judged with recall on the 'miss' class.

**Example 2. Classify.** Learning rate 0.01 → hyperparameter. Coefficient of age = 0.37 → parameter. Number of trees = 200 → hyperparameter.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Tuning on the test set (it stops being an honest estimate).
- Skipping a baseline.
- Optimising accuracy when the real cost is in missed positives.
- Deploying and never monitoring.

activity.prompt: Put the ML workflow in order.

quiz.why: Hyperparameters are set before training, like k in kNN. Weights, biases and learned thresholds are learned from the data.

quiz.q: The test set should be used…
quiz.why: The test set gives an honest estimate of final performance, so use it once at the end. Using it for tuning leaks information.

options: Input data distribution changes over time
quiz.why: Data drift is when the distribution of incoming data changes from what the model was trained on, which can make performance fall.
A baseline is a simple reference model, such as predicting the mean. A real model should beat it to be worthwhile.

quiz.q: 95% of emails are not spam. Always predicting 'not spam' gives accuracy…
quiz.why: If 95% of emails are not spam, always predicting not spam is right 95% of the time. High accuracy can hide a useless model on imbalanced data.

story.title: The salary column in lakhs and rupees

scenes.text: Half the salary values are in rupees and half in lakhs; city is text; some ages are blank.
Rahul standardises units, encodes cities, fills gaps and scales features before training.

steps.title: Missing values and outliers
steps.body:
- Drop rows/columns only if few are missing and data is plentiful.
- **Impute**: mean/median (numeric; median is robust to outliers), mode (categorical), or model-based.
- Add a 'was_missing' indicator when missingness itself carries information.
- Outliers: check if errors (fix/remove) or genuine (keep; use robust methods). IQR rule: outlier if < Q1 − 1.5·IQR or > Q3 + 1.5·IQR.

steps.title: Encoding categories
steps.body:
- **One-hot** for nominal categories (city): one 0/1 column per value.
- **Ordinal** encoding for ordered categories (low < medium < high).
- Label-encoding nominal data as 0,1,2 implies a false order for linear models.

steps.title: Scaling
steps.body:
- **Standardisation** z = (x − μ)/σ → mean 0, std 1.
- **Min–max** x' = (x − min)/(max − min) → [0, 1].
- Needed for distance-based (kNN, k-means, SVM) and gradient-based models; trees don't need it.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Computing scaling statistics on the whole dataset before splitting (leakage).
- Mean-imputing heavily skewed data.
- Label-encoding nominal features for linear models.
- One-hot encoding a feature with 10,000 categories without thinking (use hashing/target encoding carefully or grouping).

activity.prompt: Min–max scale the list to [0, 1] and print values rounded to 2 decimals.
activity.starter:
xs = [10, 20, 35, 60]
# scaled = ...
print(scaled)
activity.solution:
xs = [10, 20, 35, 60]
lo, hi = min(xs), max(xs)
scaled = [round((x - lo) / (hi - lo), 2) for x in xs]
print(scaled)
activity.hint: (x - min) / (max - min) for each x.

quiz.q: Best imputation for a skewed income column?
quiz.why: Income is skewed with outliers that pull the mean. The median is robust, so it is a better fill value.

quiz.q: Nominal 'city' for a linear model should be…
quiz.why: City has no order. One-hot encoding gives each city its own column, whereas 0, 1, 2 would imply a false ordering to a linear model.

quiz.q: Which model does NOT need feature scaling?
quiz.why: Decision trees split on thresholds of single features, so scaling does not change the splits. kNN, SVM and k-means depend on distances.
IQR = 30 − 10 = 20. The upper fence is Q3 + 1.5·IQR = 30 + 30 = 60.

scenes.text: A student's churn model scores 99% in the lab.
In production it fails: a feature 'cancellation_date' only exists after the customer has churned.

steps.title: Splitting
steps.body:
- Typical: 70–80% train, 10–15% validation, 10–15% test.
- **Stratified** split keeps class proportions (important for imbalanced data).
- **Time-series**: split by time (train on past, test on future), never shuffle.
- Group splits: keep all records of a patient/user in the same split.

steps.title: Data leakage
steps.body:
Leakage = information unavailable at prediction time sneaks into training.

- **Target leakage**: features derived from the label (cancellation_date).
- **Train–test contamination**: fitting scalers/imputers/feature selection on all data.
- Duplicate rows across splits.
Fix: build a **pipeline** that fits preprocessing on training folds only.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 1,000 samples, 10% positive, stratified 80/20 split → test has 200 samples with **20** positives.

**Example 2. Spot the leak.** Predicting hospital readmission using 'number of days readmitted' → target leakage, remove it.

**Example 3. Time series.** Sales Jan 2020–Dec 2024: train 2020–2023, test 2024.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Shuffling time-series data.
- Normalising before splitting.
- Same user's images in both train and test (model memorises the person).
- Peeking at test results repeatedly.

activity.prompt: Split the list into train (first 80%) and test (last 20%) without shuffling (time order). Print the lengths.
activity.starter:
data = list(range(50))
# train, test = ...
print(len(train), len(test))
activity.solution:
data = list(range(50))
cut = int(0.8 * len(data))
train, test = data[:cut], data[cut:]
print(len(train), len(test))
activity.hint: cut = int(0.8 * len(data)); slice before and after.

quiz.why: Stratified splitting keeps the class proportions the same in each split. This matters for imbalanced data.

options: Train on past, test on future
quiz.why: For forecasting, train on the past and test on the future, like real use. Random shuffling would let the model see future data.

quiz.q: Fitting a scaler on all data before splitting causes…
quiz.why: Fitting a scaler on all data lets statistics from the test set influence training. That is data leakage.

quiz.q: A feature only known after the outcome is…
quiz.why: A feature only known after the outcome would not be available at prediction time. That is target leakage and makes results look unrealistically good.

quiz.q: 2,000 samples, 5% positive, stratified 75/25. Positives in test?
quiz.why: Test set = 25% of 2,000 = 500 samples. Stratification keeps 5%: 500 × 0.05 = 25 positives.

questions.q: Predicting whether a tumour is malignant is…
questions.why: Malignant versus benign is a discrete label, so this is classification.

questions.q: Which is learned during training?
questions.why: Model weights are learned from data during training. Learning rate, tree depth and number of folds are set beforehand.

questions.q: Unlabelled grouping of customers is…
questions.why: Grouping customers without labels is clustering, an unsupervised task.

questions.q: Min–max of 40 in range [20, 100]?
z-score of 35 with μ = 50, σ = 5?
Q1=40, Q3=60. Lower fence?
questions.why: IQR = 60 − 40 = 20. The lower fence is Q1 − 1.5·IQR = 40 − 30 = 10.

questions.q: Assertion: Decision trees need standardised features. Reason: Trees split on thresholds of single features.
questions.why: Trees split on a threshold for one feature, so scaling does not matter. So the reason is true, but the assertion that trees need standardised features is false.

questions.q: Which encoding suits 'size: S < M < L'?
questions.why: Sizes S < M < L have a natural order, so ordinal encoding (1, 2, 3) keeps it. One-hot would discard the order.

questions.q: Case: a credit model uses 'number of collection calls after default'. Problem?
questions.why: Collection calls after default happen only because the loan has defaulted. The feature uses information from after the outcome, which is target leakage.

questions.q: Which split is correct for monthly sales forecasting?
questions.why: For sales over time, split chronologically, training on earlier months and testing on later ones. Random splits would leak future information.

questions.q: Why must preprocessing be fitted only on training data?
options: To prevent test information leaking into training
questions.why: Fitting on test data lets its information influence training, making evaluation too optimistic. So fit preprocessing on training data only, then apply it to the test set.

questions.q: 1,000 rows, 2% fraud. Accuracy of always predicting 'not fraud'?
questions.why: If 98% of rows are not fraud, always predicting not fraud is right 98% of the time, yet it catches no fraud at all.

questions.q: Photos of the same 50 people are randomly split. Risk?
questions.why: If photos of the same person are in both train and test, the model can recognise the person rather than generalise. Split by person (group split).

questions.q: Std of [2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9] (population)?
questions.why: The mean is (2+4+4+4+5+5+7+9)/8 = 5. Squared deviations sum to 32, so variance 4 and standard deviation √4 = 2.

questions.q: Which is NOT a valid reason to add a missing-indicator column?
options: It preserves information lost by imputation
Values are missing not at random
questions.why: A missing-indicator can preserve useful information about missingness, but it cannot guarantee higher accuracy. No technique guarantees that.

questions.q: Case: a model scores 0.99 AUC on validation but 0.62 live. Most likely first check?
questions.why: A big gap between validation (0.99) and real-world (0.62) performance usually points to leakage or a validation set that is not like the real data. Check this first.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Regression and Gradient Descent
courses.summary: Simple and multiple linear regression, least squares and the normal equation, gradient descent, polynomial features, bias–variance and regularisation (ridge, lasso).
outcomes: Learners can fit simple linear regression by least squares
Learners can perform gradient descent updates by hand and in code
Learners can explain bias–variance and over/underfitting
Learners can apply ridge and lasso regularisation and interpret R²

lessons.title: Simple linear regression and least squares

scenes.text: A teacher collects study hours and marks for five students.
The best-fit line predicts marks for a new student and shows about how many marks each extra hour is worth.

steps.title: Model and loss
steps.body:
Model: ŷ = w·x + b. Residual eᵢ = yᵢ − ŷᵢ.

**Least squares** minimises the sum of squared errors SSE = Σ(yᵢ − ŷᵢ)²; MSE = SSE/n.

Closed form: **w = Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ) / Σ(x − x̄)²**, **b = ȳ − w·x̄**.

steps.title: Goodness of fit
steps.body:
**R² = 1 − SSE/SST**, where SST = Σ(y − ȳ)². R² = 1 is a perfect fit; 0 means no better than predicting the mean; it can be negative on test data.

Other metrics: MAE (mean absolute error), RMSE = √MSE (same units as y).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Interpreting correlation/slope as causation.
- Extrapolating far outside the data range.
- Comparing R² across different datasets/targets.
- Ignoring residual plots (patterns mean the model is missing structure).

activity.prompt: Compute least-squares slope w and intercept b for the data and print them rounded to 2 decimals.
activity.starter:
x = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
y = [2, 4, 5, 4, 5]
# compute w, b
print(round(w, 2), round(b, 2))
activity.solution:
x = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
y = [2, 4, 5, 4, 5]
mx, my = sum(x) / len(x), sum(y) / len(y)
w = sum((a - mx) * (c - my) for a, c in zip(x, y)) / sum((a - mx) ** 2 for a in x)
b = my - w * mx
print(round(w, 2), round(b, 2))
activity.hint: w = Σ(x−x̄)(y−ȳ)/Σ(x−x̄)²; b = ȳ − w·x̄.

quiz.why: Least squares chooses the line that minimises the sum of squared residuals, Σe².

quiz.q: If x̄ = 4, ȳ = 10, w = 2, then b =
quiz.why: The line passes through (x̄, ȳ), so b = ȳ − w·x̄ = 10 − 2·4 = 2.

options: No better than predicting the mean
quiz.why: R² = 0 means the model explains none of the variance, so its error equals that of always predicting the mean.
RMSE is the square root of the mean squared error, so it is in the same units as y.
A residual is the observed value minus the predicted value: y − ŷ.

lessons.title: Multiple regression, normal equation and gradient descent

scenes.text: A hiker in thick fog wants the valley floor. She feels the slope under her feet and steps downhill.
Gradient descent does exactly this on the loss surface, with the learning rate as step size.

steps.title: Vector form
steps.body:
ŷ = Xw (with a column of 1s for the bias). MSE J(w) = (1/n)‖y − Xw‖².

**Normal equation**: w = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy — exact, but costs about O(d³) for d features and fails if XᵀX is singular (perfect multicollinearity).

steps.title: Gradient descent
steps.body:
Update: **w ← w − α·∇J(w)**. For MSE, ∇J = (2/n)Xᵀ(Xw − y).

- **Batch** GD uses all data per step; **stochastic** (SGD) one sample; **mini-batch** a small batch (most common).
- α too small → slow; too large → overshoot/diverge.
- Scale features so contours are round and GD converges faster.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1. One GD step.** J(w) = (w − 3)², w₀ = 0, α = 0.1. Gradient = 2(w − 3) = −6. w₁ = 0 − 0.1×(−6) = **0.6**. Next: gradient 2(0.6−3) = −4.8 → w₂ = **1.08**.

**Example 2. Divergence.** Same J with α = 1.1: w₁ = 0 + 1.1×6 = 6.6, gradient = 7.2, w₂ = 6.6 − 7.92 = −1.32 — it oscillates with growing amplitude.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the bias column.
- Unscaled features making GD zig-zag.
- Using the normal equation with huge d.
- Stopping too early without checking the loss curve.

activity.prompt: Run 50 steps of gradient descent on J(w) = (w − 3)² from w = 0 with alpha = 0.1. Print w rounded to 3 decimals.
activity.starter:
w = 0.0
alpha = 0.1
for _ in range(50):
    grad = 0  # fix: derivative of (w-3)^2
    w = w - alpha * grad
print(round(w, 3))
activity.solution:
w = 0.0
alpha = 0.1
for _ in range(50):
    grad = 2 * (w - 3)
    w = w - alpha * grad
print(round(w, 3))

quiz.why: The gradient points uphill, so gradient descent steps in the opposite direction to reduce the cost.

options: Expensive for many features; needs invertible XᵀX
quiz.why: The normal equation needs (XᵀX)⁻¹, which is costly with many features and fails if XᵀX is not invertible. Gradient descent scales better.
Mini-batch gradient descent updates using a small subset of the data per step, balancing the speed of SGD and the stability of full batch.
If the learning rate is too large, each step jumps past the minimum. The cost can bounce around or diverge.

lessons.title: Polynomial features and the bias–variance trade-off

scenes.text: A degree-15 polynomial passes through every training point but wiggles wildly between them.
A degree-2 model is less perfect on training data but far better on new data.

steps.title: Polynomial regression
steps.body: Add features x², x³, … and still fit a **linear** model in the parameters: ŷ = w₀ + w₁x + w₂x². Higher degree → more flexible.

steps.title: Bias and variance
steps.body:
Expected test error = **bias²** + **variance** + irreducible noise.

- **High bias (underfitting)**: too simple; high training and test error.
- **High variance (overfitting)**: too complex; low training error, high test error.
- More data reduces variance; more features/complexity reduce bias.
- Learning curves (error vs training size) diagnose which problem you have.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1. Diagnose.** Train MSE 2, validation MSE 30 → overfitting (variance). Fixes: regularise, simplify, more data.

**Example 2.** Train MSE 25, validation MSE 27, target error 5 → underfitting (bias). Fixes: add features, more flexible model, less regularisation.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Judging a model by training error alone.
- Adding more data to fix underfitting (it rarely helps).
- Polynomial features without scaling (x¹⁰ explodes).

activity.label: Polynomial degree for a curved dataset

bands.text: Straight line: underfits a curve — high bias.
Sweet spot: captures the shape; train and validation error both low.
Too flexible: fits noise; training error tiny, validation error high — high variance.

quiz.q: Low train error, high validation error indicates…
quiz.why: Low training error but high validation error means the model memorised the training data and fails to generalise. That is overfitting (high variance).
Polynomial regression uses non-linear features such as x², but the model is a weighted sum of them. So it is linear in the parameters.
More training data makes the learned model less sensitive to noise in any one sample, reducing variance. More features or complexity increase it.
Irreducible error is randomness in the data itself. No model, however good, can remove it.

quiz.q: Both train and validation errors are high and close. Fix?
options: Get more of the same data
quiz.why: When both training and validation errors are high and close, the model is too simple (underfitting, high bias). Increase its complexity.

scenes.text: A gene dataset has 20,000 features and only 300 patients.
Lasso drives most weights to exactly zero, keeping a small, interpretable set of genes.

steps.title: Penalised losses
steps.body:
- **Ridge (L2)**: J = MSE + λ·Σw². Shrinks weights smoothly; handles multicollinearity; closed form w = (XᵀX + λI)⁻¹Xᵀy.
- **Lasso (L1)**: J = MSE + λ·Σ|w|. Can set weights exactly to 0 → feature selection.
- **Elastic net**: mix of L1 and L2.
- λ = 0 → ordinary least squares; large λ → simpler model (more bias, less variance). The bias term is usually not penalised.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1. One-feature ridge.** With centred data, w_ridge = Σxy / (Σx² + λ). If Σxy = 20, Σx² = 10: λ = 0 → w = 2; λ = 10 → w = **1**.

**Example 2. Choosing λ.** Try λ ∈ {0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, 100} with 5-fold cross-validation; pick the one with the lowest mean validation error.

steps.title: Scale first
steps.body: Penalties treat all weights equally, so standardise features first; otherwise features in small units get unfairly penalised.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Choosing λ on the test set.
- Forgetting to scale.
- Expecting ridge to zero out features (that is lasso).
- Interpreting lasso's chosen features as causal.

activity.prompt: Centred one-feature ridge: Σxy = 30, Σx² = 10, λ = 5. What is w?

quiz.q: Which penalty can produce exactly zero weights?
quiz.why: The L1 (lasso) penalty has corners at zero, so it can shrink some weights to exactly 0. L2 shrinks weights but rarely makes them exactly zero.
A larger λ penalises large weights more, producing a simpler model. This increases bias and reduces variance.

quiz.q: Ridge closed form adds λI to…
quiz.why: Ridge regression's closed form is w = (XᵀX + λI)⁻¹Xᵀy, so λI is added to XᵀX.

options: So the penalty treats features fairly
quiz.why: The penalty acts on weight size, which depends on a feature's units. Standardising puts features on the same scale so the penalty is fair.
λ is a hyperparameter, so choose it by cross-validation on the training data. Using the test set to pick it would leak test information and give an over-optimistic score.

questions.q: In ŷ = wx + b, w is the…
questions.why: In ŷ = wx + b, w multiplies x, so it sets how steeply the prediction changes. That is the slope, while b is the intercept.
The line passes through the means, so b = ȳ − w·x̄ = 7 − 3·2 = 7 − 6 = 1.
The least-squares slope is w = Σ(x−x̄)(y−ȳ) / Σ(x−x̄)² = 12/4 = 3.

questions.q: SSE = 20, SST = 80 → R² =
MSE = 16 → RMSE =
questions.why: RMSE is the square root of MSE, so √16 = 4.

questions.q: J = w², w = 4, α = 0.25. After one step w =
questions.why: For J = w², the gradient is 2w = 8 at w = 4. New w = 4 − 0.25·8 = 4 − 2 = 2.

questions.q: J = w², α = 1.0 from w = 4 gives…
questions.why: With α = 1, w_new = w − 1·2w = −w. So w flips sign each step (4, −4, 4, ...) and never settles, because the step size is too big.

questions.q: Assertion: Lasso performs feature selection. Reason: The L1 penalty can drive coefficients exactly to zero.
questions.why: The L1 penalty can make coefficients exactly zero, so lasso removes features, i.e. performs feature selection. Both statements are true and the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Train RMSE 1.2, validation RMSE 9.8 →
questions.why: Very low training error (1.2) but much higher validation error (9.8) means the model fits training noise and does not generalise. That is high variance, i.e. overfitting.

questions.q: Ridge with Σxy = 40, Σx² = 15, λ = 5 → w =
questions.why: Ridge in one dimension: w = Σxy / (Σx² + λ) = 40 / (15 + 5) = 40/20 = 2.

questions.q: Normal-equation cost grows roughly as…
questions.why: The normal equation needs to invert a d × d matrix, which costs about O(d³) in the number of features.

questions.q: Which statement about R² is correct?
options: It can be negative on test data
questions.why: R² = 1 − SSE/SST. On new data a model can be worse than just predicting the mean, which makes SSE > SST and R² negative.

questions.q: Case: features are house area (sq ft, ~1000s) and rooms (1–5). GD zig-zags slowly. Fix?
questions.why: When features have very different scales (1000s versus 1–5), the cost contours are long ellipses and gradient descent zig-zags. Standardising makes them rounder, so it converges faster.

questions.q: Perfectly collinear features make XᵀX…
questions.why: If one feature is an exact linear combination of others, the columns of X are dependent. Then XᵀX is singular and cannot be inverted; adding ridge (λI) fixes this.

questions.q: SGD vs batch GD: SGD typically…
questions.why: SGD updates after each sample (or a tiny batch), so each step is cheap but noisy. Batch GD uses all data per update.

questions.q: Data x=[0,1,2], y=[1,3,5]. Least-squares line?
questions.why: The points (0,1), (1,3), (2,5) all lie on y = 2x + 1. So that line fits exactly, giving zero error.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Classification Algorithms
courses.summary: Logistic regression, k-nearest neighbours, Naive Bayes, decision trees and ensembles, and support vector machines — the core classifiers of a B.Tech ML syllabus.
outcomes: Learners can compute sigmoid outputs and log-loss for logistic regression
Learners can apply kNN and Naive Bayes by hand
Learners can compute entropy, Gini and information gain for tree splits
Learners can explain margins, support vectors and kernels in SVMs

scenes.text: Using hours studied, a model outputs a probability of passing between 0 and 1.
The college sets a threshold: above 0.5 predicts pass — but for early help they use 0.7 to catch more at-risk students.

steps.title: Sigmoid and decision boundary
steps.body:
z = wᵀx + b; **p = σ(z) = 1 / (1 + e^(−z))**. σ(0) = 0.5.

Predict class 1 if p ≥ threshold (often 0.5, i.e. z ≥ 0). The decision boundary wᵀx + b = 0 is linear.

Odds = p/(1 − p); log-odds = z, so each unit of xⱼ multiplies the odds by e^(wⱼ).

steps.title: Log-loss (cross-entropy)
steps.body:
L = −[y·log p + (1 − y)·log(1 − p)], averaged over samples. It is convex for logistic regression, so gradient descent finds the global minimum. Gradient: (p − y)·x.

Multi-class: **softmax** pᵢ = e^(zᵢ)/Σe^(zⱼ) with categorical cross-entropy.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** w = 0.8, b = −4, x = 6 hours. z = 4.8 − 4 = 0.8; p = 1/(1 + e^(−0.8)) ≈ 1/(1 + 0.449) ≈ **0.69** → pass at 0.5 threshold.

**Example 2. Log-loss.** True y = 1, p = 0.9 → −ln 0.9 ≈ **0.105**. If p = 0.1 → −ln 0.1 ≈ **2.30** (confident and wrong is punished heavily).

**Example 3.** w = 0.7 → odds multiply by e^0.7 ≈ 2.01 per extra hour.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using MSE as the loss for logistic regression (non-convex with sigmoid).
- Treating probability outputs as calibrated without checking.
- Always using 0.5 regardless of the cost of errors.
- Forgetting that the boundary is linear unless you add features.

activity.prompt: Compute the sigmoid probability for w = 0.8, b = -4, x = 6 and print it rounded to 2 decimals.
activity.starter:
import math
w, b, x = 0.8, -4, 6
# p = ...
print(round(p, 2))
activity.solution:
import math
w, b, x = 0.8, -4, 6
z = w * x + b
p = 1 / (1 + math.exp(-z))
print(round(p, 2))

quiz.q: Logistic regression's decision boundary (no extra features) is…
quiz.why: The boundary is where σ(z) = 0.5, i.e. wᵀx + b = 0. That equation is a straight line or plane, so it is linear.
Log-loss for y = 1 is −ln p. With p = 1.0, −ln 1 = 0, i.e. a perfect prediction has no loss.
For more than two classes, softmax turns the class scores into probabilities that sum to 1.

quiz.q: Weight 0.69 (≈ ln 2) means one unit of x…
quiz.why: Each unit rise in x adds the weight to the log-odds. So the odds are multiplied by e^0.69 ≈ 2, doubling them. It does not add 0.69 to the probability.

story.title: Judging a fruit by its neighbours

scenes.text: A new fruit is small and orange. Among its 3 most similar known fruits, 2 are oranges.
Meanwhile the spam filter multiplies word probabilities — the 'naive' trick that works surprisingly well.

steps.title: kNN
steps.body:
To classify x: find the k closest training points (Euclidean distance √Σ(xᵢ − yᵢ)², or Manhattan Σ|xᵢ − yᵢ|) and take a majority vote (or average for regression).

- No training phase ('lazy learner'); prediction cost grows with data size.
- Small k → noisy (high variance); large k → smooth (high bias). Odd k avoids ties in binary problems.
- Must scale features; suffers in very high dimensions (curse of dimensionality).

steps.title: Naive Bayes
steps.body:
Bayes: P(C | x) ∝ P(C)·P(x | C). Naive assumption: features are conditionally independent given the class, so P(x | C) = Π P(xⱼ | C).

- Variants: Gaussian (continuous), Multinomial (word counts), Bernoulli (binary).
- **Laplace smoothing** adds 1 to counts so unseen words don't give zero probability.
- Fast, good for text, works with little data.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1. kNN.** Points A(1,1) red, B(2,2) red, C(5,5) blue, D(6,5) blue, E(2,1) red. Query (3,3), k = 3. Distances: A √8≈2.83, B √2≈1.41, C √8≈2.83, D √13≈3.61, E √5≈2.24. Nearest 3: B, E, then a tie A/C at 2.83 — tie-breaking rule matters; with A: red wins 3–0; with C: red wins 2–1. Either way **red**.

**Example 2. Naive Bayes.** P(spam) = 0.4. P('offer'|spam) = 0.5, P('offer'|ham) = 0.1. Email contains 'offer': spam score 0.4×0.5 = 0.20; ham score 0.6×0.1 = 0.06. P(spam | offer) = 0.20/0.26 ≈ **0.77**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- kNN on unscaled features (income dominates age).
- Forgetting Laplace smoothing (one unseen word → probability 0).
- Multiplying many small probabilities (underflow) — sum log-probabilities instead.
- Treating Naive Bayes probabilities as well-calibrated.

activity.prompt: Implement 3-NN: print the predicted label for query (3, 3).
activity.solution:
pts = [((1,1),'red'), ((2,2),'red'), ((5,5),'blue'), ((6,5),'blue'), ((2,1),'red')]
q = (3, 3)
k = 3
d = sorted(pts, key=lambda p: (p[0][0]-q[0])**2 + (p[0][1]-q[1])**2)
labels = [lab for _, lab in d[:k]]
print(max(set(labels), key=labels.count))
activity.hint: Sort by squared distance, take first k labels, return the most common.

quiz.why: With k = 1, each prediction copies the single nearest neighbour, including noise. The boundary follows every point, so it overfits (high variance).
Distance = √(3² + 4²) = √25 = 5.
Naive Bayes assumes features are conditionally independent given the class. That simplifies the likelihood into a product.
Laplace (add-one) smoothing adds a count to every feature. A feature never seen with a class then gets a small non-zero probability instead of 0 wiping out the whole product.

quiz.q: Why sum log-probabilities in Naive Bayes?
quiz.why: Multiplying many small probabilities can underflow to 0 on a computer. Summing their logarithms gives the same ordering and stays numerically safe.

scenes.text: A loan officer asks: income above 5 lakh? existing EMIs? credit history? — a decision tree.
A random forest asks hundreds of slightly different trees and takes a vote — more stable than any one.

steps.title: Impurity measures
steps.body:
- **Entropy** H = −Σ pᵢ log₂ pᵢ (0 for pure, 1 for a 50/50 binary node).
- **Gini** G = 1 − Σ pᵢ² (0 pure, 0.5 max for binary).
- **Information gain** = H(parent) − Σ (nₖ/n)·H(childₖ). Greedy algorithms (ID3, C4.5, CART) pick the split with the highest gain / lowest weighted Gini.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Parent: 8 yes, 8 no → H = 1. Split → left (6 yes, 2 no), right (2 yes, 6 no). H(left) = −(0.75 log₂ 0.75 + 0.25 log₂ 0.25) ≈ 0.811; same for right. Weighted = 0.811. **Gain ≈ 0.189**.

**Example 2. Gini** of (6 yes, 2 no) = 1 − (0.75² + 0.25²) = 1 − 0.625 = **0.375**.

steps.title: Overfitting control and ensembles
steps.body:
- Trees overfit when deep; control with max_depth, min_samples_leaf, pruning.
- **Bagging**: train trees on bootstrap samples and average → lower variance. **Random forest** = bagging + random feature subsets at each split; gives feature importances and out-of-bag error.
- **Boosting** (AdaBoost, gradient boosting, XGBoost/LightGBM): trees built sequentially, each correcting previous errors → lower bias; needs careful tuning (learning rate, number of trees).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Growing trees to full depth on small data.
- Thinking random forests can't overfit at all.
- Using too high a learning rate in boosting.
- Trusting impurity-based importances for high-cardinality features (they are biased).

activity.prompt: Write entropy(counts) using log base 2. Print entropy([8, 8]) and entropy([6, 2]) rounded to 3 decimals.
activity.starter:
import math
def entropy(counts):
    # your code
    pass
print(round(entropy([8, 8]), 3), round(entropy([6, 2]), 3))
activity.hint: Sum −p·log2(p) over non-zero counts.

quiz.q: Entropy of a pure node is…
quiz.why: A pure node has only one class, so there is no uncertainty and the entropy is 0.
A random forest averages many trees trained on different samples. Averaging reduces variance, while bias stays about the same as for a single deep tree.
Boosting adds trees one after another. Each new tree focuses on the mistakes of the ensemble so far. Bagging builds trees independently in parallel.
Requiring a minimum number of samples per leaf and pruning give simpler trees that fit less noise. A larger max_depth or more features makes overfitting worse.

scenes.text: Two villages must be separated by a straight road. Many roads work, but the widest one is safest.
Only the houses nearest the road — the support vectors — decide where it goes.

steps.title: Maximum margin
steps.body:
Hyperplane wᵀx + b = 0. For labels y ∈ {−1, +1}, hard-margin SVM requires yᵢ(wᵀxᵢ + b) ≥ 1 and **minimises ½‖w‖²**. Margin width = **2/‖w‖**.

Points on the margin are **support vectors**; others don't affect the solution.

steps.title: Soft margin and kernels
steps.body:
- **Soft margin**: allow violations with slack ξᵢ; minimise ½‖w‖² + C·Σξᵢ. Large C → fewer violations, narrower margin (risk of overfitting); small C → wider, more tolerant. Equivalent to hinge loss max(0, 1 − y·f(x)).
- **Kernel trick**: replace dot products with K(x, z) to get nonlinear boundaries without computing features: linear, polynomial (xᵀz + c)^d, RBF exp(−γ‖x − z‖²). Large γ → very wiggly boundary.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Unscaled features (SVMs are distance-based).
- Huge C and γ together → memorises training data.
- Expecting probability outputs by default (SVM gives scores).
- Using kernel SVMs on millions of rows (training is roughly quadratic or worse).

activity.prompt: An SVM has w = (6, 8). What is the margin width 2/‖w‖?

quiz.why: An SVM chooses the separating line with the widest margin between the classes. A wider margin tends to generalise better.
For the constraints y(wᵀx + b) ≥ 1, the distance between the two margin lines is 2/‖w‖. So a smaller ‖w‖ means a wider margin.
A large C penalises margin violations heavily. So the SVM tries to classify every point correctly, giving a narrower margin with fewer violations.
Hinge loss = max(0, 1 − y·f(x)) = max(0, 1 − 1.5) = 0. The point is on the correct side beyond the margin, so there is no penalty.
The kernel trick replaces dot products with a kernel function. This gives nonlinear boundaries without explicitly building the high-dimensional features.

questions.q: Logistic regression outputs…
questions.why: Logistic regression passes the linear score through the sigmoid, giving a probability between 0 and 1.

questions.q: σ(z) > 0.5 exactly when…
questions.why: σ(0) = 0.5 and σ increases with z. So σ(z) > 0.5 exactly when z > 0.

questions.q: Log-loss for y = 0, p = 0.2 (natural log)?
questions.why: For y = 0, the log-loss is −ln(1 − p) = −ln(0.8) ≈ 0.223. A mild error gives a small loss.

questions.q: kNN is called a lazy learner because…
options: It defers computation to prediction time
questions.why: kNN does no real training. It just stores the data and does the computation when a prediction is requested, which is why it is called lazy.

questions.q: Manhattan distance between (1,2) and (4,6)?
questions.why: Manhattan distance = |4 − 1| + |6 − 2| = 3 + 4 = 7.

questions.q: Entropy of (3 yes, 1 no) ≈
Gini of (2 yes, 2 no, 0 maybe) three-class node?
questions.why: Proportions are 0.5, 0.5 and 0. Gini = 1 − (0.25 + 0.25 + 0) = 0.5; an empty class adds nothing.

questions.q: Assertion: Bagging reduces variance. Reason: Averaging many models trained on bootstrap samples smooths out individual fluctuations.
questions.why: Bagging trains models on bootstrap samples and averages them. The averaging smooths out individual fluctuations, reducing variance. Both statements are true and the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Random forest adds which randomness beyond bagging?
options: Random feature subsets at each split
questions.why: Besides bootstrap samples, a random forest considers only a random subset of features at each split. This makes the trees less alike (decorrelated), so averaging helps more.

questions.q: Hard-margin SVM with w = (1, 1): width of the margin between the supporting hyperplanes w·x + b = +1 and w·x + b = −1?
questions.why: The margin width is 2/‖w‖, and ‖w‖ = √(1² + 1²) = √2. So the width is 2/√2 = √2 ≈ 1.414; 1/√2 is only the distance from the decision boundary to one supporting hyperplane.

questions.q: Hinge loss for y = −1, f(x) = −0.4?
questions.why: Hinge loss = max(0, 1 − y·f(x)) = max(0, 1 − (−1)(−0.4)) = max(0, 0.6) = 0.6. The point is on the correct side but inside the margin.

questions.q: Case: kNN performs poorly; features are income (₹ lakhs ×1000) and age. First fix?
questions.why: Income values are about 1000 times larger, so they dominate the distance and age is ignored. Scale the features so both contribute.

questions.q: RBF SVM with very large γ tends to…
questions.why: A very large γ makes each point's influence extremely local. The boundary then twists around individual points, which means overfitting.

questions.q: Parent H = 1 (8/8). Split: left 8 (all yes), right 8 (all no). Information gain?
questions.why: Information gain = parent entropy − weighted child entropy = 1 − 0 = 1. Both children are pure, so they have no uncertainty.

questions.q: Case: a text classifier with 50,000 word features and 2,000 documents needs a fast, decent baseline. Best choice?
questions.why: Multinomial Naive Bayes is fast, works well with many sparse word features and few documents, and is a standard baseline for text. A deep tree or k = 1 would overfit.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Model Evaluation and Selection
courses.summary: Confusion matrix, precision, recall, F1, ROC–AUC and PR curves, cross-validation, hyperparameter search, imbalanced data and fairness.
outcomes: Learners can compute precision, recall, F1 and specificity from a confusion matrix
Learners can interpret ROC–AUC and choose thresholds
Learners can use k-fold cross-validation and grid/random search correctly
Learners can handle class imbalance and check models for unfair bias

scenes.text: A screening model is 97% accurate — but it misses half the actual cancer cases.
The doctors care about recall: catching as many true cases as possible, then confirming with further tests.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
Confusion matrix: TP, FP, FN, TN.

- Accuracy = (TP + TN)/total
- **Precision** = TP/(TP + FP) — of predicted positives, how many are right?
- **Recall (sensitivity, TPR)** = TP/(TP + FN) — of actual positives, how many did we catch?
- Specificity = TN/(TN + FP); FPR = 1 − specificity.
- **F1** = 2PR/(P + R) — harmonic mean.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** TP = 40, FP = 10, FN = 20, TN = 930.
- Accuracy = 970/1000 = 0.97.
- Precision = 40/50 = **0.8**.
- Recall = 40/60 ≈ **0.667**.
- F1 = 2×0.8×0.667/(1.467) ≈ **0.727**.
- Specificity = 930/940 ≈ 0.989.

**Example 2. Which metric?** Spam filter (don't lose real mail) → precision. Disease screening (don't miss cases) → recall. Balanced need → F1.

steps.title: Multi-class averaging
steps.body: Macro-average treats each class equally; micro-average pools all decisions (equals accuracy for single-label problems); weighted-average weights by class support.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reporting accuracy alone on imbalanced data.
- Swapping FP and FN.
- Using arithmetic mean instead of harmonic mean for F1.
- Comparing precision across datasets with different base rates.

activity.prompt: Compute precision, recall and F1 for TP=40, FP=10, FN=20. Print them rounded to 3 decimals.
activity.starter:
TP, FP, FN = 40, 10, 20
# p, r, f1 = ...
print(round(p, 3), round(r, 3), round(f1, 3))
activity.solution:
TP, FP, FN = 40, 10, 20
p = TP / (TP + FP)
r = TP / (TP + FN)
f1 = 2 * p * r / (p + r)
print(round(p, 3), round(r, 3), round(f1, 3))

quiz.why: Recall = TP/(TP + FN): of all real positives, the fraction found.
In disease screening, missing a sick person (false negative) is costly. So high recall matters most, even at the price of some false alarms.
A false positive is predicted positive when the actual class is negative, i.e. a false alarm.
Specificity is the true negative rate: TN/(TN + FP), the share of real negatives correctly identified.

lessons.title: ROC, AUC, PR curves and thresholds

scenes.text: A fraud team lowers the alert threshold from 0.5 to 0.3.
They catch more fraud (recall up) but analysts face more false alarms (precision down).

steps.title: ROC curve and AUC
steps.body:
Plot TPR (y) vs FPR (x) for every threshold. Diagonal = random guessing (AUC 0.5); top-left corner = perfect (AUC 1).

**AUC** = probability that a random positive gets a higher score than a random negative. It is threshold-independent.

steps.title: Precision–recall curve
steps.body: On heavily imbalanced data (fraud 0.1%), ROC can look great while precision is poor. The **PR curve** and **average precision** are more informative. The PR baseline is the positive rate, not 0.5.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1. AUC by pairs.** Positives scores {0.9, 0.6}; negatives {0.7, 0.2}. Pairs (pos > neg): 0.9>0.7 ✓, 0.9>0.2 ✓, 0.6>0.7 ✗, 0.6>0.2 ✓ → 3/4 = **AUC 0.75**.

**Example 2. Choosing a threshold.** If a missed fraud costs ₹10,000 and a false alarm costs ₹200, choose the threshold that minimises 10000·FN + 200·FP on validation data.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking AUC tells you the best threshold.
- Using ROC alone for rare-event problems.
- Choosing thresholds on the test set.
- An AUC below 0.5 usually means labels or scores are flipped.

activity.prompt: Compute AUC by counting positive–negative pairs where the positive scores higher (ties count 0.5). Print the result.
activity.solution:
pos = [0.9, 0.6]
neg = [0.7, 0.2]
s = 0
for p in pos:
    for n in neg:
        s += 1 if p > n else (0.5 if p == n else 0)
auc = s / (len(pos) * len(neg))
print(auc)
activity.hint: Loop over all pairs and divide by the number of pairs.

quiz.q: A random classifier's AUC is about…
quiz.why: A random classifier ranks positives above negatives only half the time, so its ROC curve is the diagonal and its AUC is about 0.5.
The ROC curve plots true positive rate against false positive rate as the threshold varies.
A lower threshold labels more cases positive. So more real positives are found (higher recall), but more false positives appear (lower precision).

quiz.q: For a 0.1% positive rate problem prefer…
quiz.why: With only 0.1% positives, accuracy and ROC can look great while the model is poor on the rare class. The PR curve / average precision focuses on the positives.
An AUC of 0.3 is worse than random (0.5). Often the scores are inverted, and flipping them would give about 0.7.

scenes.text: Model A beats B on one random split — but on another split B wins.
5-fold cross-validation averages over five splits and gives a more reliable comparison.

steps.title: k-fold cross-validation
steps.body:
Split training data into k folds; train on k − 1, validate on the remaining one; repeat k times; average the scores (report mean ± std).

- Stratified k-fold for classification; TimeSeriesSplit for time data; GroupKFold for grouped data.
- Leave-one-out = k equal to n (expensive, high variance).
- **Nested CV**: inner loop tunes, outer loop estimates performance honestly.

steps.title: Search strategies
steps.body:
- **Grid search**: all combinations (cost multiplies).
- **Random search**: sample combinations; often finds good regions faster when few hyperparameters matter.
- **Bayesian optimisation**: uses past results to choose the next trial.
- **Early stopping** for iterative models.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1. Cost.** Grid with C ∈ {0.1, 1, 10, 100} and γ ∈ {0.01, 0.1, 1} = 12 combinations; with 5-fold CV → **60** model fits (plus one final refit).

**Example 2. Fold sizes.** 1,000 samples, 5-fold → each fold trains on 800 and validates on 200.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Preprocessing outside the CV loop (leakage) — use pipelines.
- Reporting the best CV score from tuning as the final performance (optimistic).
- Shuffled CV on time series.
- Huge grids that waste compute.

activity.prompt: Grid search: 3 values of max_depth × 4 values of n_estimators × 2 values of learning_rate, with 5-fold CV. How many model fits (excluding the final refit)?

quiz.q: In 10-fold CV each model trains on…
quiz.why: In k-fold CV each model trains on k − 1 folds. For 10 folds that is 9/10 = 90% of the training data.

options: Tune and estimate performance without optimistic bias
quiz.why: Nested CV uses an inner loop for tuning and an outer loop for evaluation. Performance is then not biased by the tuning, which would be optimistic otherwise.

quiz.q: Random search often beats grid search because…
options: It explores more distinct values of important hyperparameters
quiz.why: With a few important hyperparameters, random search tries many different values of each one. Grid search repeats the same few values, so random search covers important ones better.
The grid has 5 × 4 = 20 combinations, and each is fitted in 3 folds. So 20 × 3 = 60 fits.

quiz.q: Fitting a scaler before CV splitting causes…
quiz.why: Fitting a scaler on all data before CV lets the validation folds influence preprocessing. That is leakage, and the CV score becomes too optimistic.

lessons.title: Imbalanced data, fairness and responsible ML

scenes.text: A company trains a résumé screener on 10 years of past hiring decisions.
An audit finds it ranks equally qualified women lower — it learned past bias. The team fixes data, features and adds monitoring.

steps.title: Handling imbalance
steps.body:
- Use the right metrics (recall, precision, PR-AUC).
- **Class weights** in the loss (penalise errors on the rare class more).
- **Resampling**: oversample minority (e.g. SMOTE creates synthetic points), undersample majority — **only on training folds**.
- Threshold tuning on validation data.
- Collect more minority examples where possible.

steps.title: Fairness and responsible AI
steps.body:
- Bias can come from historical data, sampling, labels, or proxies (pin code can proxy for community).
- Check metrics per group (e.g. recall and false positive rate by gender or region).
- Fairness definitions (demographic parity, equal opportunity) can conflict — choose with stakeholders.
- Document data and models (datasheets, model cards), keep humans in the loop for high-stakes decisions, protect privacy (India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 governs personal data processing).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1. Class weights.** 950 negatives, 50 positives. Balanced weight wₖ = n/(K·nₖ): negatives 1000/(2×950) ≈ 0.526; positives 1000/(2×50) = **10**.

**Example 2. Group check.** Recall for group A = 0.85, group B = 0.60 → equal-opportunity gap 0.25 → investigate data coverage for B.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Oversampling before splitting (copies leak into validation).
- Dropping the sensitive attribute and assuming the model is fair (proxies remain).
- Only checking overall accuracy.
- Deploying high-stakes models without human review or appeal processes.

a.text: Your loan-approval model has 92% accuracy overall, but approval recall for applicants from rural pin codes is much lower. What do you do first?

choices.label: Ship it — 92% is great
choices.feedback: Overall accuracy hides a group-level harm.

choices.label: Investigate data coverage, proxy features and per-group metrics before deploying

bad.text: Qualified rural applicants are systematically rejected. This is unfair and a reputational and regulatory risk.

good.text: You find rural applicants are under-represented in training data. You gather more data, reweight, re-evaluate per group and add human review.

quiz.why: SMOTE creates synthetic minority samples, so apply it only to the training folds. Using it before splitting leaks copies of validation points into training.

quiz.q: Balanced class weight for 100 positives out of 1,000 (2 classes)?
quiz.why: Balanced weight = n_samples / (n_classes × n_class_samples) = 1000 / (2 × 100) = 5 for the positive class.

quiz.q: Removing a sensitive attribute guarantees fairness?
quiz.why: Other features can be correlated with the removed attribute (proxies, like postcode). So the model may still discriminate, and removing the attribute does not guarantee fairness.

options: Intended use, data, metrics and limitations of a model
quiz.why: A model card is a short document describing a model's intended use, training data, performance metrics and limitations, to promote transparency.

quiz.q: India's main personal data protection law (2023) is…
quiz.why: India's personal data protection law is the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. GDPR is the EU law and POCSO deals with child protection.

questions.q: Precision =
questions.why: Precision = TP/(TP + FP): of everything predicted positive, the fraction that is truly positive.

questions.q: TP=30, FN=10 → recall =
TP=20, FP=5, FN=20, TN=955. Accuracy?
questions.why: Accuracy = (TP + TN)/N = (20 + 955)/1000 = 0.975. High accuracy here hides that half the positives are missed.

questions.q: Same numbers: precision and recall?
AUC equals the probability that…
options: A random positive is scored above a random negative
questions.why: AUC equals the probability that a randomly chosen positive gets a higher score than a randomly chosen negative. It is a ranking measure, not accuracy at a threshold.

questions.q: Positives {0.8, 0.4}, negatives {0.5, 0.1}. AUC?
questions.why: Compare all 4 positive–negative pairs: 0.8 beats 0.5 and 0.1, 0.4 beats 0.1 but loses to 0.5. So 3 of 4 pairs are ranked correctly, AUC = 0.75.

questions.q: Assertion: ROC–AUC can look strong on very imbalanced data while precision is poor. Reason: FPR divides by the large number of negatives.
questions.why: FPR = FP/(all negatives). With a huge number of negatives, many false positives still give a small FPR, so AUC stays high while precision is poor. Both are true and the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: 5-fold CV on 2,000 samples: validation fold size?
questions.why: In 5-fold CV the data is split into 5 equal folds. Each validation fold has 2000/5 = 400 samples.

questions.q: Grid 4×3×2 with 10-fold CV → fits?
questions.why: The grid has 4 × 3 × 2 = 24 combinations. With 10-fold CV each is fitted 10 times: 24 × 10 = 240 fits.

questions.q: Correct CV for stock-price prediction?
questions.why: Stock prices depend on time order. Forward-chaining splits always train on the past and validate on the future, so there is no peeking ahead.

questions.q: Which is leakage?
options: Oversampling the full dataset before CV
Scaling inside a pipeline per fold
questions.why: Oversampling before CV puts synthetic copies of points in both training and validation folds. That is leakage. Scaling inside a pipeline fits per fold, so it is safe.

questions.q: Spam filter where losing real mail is worst — optimise…
questions.why: If losing real mail is the worst outcome, avoid false spam flags. That means optimising precision for the spam class, so that what is flagged is truly spam.

questions.q: Case: missed fraud costs ₹5,000; false alarm ₹100. Threshold A: FN 20, FP 300. Threshold B: FN 35, FP 100. Cheaper?
Recall group A = 0.9, group B = 0.6. Which fairness notion is violated?
questions.why: Recall is the true positive rate. If it differs between groups (0.9 vs 0.6), equal opportunity, which asks for equal TPR, is violated.

questions.q: Macro-averaged F1 …
questions.why: Macro-averaging computes F1 for each class and takes the plain mean. So every class counts equally, regardless of its size.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Unsupervised Learning
courses.summary: k-means and its variants, hierarchical and density-based clustering, cluster evaluation, and dimensionality reduction with PCA.
outcomes: Learners can run k-means iterations by hand and choose k
Learners can compare hierarchical, DBSCAN and k-means clustering
Learners can compute and interpret silhouette scores
Learners can explain PCA via variance, eigenvectors and explained variance ratio

scenes.text: A grocery startup must place 3 warehouses to serve 500 customer addresses.
k-means repeatedly assigns customers to the nearest hub and moves each hub to its customers' centre.

steps.title: Lloyd's algorithm
steps.body:
- Choose k initial centroids (k-means++ spreads them out).
- **Assign** each point to the nearest centroid.
- **Update** each centroid to the mean of its points.
- Repeat until assignments stop changing.

Objective: minimise within-cluster sum of squares (WCSS / inertia). It always converges, but to a **local** optimum — run several initialisations.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 1-D points {1, 2, 3, 10, 11, 12}, k = 2, initial centroids 1 and 12.
- Assign: {1,2,3} → c1; {10,11,12} → c2.
- Update: c1 = 2, c2 = 11. Reassign: no change → converged. WCSS = (1+0+1)+(1+0+1) = **4**.

**Example 2. Choosing k.** Elbow method: plot WCSS vs k and pick where the drop flattens; or pick k with the highest silhouette score.

steps.title: Assumptions
steps.body: k-means prefers roughly spherical, similarly sized clusters and is sensitive to scale and outliers. k-medoids uses actual points as centres and is more robust.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Not scaling features.
- Expecting k-means to find crescent or ring shapes.
- Running once and trusting the result.
- Choosing k only because WCSS keeps decreasing (it always decreases as k increases).

activity.prompt: Run k-means (k=2) on 1-D data from initial centroids 1 and 12 until convergence. Print the final centroids.
activity.starter:
pts = [1, 2, 3, 10, 11, 12]
c = [1.0, 12.0]
# loop: assign then update
print(c)
activity.solution:
pts = [1, 2, 3, 10, 11, 12]
c = [1.0, 12.0]
while True:
    groups = [[], []]
    for p in pts:
        groups[0 if abs(p - c[0]) <= abs(p - c[1]) else 1].append(p)
    new = [sum(g) / len(g) for g in groups]
    if new == c:
        break
    c = new
print(c)
activity.hint: Assign each point to the nearer centroid, recompute means, stop when unchanged.

quiz.why: k-means minimises the within-cluster sum of squared distances to centroids (WCSS or inertia).
k-means++ picks initial centroids that are spread far apart. That gives better starting points and often better final clusters.
Adding more centroids lets points sit closer to a centre, so WCSS does not increase as k grows (and usually decreases). It reaches 0 when k equals the number of points.
k-means assigns points to the nearest mean, which gives convex, roughly round clusters. It cannot capture non-convex shapes like rings.
The centroid is the mean: (2 + 4 + 9)/3 = 15/3 = 5.

scenes.text: Biologists merge the most similar species step by step and draw a tree called a dendrogram.
A city planner uses DBSCAN on GPS points to find crowded areas of any shape and ignore isolated noise.

steps.title: Agglomerative clustering
steps.body:
Start with each point as its own cluster; repeatedly merge the two closest clusters. **Linkage** defines cluster distance:

- Single (min distance) — can chain.
- Complete (max distance) — compact clusters.
- Average.
- Ward — merge that least increases variance.
Cut the dendrogram at a height to get clusters; no need to fix k in advance. Cost is roughly O(n²) memory or more.

steps.title: DBSCAN
steps.body:
Parameters **ε** (neighbourhood radius) and **minPts**.

- Core point: ≥ minPts points within ε (including itself).
- Border point: within ε of a core point but not core.
- Noise: neither.
Finds arbitrary shapes, labels outliers, no k needed; struggles when density varies a lot.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1. Single linkage.** Points 1, 2, 6, 7, 20. Merge 1–2 (d=1), 6–7 (d=1), then {1,2}–{6,7} (d = 6 − 2 = 4), then with 20 (d = 13).

**Example 2. DBSCAN.** ε = 1.5, minPts = 3 on 1-D points {1, 2, 3, 8}. Point 2 has neighbours {1,2,3} → core. 1 and 3 have 2 neighbours each → border. 8 → **noise**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Single linkage on noisy data (chaining).
- Using DBSCAN without scaling.
- One global ε for clusters of very different densities.
- Running hierarchical clustering on millions of points.

activity.prompt: Match the method to its key property.
pairs: Tree of merges, cut to get clusters

quiz.why: DBSCAN finds clusters from density using ε and minPts, so it does not need the number of clusters k in advance.

quiz.q: A point with fewer than minPts neighbours and not near a core point is…
quiz.why: A point that is not a core point and is not within ε of one is labelled noise (an outlier).
Complete linkage measures the distance between two clusters as the largest distance between a member of each, i.e. the farthest pair.

options: Each point as its own cluster
quiz.why: Agglomerative clustering works bottom-up. It begins with every point as its own cluster and repeatedly merges the closest pair.
DBSCAN groups dense regions of any shape, so it can follow crescents. k-means assumes round clusters, and PCA and linear regression are not clustering methods.

scenes.text: Marketing gets 6 customer segments from a clustering run.
Before acting, the analyst checks silhouette scores and whether segments make business sense.

steps.title: Silhouette score
steps.body:
For point i: a = mean distance to its own cluster; b = mean distance to the nearest other cluster.

**s = (b − a)/max(a, b)**, ranging from −1 to 1. Near 1: well clustered; near 0: on a boundary; negative: probably in the wrong cluster. Average over all points.

steps.title: Other measures
steps.body:
- Internal: WCSS, Davies–Bouldin (lower better), Calinski–Harabasz (higher better).
- External (when true labels exist): Adjusted Rand Index, normalised mutual information, purity.
- Always add **domain validation**: can people describe and use each cluster?

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** a = 2, b = 8 → s = 6/8 = **0.75**.

**Example 2.** a = 5, b = 4 → s = −1/5 = **−0.2** → point is closer to another cluster.

**Example 3.** Silhouette for k = 2, 3, 4, 5: 0.41, 0.58, 0.47, 0.39 → choose **k = 3**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating clusters as ground truth.
- Using silhouette for DBSCAN noise points without excluding them.
- Comparing WCSS across different k as if lower always means better.

activity.prompt: Silhouette: a = 3, b = 12. What is s?

quiz.why: The silhouette is s = (b − a)/max(a, b), which always lies between −1 and 1.
With a = b, s = (b − a)/max(a, b) = 0. The point is as close to its own cluster as to the next one, i.e. on the boundary.
The Davies–Bouldin index compares within-cluster spread with between-cluster separation. Lower values mean tighter, better-separated clusters.
The Adjusted Rand Index compares a clustering with known true labels. So it is an external measure that needs ground truth.

options: The point may be in the wrong cluster
quiz.why: A negative silhouette means the point is closer on average to another cluster than to its own. It may be assigned to the wrong cluster.

scenes.text: A survey has 100 correlated questions.
PCA finds a few directions — like 'satisfaction', 'price sensitivity' — that capture most of the variation.

steps.title: Idea and steps
steps.body:
PCA finds orthogonal directions of maximum variance.

- Centre (and usually standardise) the data.
- Compute the covariance matrix Σ = (1/(n−1)) XᵀX.
- Find eigenvectors (principal components) and eigenvalues (variance along each).
- Sort by eigenvalue; project onto the top k components.
- **Explained variance ratio** = λᵢ / Σλ.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Eigenvalues 4.0, 0.8, 0.2 (total 5). Ratios 0.80, 0.16, 0.04. Keeping 2 components retains **96%** of variance.

**Example 2. 2×2 covariance** [[2, 1], [1, 2]]: eigenvalues from (2 − λ)² − 1 = 0 → λ = 3 and 1. PC1 direction (1, 1)/√2 explains 3/4 = **75%**.

steps.title: Uses and alternatives
steps.body:
- Uses: visualisation (2-D plots), noise reduction, speeding up models, removing multicollinearity.
- PCA is linear and unsupervised (it ignores labels).
- Nonlinear visualisation: t-SNE, UMAP (good for plots, not for distances between far clusters).
- Computed in practice through SVD.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Not standardising features with different units.
- Fitting PCA on all data before the train/test split.
- Interpreting components as if they were original features.
- Assuming high-variance directions are the most predictive.

activity.prompt: Given eigenvalues, print the minimum number of components needed to retain at least 95% of the variance.
activity.solution:
eig = sorted([5.0, 2.5, 1.5, 0.6, 0.4], reverse=True)
total = sum(eig)
cum, k = 0.0, 0
for v in eig:
    cum += v
    k += 1
    if cum / total >= 0.95:
        break
print(k)
activity.hint: Accumulate sorted eigenvalues until the ratio reaches 0.95 (total is 10).

quiz.why: Principal components are orthogonal directions along which the data has the most variance. They are the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix.
The explained variance ratio of PC1 is its eigenvalue over the total: 6/(6 + 3 + 1) = 6/10 = 0.6.
PCA looks only at the variance of the features, not at labels. So it is unsupervised.

options: So large-unit features don't dominate variance
quiz.why: PCA follows variance, which depends on units. A feature measured in large units would dominate, so standardise first so that all features count fairly.
PCA is usually computed with the singular value decomposition (SVD) of the centred data. It is numerically stable.

questions.q: Clustering uses…
questions.why: Clustering has no labels to learn from. It finds structure in unlabelled data, so it is unsupervised.

questions.q: k-means update step sets each centroid to…
questions.why: After assigning points to the nearest centroid, k-means moves each centroid to the mean of the points assigned to it.

questions.q: Points {0, 2, 10, 12}, k = 2, centroids 0 and 12. After convergence WCSS?
questions.why: Clusters {0, 2} and {10, 12} have centroids 1 and 11. Each point is 1 away from its centroid, so WCSS = 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 4.

questions.q: Elbow method plots…
questions.why: The elbow method plots WCSS against k and looks for the bend where adding more clusters gives little improvement.

questions.q: DBSCAN core point definition?
questions.why: A DBSCAN core point has at least minPts points (including itself) within distance ε. This shows it lies in a dense region.

questions.q: Which linkage tends to chain?
questions.why: Single linkage merges using the smallest distance between clusters, so a chain of close points can link far-apart groups. This is the chaining effect.

questions.q: a = 6, b = 10 → silhouette?
Assertion: k-means always finds the global optimum. Reason: Each iteration never increases WCSS.
questions.why: Each k-means iteration never increases WCSS, so the reason is true. But it converges to a local optimum that depends on the start, so it does not always find the global optimum; the assertion is false.

questions.q: Covariance [[3,0],[0,1]]: fraction of variance on PC1?
questions.why: The eigenvalues of the diagonal covariance are 3 and 1. PC1's share is 3/(3 + 1) = 0.75.

questions.q: Eigenvalues 8, 1, 0.5, 0.5 → components for ≥ 90%?
questions.why: The total is 10. One component explains 8/10 = 80%, and two explain 9/10 = 90%. So 2 components are needed.

questions.q: t-SNE is mainly used for…
questions.why: t-SNE is a nonlinear method that embeds high-dimensional data into 2-D or 3-D for visualisation. It is not used for regression or classification.

questions.q: Case: GPS points form winding road-shaped clusters with scattered noise. Best algorithm?
questions.why: DBSCAN finds clusters of any shape, like winding roads, and marks scattered points as noise. k-means would force round clusters.

questions.q: Silhouette scores k=2:0.35, k=3:0.52, k=4:0.61, k=5:0.44. Choose k =
questions.why: Choose the k with the highest silhouette score. Here that is k = 4 with 0.61.

questions.q: Covariance [[2,1],[1,2]] eigenvalues?
Case: features are height (cm) and income (₹). PCA without scaling gives PC1 ≈ income. Why?
options: Income has far larger variance in its units
questions.why: Income in rupees has a far bigger numerical variance than height in cm. PCA follows variance, so PC1 is mostly income; standardise first.

questions.q: DBSCAN ε = 1, minPts = 3 on {1, 1.5, 2, 5}: point 5 is…
questions.why: The point 5 has no other point within ε = 1. So it has no neighbours and cannot be a core or border point; it is noise.

courses.title: Revision & Practice · Machine Learning
courses.summary: Formula sheet for every unit and a full-length mixed mock paper with numericals.
outcomes: Learners can recall all key ML formulas
Learners can solve mixed numericals quickly
Learners can choose the right algorithm and metric for a scenario

scenes.text: The end-semester exam allows no notes. You make one memory sheet.
Here it is — learn it, then test yourself.

steps.title: Regression
steps.body:
- w = Σ(x−x̄)(y−ȳ)/Σ(x−x̄)², b = ȳ − w·x̄
- MSE = (1/n)Σ(y−ŷ)²; RMSE = √MSE; R² = 1 − SSE/SST
- GD: w ← w − α∇J; MSE gradient (2/n)Xᵀ(Xw − y)
- Normal eq. w = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy; ridge (XᵀX + λI)⁻¹Xᵀy

steps.title: Classification
steps.body:
- σ(z) = 1/(1+e^(−z)); log-loss −[y ln p + (1−y) ln(1−p)]
- Bayes P(C|x) ∝ P(C)ΠP(xⱼ|C)
- Entropy −Σp log₂ p; Gini 1 − Σp²; IG = H(parent) − weighted H(children)
- SVM margin 2/‖w‖; hinge max(0, 1 − y f(x))

steps.title: Evaluation and unsupervised
steps.body:
- Precision TP/(TP+FP); Recall TP/(TP+FN); F1 = 2PR/(P+R); Specificity TN/(TN+FP)
- AUC = P(score⁺ > score⁻)
- Fits = combinations × folds
- Silhouette (b − a)/max(a, b)
- PCA explained ratio λᵢ/Σλ; z = (x − μ)/σ; min–max (x − min)/(max − min)

scenes.text: 'Which algorithm would you use and why?' — the most common viva question.
Use this decision guide to answer with reasons.

steps.title: Quick guide
steps.body:
- Small tabular data, need interpretability → logistic regression or a shallow tree.
- Tabular data, best accuracy → gradient-boosted trees / random forest.
- Text with many sparse features → Naive Bayes or linear models.
- Few features, nonlinear, moderate size → kernel SVM or kNN (scaled).
- No labels → k-means (spherical), DBSCAN (arbitrary shapes), hierarchical (dendrogram).
- Too many features → regularisation or PCA.

steps.title: Metric guide
steps.body:
- Missing positives is costly → recall.
- False alarms costly → precision.
- Imbalanced → PR-AUC, F1.
- Regression → RMSE (penalises big errors) or MAE (robust).

steps.title: Top exam traps
steps.body:
- Scaling for trees (not needed) vs kNN/SVM/k-means/PCA (needed).
- Leakage from preprocessing before splitting.
- Test set used for tuning.
- Accuracy on imbalanced data.

activity.prompt: Does the method need feature scaling?

quiz.q: Best first model for interpretable credit scoring?
quiz.why: Logistic regression has coefficients that can be explained, so it is a good first model when reasons for decisions matter, as in credit scoring.

quiz.q: Metric when big errors are especially bad (regression)?
quiz.why: RMSE squares the errors before averaging, so large errors count extra. MAE treats all errors in proportion.

quiz.q: Unlabelled data with noise and odd shapes?
quiz.why: For unlabelled data with noise and irregular shapes, use a density-based method like DBSCAN. k-means assumes round clusters and the other options are supervised.

scenes.text: Attempt the course exam below as a timed mock — about 1.5 minutes per question.
Mark your weak unit and revisit its lessons.

steps.title: Numerical method
steps.body:
- Write the formula.
- Substitute with units/labels.
- Compute step by step.
- Sanity check (probabilities in [0,1], R² ≤ 1, silhouette in [−1,1]).

steps.title: Long answers
steps.body: For 'explain' questions use: definition → diagram described in words → formula → example → advantages/limitations.

steps.title: Check before submitting
steps.body:
- log base 2 for entropy.
- Harmonic (not arithmetic) mean for F1.
- Multiply grid size by folds.
- 2/‖w‖, not 1/‖w‖, for margin width.

activity.prompt: I can do these without notes:

quiz.why: For a 50/50 binary node, entropy = −2·0.5·log₂0.5 = 1. This is the maximum for two classes.
There are 6 settings, each fitted once per fold. So 6 × 5 = 30 fits.

questions.q: Which is unsupervised?
questions.why: PCA does not use labels, so it is unsupervised. Logistic regression, SVM and linear regression all need labelled targets.

questions.q: Hyperparameter example?
questions.why: The learning rate is set before training, so it is a hyperparameter. Weights, residuals and predictions come from the data.

questions.q: J=(w−2)², w=0, α=0.5 → w after one step?
questions.why: The gradient is 2(w − 2) = −4 at w = 0. New w = 0 − 0.5·(−4) = 2, which is exactly the minimum.

questions.q: σ(z) with z = 0 and threshold 0.5 predicts…
questions.why: σ(0) = 0.5, so the point lies exactly on the decision boundary. With a 0.5 threshold, the class is a tie.

questions.q: P(spam)=0.5, P(w|spam)=0.4, P(w|ham)=0.1 → P(spam|w)?
Parent (4 yes, 4 no) split into (4,0) and (0,4). Weighted Gini after split?
questions.why: Both children are pure (all one class), so each has Gini 0. The weighted average after the split is 0.

questions.q: TP=45, FP=15, FN=5 → precision, recall?
questions.why: Precision = TP/(TP + FP) = 45/60 = 0.75. Recall = TP/(TP + FN) = 45/50 = 0.9.

questions.q: Assertion: Increasing k in kNN reduces variance. Reason: Predictions average over more neighbours.
questions.why: A larger k averages over more neighbours, so predictions change less with individual points. That gives a smoother boundary and lower variance. Both statements are true and the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Which regulariser zeroes coefficients?
questions.why: Lasso uses an L1 penalty, which can make coefficients exactly zero. Ridge only shrinks them, and PCA and dropout are not regularisers of this kind.

questions.q: a = 1, b = 5 → silhouette?
Eigenvalues 3, 1, 1 → ratio for first two PCs?
questions.why: The total is 5. The first two components explain (3 + 1)/5 = 4/5 = 0.8.

questions.q: Case: 0.5% fraud rate; model AUC 0.97 but precision 0.08 at chosen threshold. Best next step?
options: Examine PR curve and tune threshold by cost
questions.why: With a 0.5% fraud rate, AUC can look excellent while precision is low. Look at the PR curve and choose a threshold using the costs of misses and false alarms.

questions.q: Grid 3×3×3 with 5-fold CV fits?
questions.why: The grid has 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 combinations, each fitted in 5 folds: 27 × 5 = 135 fits.

questions.q: Case: scaler fitted on full data, then 5-fold CV; CV score 0.95, test 0.81. Most likely cause?
questions.why: Fitting the scaler on all data before CV leaks information from validation folds. The CV score is then too high compared with the true test score.

questions.q: Data x = [1,2,3], y = [2,2,2]. Least-squares slope?
questions.why: y is constant, so it does not change with x. The covariance of x and y is 0, so the least-squares slope is 0.

questions.q: Hinge loss for y = +1, f(x) = −1?
Case: a 30-feature dataset, 200 rows, linear model overfits. Most suitable fix?
questions.why: With 30 features and only 200 rows, the model overfits (high variance). Ridge or lasso with λ chosen by cross-validation shrinks the weights and reduces overfitting.

uni-cse-oop.title: Object-Oriented Programming in Java and C++ (B.Tech CSE)
uni-cse-oop.description: Unit-by-unit OOP for B.Tech/B.E. CSE in both C++ and Java: classes and encapsulation, inheritance and polymorphism, C++ templates, STL and smart pointers, Java strings, exceptions, collections, streams and threads, and object-oriented design with SOLID and patterns — with many runnable code activities.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Classes, Objects and Encapsulation (C++ and Java)
courses.summary: Procedural vs object-oriented thinking, classes and objects, access specifiers and encapsulation, constructors and destructors, this, static members, and object memory in C++ and Java. Covers topics commonly taught in B.Tech OOP courses.
outcomes: Learners can explain the four pillars of OOP with examples
Learners can write classes with private data and public methods in C++ and Java
Learners can use default, parameterised and copy constructors correctly
Learners can explain static members and object lifetime

scenes.text: The college canteen's C program has 40 global variables and 60 functions. Changing the GST rate breaks the receipt printer.
Rewriting it with an Order class that owns its items and totals makes each change local and safe.

steps.title: Four pillars
steps.body:
- **Encapsulation**: bundle data with the methods that use it; hide internals.
- **Abstraction**: expose *what* an object does, not *how*.
- **Inheritance**: build new classes from existing ones (is-a).
- **Polymorphism**: one interface, many implementations.

A **class** is a blueprint; an **object** is an instance with its own state.

steps.title: Solved example: same class in C++ and Java
Members and memory
steps.body:
- C++ default access in `class` is **private**; in `struct` it is public.
- Java default (no modifier) is **package-private**.
- C++ objects can live on the stack or heap (`new`); Java objects always live on the heap, managed by the garbage collector.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the semicolon after a C++ class definition.
- In Java, declaring `Rect r;` and calling `r.area()` → NullPointerException (no object created).
- Calling an object 'a class' — the class is the type.

activity.prompt:
Write class Rect with private width and height, a constructor, area() and perimeter(). Read w h and print `Area= Perimeter=

`.
activity.hint: Use an initialiser list: Rect(int a,int b): w(a), h(b) {}

quiz.q: Default access of members in a C++ class
quiz.why: In a C++ class, members are private by default. A struct is the same except that its members are public by default.
In Java, objects are created with new and live on the heap. References to them may be on the stack.

quiz.q: Hiding internal data behind methods is
quiz.why: Hiding internal data and exposing it only through methods is encapsulation.
A class is the blueprint and an object is a concrete instance created from it.

quiz.q: `Rect r;` in Java followed by `r.area()` causes
options: NullPointerException / compile error for uninitialised local
quiz.why: Declaring a reference does not create an object. Using r without new fails: the compiler rejects an uninitialised local, and a null field would throw NullPointerException.

scenes.text: A C++ logger opens a resource in every object but never closes it. After a day the server runs out of handles.
Putting cleanup in the destructor guarantees it runs when each object goes out of scope.

steps.title: Constructors
steps.body:
Same name as the class, no return type, run automatically at creation.
- **Default** (no arguments), **parameterised**, **copy** constructor `T(const T&)` in C++.
- If you write any constructor, the compiler no longer generates the default one.
- C++ initialiser lists initialise members before the body runs (required for const and reference members).

steps.title: Destructors and finalisation
steps.body:
- C++ `~T()` runs when the object's lifetime ends — stack objects at scope exit, heap objects at `delete`. Order: reverse of construction.
- This is **RAII**: acquire in the constructor, release in the destructor.
- Java has no destructors; the GC reclaims memory. Use try-with-resources and `AutoCloseable` for other resources (`finalize` is deprecated).

steps.title: Solved example: order of calls
steps.body:
```
struct A { A(){cout<<"A+";} ~A(){cout<<"A-";} };
int main(){ A x; { A y; } A z; }
```
- x constructed: A+
- y constructed and destroyed at the inner brace: A+ A-
- z constructed: A+
- end of main destroys z then x: A- A-
Output: **A+A+A-A+A-A-**

steps.title: Solved example: shallow vs deep copy
steps.body:
A class holding `int* data` with the default copy constructor copies only the pointer → two objects free the same memory (double delete).
- Fix: write a copy constructor that allocates new memory and copies the values (**rule of three**: destructor, copy constructor, copy assignment).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Giving a constructor a return type (it becomes an ordinary function or an error).
- Relying on Java GC to close files or sockets.
- Forgetting `delete` for `new` in C++ (prefer smart pointers, Unit 3).

activity.prompt: Complete struct A so that its constructor prints `A+` and its destructor prints `A-`. Running the given main must print exactly A+A+A-A+A-A- (the NL guard object, destroyed last, prints the final newline).
activity.hint: Destruction happens in reverse order of construction; nl is destroyed last and prints the newline.

quiz.why: A constructor has the class name and no return type, not even void.

quiz.q: C++ destructors of local objects run
quiz.why: Local objects in C++ are destroyed in the reverse order of their construction when they go out of scope.

options: resource lifetime tied to object lifetime
quiz.why: RAII (Resource Acquisition Is Initialisation) ties a resource's lifetime to an object's lifetime. It is acquired in the constructor and released in the destructor.

quiz.q: Java's way to release a file reliably
quiz.why: try-with-resources automatically closes any AutoCloseable (such as a file) at the end of the block, even on exceptions. Java has no destructors, and finalize is unreliable.

quiz.q: Default copy of a class with a raw pointer member is
quiz.why: The default copy copies each member, so a raw pointer is copied as an address. Both objects then point to the same data, i.e. a shallow copy.

lessons.title: Encapsulation in practice: getters, setters and invariants

scenes.text: In a student bank app, any code could write `acc.balance = -5000`. Audits found impossible balances.
Making balance private and allowing changes only through deposit() and withdraw() with checks fixed it.

steps.title: Class invariants
steps.body:
An **invariant** is a rule that must always hold for an object (balance ≥ 0, age ≥ 0). Encapsulation lets methods enforce it: all writes go through code that validates input.

Getters expose state read-only; setters (if any) must validate.

steps.title: Solved example: Java account
Access modifiers compared
steps.body:
- C++: private, protected, public (+ `friend` to grant access).
- Java: private, (default) package-private, protected (package + subclasses), public.
- Immutable objects (all fields final/const, no setters) are naturally thread-safe — e.g. Java `String`.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Auto-generating a setter for every field — that destroys encapsulation.
