- Java: bytecode on JVM; objects on heap; garbage collection; single class inheritance + interfaces; no operator overloading (except + on String); generics (erasure).

steps.title: Polymorphism
steps.body:
- C++: `virtual` needed; `override`, `final`; pure virtual `= 0`; virtual destructor for polymorphic bases.
- Java: methods virtual by default (not static/private/final); `abstract`; `@Override`; interfaces with default methods.

steps.title: Errors and resources
steps.body:
- C++: exceptions unchecked; RAII destructors during unwinding; smart pointers.
- Java: checked vs unchecked exceptions; finally; try-with-resources (AutoCloseable).

steps.title: Access
steps.body:
- C++: private / protected / public; `friend`; class default private, struct default public.
- Java: private / default (package) / protected / public.

steps.title: Top viva traps
steps.body: - 'Java is pass-by-reference' ✗ · 'Overloading = overriding' ✗ · 'Abstract classes can't have constructors' ✗ · 'Static methods can be overridden' ✗ · 'struct can't have methods in C++' ✗

statements.s: Java supports operator overloading for user classes.
In C++, a function must be declared virtual to be dispatched dynamically.
Java abstract classes can have constructors.
A C++ struct can have member functions and constructors.
statements.why: Only default access differs from class.

statements.s: Java static methods can be overridden.
C++ templates use type erasure like Java generics.

quiz.why: Java has checked exceptions, enforced by the compiler. C++ has no checked exceptions.

quiz.q: Multiple class inheritance is allowed in
quiz.why: C++ allows a class to inherit from several classes. Java allows only one superclass and uses interfaces for multiple inheritance of type.

quiz.q: Deterministic destruction at scope end is a feature of
quiz.why: C++ destroys local objects at the end of scope, running the destructor immediately (RAII). Java uses garbage collection at an unspecified time.

quiz.q: Default member access in a C++ struct
quiz.why: In C++, struct members are public by default. This is the only difference from class, where they are private.
Java generics cannot take primitive types, so List<int> is invalid. Use the wrapper List<Integer>.

scenes.text: A senior trains juniors by asking them to predict output before running any snippet.
Within a month, they spot construction-order and virtual-call bugs on sight.

steps.title: Snippet 1 (C++)
Snippet 2 (Java)
Snippet 3 (Java)
Patterns to remember
steps.body:
- Constructors: base → derived; destructors reverse.
- Virtual calls inside constructors use the class being constructed (C++); Java calls the overridden version (danger: fields not initialised yet).
- Static = declared type; instance = runtime type.

activity.prompt: Reproduce Snippet 2: classes P and C with static s() and instance i() printing as shown. In main, do `P p = new C(); p.s(); p.i();` and then print a newline. Expected output: `Ps Ci `.
activity.starter:
// classes P and C
public class Main{ public static void main(String[] a){ P p = new C(); p.s(); p.i(); System.out.println(); } }
activity.hint: Calling a static method through an instance uses the declared type.

quiz.q: C++: virtual call inside base constructor dispatches to
quiz.why: While the base constructor runs, the object is still only a base object. So a virtual call there goes to the base version.

quiz.q: Java: p.s() where s is static and p is declared P
quiz.why: Static methods are bound at compile time using the declared type of the reference. So p.s() calls P.s(), not C.s().

quiz.q: Java: p.i() where i is overridden in C and p refers to a C
quiz.why: Instance methods are dispatched on the actual object at run time. Since p refers to a C, the overridden C.i() runs.

quiz.q: Output of try{print T; throw}catch{print C}finally{print F}
quiz.why: Print T, then throw is caught, so C prints, and finally always runs and prints F. Output T C F.

scenes.text: The end-sem paper asks: 'Design classes for a parking lot.' Many students write only code.
Top scorers draw a quick UML diagram, name the patterns used and justify each relationship.

steps.title: Design answer template
steps.body:
1. List nouns → candidate classes; verbs → methods.
2. Draw a class diagram with relationships and multiplicities.
3. Identify variation points → interfaces/strategies.
4. Mention SOLID checks and any pattern (Factory for vehicle creation, Strategy for fee calculation, Singleton for the lot — if justified).
5. Give a short code skeleton.

steps.title: Solved sketch: parking lot
steps.body:
- ParkingLot ◆— 1..* Level ◆— 1..* Spot
- Vehicle (abstract) ▷ Car, Bike, Truck; Spot has a size and fits(Vehicle)
- Ticket — 1 Vehicle, 1 Spot, entry time
- FeeStrategy (interface) ▷ HourlyFee, FlatFee — injected into the exit gate (DIP).

steps.title: Avoid
steps.body:
- One giant class doing everything.
- Inheritance for roles that change (a Person who is both Student and TA → use roles/composition).
- Naming patterns without explaining why they help.

activity.prompt: I can…
items: Write a class with constructors, destructor/RAII and static members
Explain virtual dispatch, vtables and slicing
Use abstract classes and interfaces correctly
Use STL and Java collections with the right complexity
Handle exceptions in Java and C++
Apply SOLID and three design patterns

quiz.q: A good first step in a design question
quiz.why: Start a design question by picking out the nouns (candidate classes) and verbs (their behaviour). This finds classes and responsibilities.

quiz.q: Fee rules that change often are best modelled as
quiz.why: Rules that change often should be separate, interchangeable objects behind a Strategy interface. Then you add new rules without editing old code, as open/closed requires.

quiz.q: A person who is both a student and a TA is best modelled with
options: multiple inheritance from Student and TA
quiz.why: A person can take on roles that change over time. Model roles with composition, not inheritance from both Student and TA.

questions.q: Mock A1. Output (C++): struct A{A(){cout<<'a';}~A(){cout<<'b';}}; int main(){A x[2];}
questions.why: Both array elements are constructed first, printing a a. At the end of main they are destroyed in reverse order, printing b b. So aabb.

questions.q: Mock A2. Which enables `Complex c = a + b;` in C++?
questions.why: Overloading operator+ lets you write a + b for your own class, so Complex c = a + b works.

questions.q: Mock A3. Java: String s1 = new String("x"); String s2 = "x"; s1.equals(s2) and s1 == s2
questions.why: equals compares contents, which are both x, so true. == compares references. new String creates a different object, so false.

questions.q: Mock A4. Which is resolved at compile time?
questions.why: Overloading is resolved by the compiler from argument types (compile time). Virtual, interface and abstract method calls are resolved at run time.

questions.q: Mock A5. Assertion: a C++ class with a pure virtual function cannot be instantiated. Reason: it has an incomplete vtable entry that must be provided by a derived class.
questions.why: A class with a pure virtual function is abstract and cannot be instantiated, because that function has no implementation to call. So the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Mock A6. Best Java collection for an LRU cache with O(1) operations
questions.why: A LinkedHashMap in access-order mode moves each accessed entry to the end. Overriding removeEldestEntry evicts the least recently used one, all in O(1).

questions.q: Mock A7. Case: two threads update a bank balance; the total sometimes drifts. First fix
options: make the update synchronized or atomic
questions.why: Two threads updating a shared balance without coordination cause a race condition. Making the update synchronized or atomic fixes it.

questions.q: Mock A8. Output (Java): class A{int f(){return 1;}} class B extends A{int f(){return 2;}} A a=new B(); System.out.println(a.f());
questions.why: a is declared as A but refers to a B. The overridden B.f() is chosen at run time, returning 2.

questions.q: Mock B1. In C++, `delete p;` where p is Base* to Derived and ~Base is not virtual
questions.why: Deleting a Derived object through a Base pointer without a virtual destructor is undefined behaviour. Make ~Base virtual.

questions.q: Mock B2. Which pattern adds responsibilities to objects dynamically?
questions.why: The Decorator pattern wraps an object to add responsibilities dynamically while keeping the same interface.

questions.q: Mock B3. Java: which is NOT allowed in an interface (Java 17)?
questions.why: Interfaces cannot hold instance fields with state. Their fields are implicitly public static final constants, though default, static and private methods are allowed.

questions.q: Mock B4. shared_ptr use_count after: auto a=make_shared<int>(1); { auto b=a; auto c=b; }
questions.why: Inside the block, b and c add to the count, but they are destroyed at the closing brace. Only a remains, so use_count is 1.

questions.q: Mock B5. Which violates Liskov substitution?
options: a subclass adding a new method
a subclass with a faster implementation
a subclass method that throws for valid base inputs
questions.why: Subclasses must be usable wherever the base is expected. A method that throws for inputs the base accepts breaks the base contract, violating Liskov substitution.

questions.q: Mock B6. Default ordering of TreeSet<String>
questions.why: TreeSet orders elements by their natural ordering. For Strings that is lexicographic (dictionary) order, via Comparable.

questions.q: Mock B7. Output (C++): Base* p = new Der; p->f(); where f is non-virtual in Base and redefined in Der
questions.why: f is non-virtual, so the call is bound at compile time to the pointer's type Base. So Base::f runs.

questions.q: Mock B8. In Java, finalize() is
options: deprecated and not guaranteed to run
questions.why: finalize() is deprecated and not guaranteed to run at all. Use try-with-resources to release resources reliably.

questions.q: Mock B9. Which statement about C++ templates is true?
options: each used type gets its own instantiation at compile time
they are resolved at run time
they cannot be used with classes
questions.why: C++ templates are instantiated by the compiler for each type used, generating separate code at compile time. They are not resolved at run time.

questions.q: Mock B10. Which is the correct way to give a Java class natural ordering?
questions.why: Implement Comparable<T> and compareTo to define a class's natural order. Comparator is a separate object for other orderings.

uni-cse-os.title: Operating Systems (B.Tech CSE)
uni-cse-os.description: A complete B.Tech operating-systems course: processes, scheduling, synchronisation, deadlocks, memory, virtual memory, storage and I/O — with GATE-style numericals and unit exams.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Introduction & OS Structures
courses.summary: What an operating system is, how it protects itself with dual mode and system calls, how kernels are structured and how a computer boots. Covers the topics commonly taught in B.Tech operating-systems courses at Indian engineering institutes.
outcomes: Learners can explain the OS as resource manager and extended machine
Learners can trace a system call from user mode to kernel mode and back
Learners can compare monolithic, layered, microkernel, modular and hybrid kernels
Learners can compute CPU utilisation under multiprogramming

scenes.text: Riya has a browser, a music player and a compiler open at once on a 4-core laptop.
Music never stutters, the compile finishes, and no app can read another app's memory.
Who is deciding which program runs, where it lives in RAM and who may open which file? The operating system.

steps.title: Two views of an OS
steps.body:
**Resource manager:** the OS allocates CPU time, memory, disk space and devices fairly and efficiently among competing programs.

**Extended machine:** it hides ugly hardware details behind clean abstractions — files instead of disk sectors, processes instead of raw CPU registers, sockets instead of NIC buffers.

The part that is always resident and runs in privileged mode is the **kernel**; everything else (shell, compilers, GUI) are system programs or applications.

steps.title: Types of operating systems
steps.body:
- **Batch:** jobs grouped and run one after another without interaction.
- **Multiprogramming:** several jobs in memory; when one waits for I/O, the CPU switches to another — goal: keep the CPU busy.
- **Time-sharing (multitasking):** CPU switched so quickly (time slices) that each user feels they own the machine — goal: fast response.
- **Real-time:** hard real-time (deadline miss = failure, e.g. airbag controller) vs soft real-time (deadline miss = degraded quality, e.g. video streaming).
- **Distributed / network OS, mobile OS, embedded OS.**

steps.title: Solved example 1 · CPU utilisation with multiprogramming
steps.body:
A simple probabilistic model: if each process spends fraction **p** of its time waiting for I/O, and n processes are in memory, the CPU is idle only when all n wait: utilisation = **1 − pⁿ**.

Given p = 0.8, n = 4:
- Step 1: pⁿ = 0.8⁴ = 0.4096
- Step 2: utilisation = 1 − 0.4096 = **0.5904 ≈ 59%**

With only one process (n = 1): 1 − 0.8 = 20%. Multiprogramming nearly tripled CPU use.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · How many processes for 90%?
steps.body:
Same p = 0.8. Find the smallest n with 1 − 0.8ⁿ ≥ 0.9, i.e. 0.8ⁿ ≤ 0.1.
- n = 10: 0.8¹⁰ ≈ 0.107 (not enough)
- n = 11: 0.8¹¹ ≈ 0.086 ✓

Answer: **11 processes**. Note the diminishing returns — memory, not CPU, becomes the limit.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling the shell or the GUI 'the kernel' — they are user-level programs.
- Mixing up multiprogramming (maximise CPU use) with time-sharing (minimise response time). Time-sharing is multiprogramming plus time slices.
- Saying a soft real-time system has no deadlines — it has them, missing them only degrades service.

activity.prompt: Match the OS type to its defining goal
pairs: Run grouped jobs without user interaction
Keep the CPU busy while others wait for I/O
Quick response to many interactive users

quiz.q: The OS component that always runs in privileged mode is the
quiz.why: The kernel is the core of the OS and runs in privileged (kernel) mode. The shell and compiler run as user programs.

quiz.q: With I/O wait fraction 0.5 and 3 processes, CPU utilisation (1 − pⁿ) is
quiz.why: CPU utilisation = 1 − pⁿ = 1 − 0.5³ = 1 − 0.125 = 0.875, i.e. 87.5%. With more processes, it is likely that at least one is ready.

quiz.q: An anti-lock braking controller is best described as
quiz.why: An anti-lock brake controller must respond by a deadline, or the result could be catastrophic. That makes it hard real-time.
Time-sharing rapidly switches the CPU among users in small slices. This gives interactive users quick response times.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a resource the OS manages?
quiz.why: The OS manages hardware resources such as CPU, memory and I/O devices. It does not manage a programmer's algorithm choices.

lessons.title: Dual mode, interrupts and system calls

story.title: Why printf can't touch the disk directly

scenes.text: Arjun's C program calls printf to write to a file.
If any program could command the disk controller, one buggy app could wipe the disk.
So the program asks the kernel through a doorway called a system call.

steps.title: Dual-mode operation
steps.body:
Hardware provides a **mode bit**: kernel (supervisor) mode = 0, user mode = 1. **Privileged instructions** — I/O instructions, changing the timer, disabling interrupts, loading the base/limit or page-table register, halting — run only in kernel mode. Attempting one in user mode causes a **trap** to the OS.

A hardware **timer** interrupts periodically so the OS regains control even if a program loops forever.

steps.title: Interrupts, traps and system calls
steps.body:
- **Interrupt:** asynchronous signal from hardware (disk done, key pressed). CPU saves state, jumps via the interrupt vector to a handler.
- **Trap/exception:** synchronous, caused by the running instruction (divide by zero, page fault, or a deliberate syscall instruction).
- **System call:** the programmatic interface to kernel services. Typical flow: library wrapper puts the syscall number and arguments in registers (or a memory block / stack) → executes trap instruction (e.g. `syscall`, `int 0x80`) → mode switches to kernel → kernel dispatches via the system-call table → result returned → mode switches back to user.

steps.title: Categories of system calls
steps.body:
- Process control: fork, exec, exit, wait
- File management: open, read, write, close
- Device management: ioctl, read/write on devices
- Information maintenance: getpid, time
- Communication: pipe, shmget, socket, send/recv
- Protection: chmod, setuid

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Tracing write()
steps.body:
`write(fd, buf, 10)` in a C program:
1. libc wrapper loads syscall number of write and the three arguments into registers.
2. Executes the trap instruction → CPU sets mode bit to kernel, jumps to the syscall entry.
3. Kernel validates fd and that buf lies in the caller's address space.
4. Copies 10 bytes into a kernel buffer and queues the device/file-system work.
5. Puts the return value (bytes written or −1 with errno) in a register, returns to user mode.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Privileged or not?
steps.body:
Classify: (a) read the clock, (b) set the timer, (c) clear memory, (d) disable interrupts, (e) switch from user to kernel mode via trap.
- (a) not privileged (reading time is harmless)
- (b) **privileged** (else a process could keep the CPU forever)
- (c) not privileged within its own memory
- (d) **privileged**
- (e) not privileged — the trap instruction itself must be callable from user mode; it is the *entry* to the kernel.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking the trap instruction is privileged — then user programs could never request services.
- Confusing an API (printf, POSIX) with the system call itself; one library call may make zero or many syscalls.
- Forgetting the kernel must validate user pointers before using them.

activity.prompt: Privileged instruction or allowed in user mode?

quiz.q: The mode bit value for kernel mode is conventionally
quiz.why: By the usual convention, mode bit 0 is kernel (privileged) mode and 1 is user mode.

quiz.q: A divide-by-zero in a user program generates a
quiz.why: Dividing by zero is detected as the instruction executes, so it raises a synchronous exception, called a trap. Device interrupts are asynchronous.

quiz.q: Which is a process-control system call?
quiz.why: fork creates a new process, so it is a process-control call. chmod is file management and ioctl is device management.

quiz.q: Why does the OS need a timer interrupt?
options: To regain control from a running process
quiz.why: The timer interrupt returns control to the OS regularly. Without it, a process stuck in a loop could keep the CPU forever.

options: a library function that may invoke write()
quiz.why: printf is a C library function that formats text in user space. When it flushes its buffer, it calls the write() system call.

scenes.text: Team A puts everything — file system, drivers, scheduler — into one big kernel. Fast, but one driver bug crashes all.
Team B keeps only IPC and scheduling in the kernel and runs drivers as servers. Safer, but slower due to messages.
Team C mixes both. Real systems mostly look like Team C.

steps.title: Main designs
steps.body:
- **Monolithic:** all services in one address space in kernel mode (traditional UNIX, Linux). Fast function calls; hard to maintain; a faulty driver can crash the system.
- **Layered:** layer i uses only layer i−1 services (THE system). Easy to verify; hard to define layers; overhead per layer.
- **Microkernel:** minimal kernel (IPC, basic scheduling, low-level memory); file systems, drivers run as user-space servers (Mach, QNX, MINIX 3). Reliable and extensible; message-passing overhead.
- **Modular (loadable kernel modules):** core kernel plus modules loaded at run time (Linux modules, Solaris).
- **Hybrid:** combination, e.g. Windows NT family, macOS XNU (Mach + BSD components).

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Choosing a design
steps.body:
A car's safety controller must keep running even if the audio driver fails. Which design?
- Step 1: requirement = fault isolation.
- Step 2: in a microkernel the audio driver is a user-space server; its crash does not take down the kernel.
- Answer: **microkernel** (QNX is widely used in automotive systems).

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Cost of messages
steps.body: A file read in a microkernel needs: app → kernel → FS server → kernel → disk driver → kernel → FS server → kernel → app. Count the user/kernel boundary crossings: each arrow touching the kernel is a crossing, so about **8 crossings** vs **2** (enter + leave) in a monolithic kernel. This is why microkernels optimise IPC heavily.

steps.title: Virtual machines
steps.body: A **hypervisor** lets several guest OSes share hardware. **Type 1 (bare-metal)** runs directly on hardware (e.g. Xen, VMware ESXi, Hyper-V). **Type 2 (hosted)** runs on a host OS (e.g. VirtualBox, VMware Workstation). **Containers** share the host kernel and isolate processes with namespaces and cgroups — lighter than VMs.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling Linux a microkernel — it is monolithic with loadable modules.
- Assuming microkernels are always slower in practice; well-tuned IPC (L4 family) narrows the gap.
- Thinking containers have their own kernel — they do not.

activity.prompt: Match the structure to an example

quiz.q: In a microkernel, device drivers usually run in
quiz.why: A microkernel keeps only minimal services in the kernel. Drivers run as user-space servers, so a crash in one does not take down the kernel.

quiz.q: Main drawback of a pure monolithic kernel:
options: one faulty component can crash the whole system
quiz.why: In a monolithic kernel, all services share one privileged address space. A bug in any one component, such as a driver, can crash the whole system.

quiz.q: Containers differ from VMs because containers
quiz.why: Containers isolate processes using the host's kernel (namespaces and cgroups). VMs emulate hardware and each runs its own OS kernel.
In layered design, the hard part is deciding the order of layers, since each layer can use only the ones below it. Some components depend on each other, such as memory management and disk drivers.
ESXi runs directly on the hardware without a host OS, so it is a Type 1 (bare-metal) hypervisor.

scenes.text: Kabir presses power. The CPU starts executing firmware from a fixed address.
Firmware tests hardware, finds a boot device and loads a bootloader.
The bootloader loads the kernel; the kernel starts the first user process, which starts everything else.

steps.title: Boot sequence
steps.body:
1. Power on → CPU jumps to firmware (BIOS or UEFI) in ROM/flash.
2. **POST** (power-on self test) checks hardware.
3. Firmware loads the **bootloader** (from MBR boot sector or an EFI system partition), e.g. GRUB or Windows Boot Manager.
4. Bootloader loads the kernel image (and an initial RAM disk) into memory and jumps to it.
5. Kernel initialises memory management, interrupts, drivers, mounts the root file system.
6. Kernel starts the first user process (on many Linux systems `systemd`, PID 1), which starts services and the login screen.

steps.title: Services an OS provides
steps.body:
User-facing: user interface (CLI/GUI), program execution, I/O operations, file-system manipulation, communication, error detection.
Efficiency-facing: resource allocation, accounting/logging, protection and security.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Where does it fail?
steps.body:
A PC shows the manufacturer logo, then 'No bootable device'. Which stage failed?
- POST passed (logo appeared).
- Firmware could not find a valid bootloader on any device.
- Answer: **bootloader discovery stage** — check boot order / EFI partition, not the kernel.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Policy vs mechanism
steps.body: Mechanism = *how* to do something; policy = *what* to do. The timer interrupt that preempts a process is a **mechanism**; deciding that interactive processes get priority is a **policy**. Separating them lets an OS change policy (e.g. a new scheduler) without rewriting mechanisms.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the BIOS loads the kernel directly on modern systems — usually a bootloader sits in between.
- Treating the init process as part of the kernel; it is the first *user-space* process.

activity.prompt: Put the boot steps in order

quiz.why: POST is the Power-On Self Test, which the firmware runs at power-on to check the hardware.
GRUB is a bootloader. It loads the kernel into memory and starts it.

options: changing decisions without changing low-level code
quiz.why: Mechanism is how something is done, and policy is what is decided. Separating them lets you change decisions without rewriting low-level code.

quiz.q: On many Linux systems PID 1 is
quiz.why: On many Linux systems the first user process, PID 1, is init or systemd. It starts other services.

quiz.q: Accounting as an OS service means
quiz.why: Accounting records how much of each resource is used by each user or process, for billing or statistics.

questions.q: The program that runs at all times in kernel mode is the
questions.why: The kernel is the part of the OS that is always loaded and runs in kernel mode. A shell, loader or editor runs as a user program.

questions.q: Which OS type is designed to minimise response time for many users?
questions.why: Time-sharing uses short time slices to give many users quick responses. Batch systems do not aim for interactivity.

questions.q: Which instruction must NOT be privileged?
questions.why: A trap (system call) is how user code asks the kernel for service. So it must be allowed in user mode. Direct I/O, disabling interrupts and setting the timer are privileged.

questions.q: Linux is best classified as
questions.why: Linux has a monolithic kernel, but it can load and unload modules (like drivers) at run time.

questions.q: A page fault is an example of
questions.why: A page fault is caused by the instruction accessing an unmapped page. It is synchronous, so it is a trap/exception, not a device interrupt.

questions.q: Assertion (A): A timer interrupt is required for time-sharing. Reason (R): Without it the OS cannot preempt a running process. Choose:
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A timer interrupt lets the OS regain the CPU so it can preempt a running process, which time-sharing needs. Both are true and the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Utilisation with p = 0.6 and n = 2 (1 − pⁿ) is
Which is a Type 2 hypervisor?
questions.why: VirtualBox runs on top of a host operating system, so it is a Type 2 hypervisor. ESXi, Xen and Hyper-V are Type 1.

questions.q: Mach + BSD components in macOS make XNU a
questions.why: XNU, the macOS kernel, combines the Mach microkernel with BSD components. That mix makes it a hybrid kernel.

questions.q: Case: a medical infusion pump must deliver a dose exactly every 5 s; a late dose is dangerous. Required OS class:
questions.why: A late dose is dangerous, so the deadline must always be met. That requires a hard real-time OS.

questions.q: Minimum n with 1 − 0.9ⁿ ≥ 0.5 (p = 0.9):
questions.why: We need 1 − 0.9ⁿ ≥ 0.5, i.e. 0.9ⁿ ≤ 0.5. 0.9⁶ ≈ 0.531 is still above 0.5, but 0.9⁷ ≈ 0.478 is below, so n = 7.

questions.q: In a microkernel file read, why is performance lower than monolithic?
options: More user/kernel crossings and message copies
questions.why: In a microkernel, a file read passes messages between user-space servers. That means more user/kernel crossings and copies, so it is slower than a monolithic call.

questions.q: Which statement about containers is correct?
options: They rely on namespaces and cgroups of a shared kernel
questions.why: Containers share the host kernel and are isolated using namespaces and cgroups. They do not have their own kernel or need hardware virtualisation.

questions.q: Choosing which process to run next is a ___; the context switch code is a ___.
questions.why: Choosing which process runs next is a decision, so a policy. The context-switch code is how the switch is done, so a mechanism.

questions.q: A system call passes a pointer to a user buffer. What must the kernel do first?
options: Validate the pointer lies in the caller's address space
questions.why: A user could pass a bad pointer to trick the kernel into reading or writing protected memory. So the kernel must first check that the pointer lies within the caller's address space.

questions.q: CPU utilisation is 1 − pⁿ. With 8 processes utilisation is 0.9. Approximately what is p?

courses.summary: Process concept, PCB, states, fork/exec/wait, context switching, schedulers, inter-process communication and threads, with fork-counting and Amdahl's-law problems.
outcomes: Learners can draw the five-state process model and its transitions
Learners can count processes and outputs created by fork()
Learners can compare shared memory and message passing

scenes.text: Neha opens three terminal windows and runs the same text editor in each.
There is one program file on disk but three processes — each with its own memory, registers and open files.

steps.title: Program vs process
steps.body:
A **program** is passive code on disk. A **process** is a program in execution: code (text) + data + heap + stack + CPU context (PC, registers) + OS bookkeeping.

The OS stores bookkeeping in a **Process Control Block (PCB)**: PID, state, program counter, CPU registers, scheduling info (priority, queue pointers), memory-management info (page table base, limits), accounting info, I/O status (open files).

steps.title: Five-state model
steps.body:
- **New → Ready:** admitted by the long-term scheduler.
- **Ready → Running:** dispatched by the short-term scheduler.
- **Running → Ready:** preempted (timer interrupt).
- **Running → Waiting (blocked):** requests I/O or waits for an event.
- **Waiting → Ready:** I/O completes/event occurs.
- **Running → Terminated:** exit.

There is **no** direct Waiting → Running transition: it must go through Ready. With swapping, add *Ready-Suspended* and *Blocked-Suspended* states (seven-state model).

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Which transition?
steps.body:
(a) A process issues read() on disk. → Running → Waiting.
(b) Its time slice expires. → Running → Ready.
(c) The disk interrupt reports completion. → Waiting → Ready.
(d) Scheduler picks it. → Ready → Running.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Counting states
steps.body:
On a single-CPU machine with 10 processes in memory, what is the maximum number in Running, Ready and Waiting?
- Running: at most **1** (one CPU).
- Ready: at most **9** (all except the running one) — or 10 if the CPU is idle momentarily switching.
- Waiting: at most **10** (all could be blocked; CPU idle).
On n CPUs, at most n are Running.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Drawing an arrow from Waiting directly to Running.
- Thinking the PCB holds the program's code — it holds pointers/metadata, not the code itself.
- Confusing 'Ready' (waiting only for CPU) with 'Waiting' (waiting for an event).

activity.prompt: Match the event to the state transition

quiz.q: Which is stored in the PCB?
quiz.why: The PCB stores a process's state, including the program counter and registers, so it can resume later.

quiz.q: On 1 CPU, how many processes can be Running at once?
quiz.why: A single CPU can execute only one process at a time. So only one process is in the Running state.

quiz.q: A process waiting for keyboard input is in
quiz.why: A process waiting for keyboard input is waiting for an event, not for the CPU. That is the Waiting (Blocked) state.

quiz.q: Which transition is impossible in the five-state model?
quiz.why: A waiting process must first become Ready after its event happens, then wait to be scheduled. It cannot go straight to Running.

quiz.q: A program becomes a process when
quiz.why: A program is just a file. It becomes a process once it is loaded into memory and executing.

scenes.text: When Sam types `ls`, the shell clones itself with fork().
The child replaces itself with the ls program using exec().
The parent shell calls wait() until ls finishes, then prints the prompt again.

steps.title: fork, exec, wait, exit
steps.body:
- `fork()` creates a child that is a copy of the parent. Returns **0 in the child**, the **child's PID in the parent**, **−1 on failure**.
- `exec*()` replaces the current process image with a new program (same PID). It does not return on success.
- `wait()` makes the parent block until a child terminates and collects its exit status.
- **Zombie:** child has exited but parent has not yet called wait — its PCB entry remains.
- **Orphan:** parent exits first; the child is adopted by init/systemd (or a subreaper), which reaps it.
- Modern kernels use **copy-on-write** so fork is cheap: pages are shared until someone writes.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Counting with sequential forks
steps.body:
`fork(); fork(); fork(); printf("hi\n");`
- After 1st fork: 2 processes; after 2nd: 4; after 3rd: 8.
- Each prints once → **8 'hi'**.
- Child processes created = 2³ − 1 = **7**.
General rule: n sequential forks → 2ⁿ processes, 2ⁿ − 1 children.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · fork in a loop
steps.body:
`for (i = 0; i < 3; i++) { fork(); printf("x"); }` (stdout unbuffered for simplicity)
- i=0: 2 processes print → 2
- i=1: 4 processes print → 4
- i=2: 8 processes print → 8
- Total **14 x's** (= 2 + 4 + 8). Total processes at the end = 8.

Beware: with buffered stdout and no newline, buffers are duplicated by fork, so the visible count can differ (it would be 24 here since each of the 8 final processes flushes its 3 buffered x's). Exam questions usually assume unbuffered or newline-terminated output.

steps.title: Solved example 3 · Using the return value
steps.body:
`if (fork() == 0) printf("C"); else printf("P");`
The child sees 0 → prints C; the parent sees the child's PID (> 0) → prints P. Output: one C and one P, in **either order** — the scheduler decides.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying fork returns the parent's PID to the child — it returns 0 to the child (the child can call getppid()).
- Assuming the parent always runs first after fork.
- Forgetting that exec keeps the PID and open file descriptors (unless close-on-exec).

activity.prompt: How many times is 'hi' printed by: fork(); fork(); fork(); fork(); printf("hi\n");

quiz.q: fork() returns what value in the child?
quiz.why: fork() returns 0 in the child and the child's PID in the parent. That is how each can tell which one it is.

quiz.q: After 5 sequential fork() calls, the number of child processes created is
quiz.why: Each sequential fork doubles the number of processes. After 5 forks there are 2⁵ = 32 processes, so 31 are children.

quiz.q: A process that has terminated but whose parent has not called wait() is a
quiz.why: A zombie has finished, but its parent has not called wait(). Its PCB stays in the process table until the exit status is collected.
A successful exec replaces the process's program image with a new one. So there is nothing to return to; it returns only on error.
With copy-on-write, parent and child share the same pages. They are copied only when one writes, so fork avoids copying everything.

scenes.text: A camera app captures frames; a filter app processes them.
They can share a memory region (fast) or send messages (simpler, safer).

steps.title: Three schedulers
steps.body:
- **Long-term (job) scheduler:** decides which jobs enter memory; controls the degree of multiprogramming. Runs infrequently.
- **Short-term (CPU) scheduler:** picks the next ready process; runs every few milliseconds, so it must be fast.
- **Medium-term scheduler:** swaps processes out/in to reduce memory pressure.

A good long-term scheduler mixes **I/O-bound** and **CPU-bound** processes.

**Dispatcher** = module that gives the CPU to the chosen process (context switch, switch to user mode, jump to PC). Its time is **dispatch latency**.

steps.title: Context switch
steps.body: Save the running process's context into its PCB, load the next process's context from its PCB. Pure overhead: no useful work. Cost includes register save/restore plus indirect costs (TLB and cache refill).

steps.title: IPC models
steps.body:
- **Shared memory:** processes map a common region; after setup, communication needs no kernel involvement → fast, but programmers must synchronise.
- **Message passing:** send/receive via the kernel (pipes, message queues, sockets) → easier, works across machines, slower per message.
- Message passing may be **blocking (synchronous)** or **non-blocking (asynchronous)**; a blocking send + blocking receive is called a **rendezvous**.
- **Pipes:** ordinary pipes are unidirectional and between related processes; named pipes (FIFOs) can connect unrelated processes.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Overhead of context switching
steps.body:
Time slice q = 10 ms, context switch s = 1 ms. Fraction of CPU wasted (all processes use their full slice) = s / (q + s) = 1/11 ≈ **9.1%**.
If q = 1 ms with s = 1 ms → 1/2 = **50%** wasted. Lesson: the quantum must be large compared with the switch time.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Pick the IPC
steps.body: A video editor sends 4K frames (≈ 24 MB each) between its decoder and renderer on the same machine, 60 times a second. Message passing would copy ~1.4 GB/s through the kernel. **Shared memory** avoids copies; use a semaphore to signal 'frame ready'.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling the dispatcher the scheduler; the scheduler decides, the dispatcher performs the switch.
- Assuming shared memory is automatically safe — it needs synchronisation.
- Thinking ordinary pipes are bidirectional.

activity.prompt: Quantum = 4 ms, context-switch time = 0.5 ms. What percentage of CPU time is overhead? (s/(q+s)×100, 1 decimal)

quiz.q: Which scheduler controls the degree of multiprogramming?
quiz.why: The long-term scheduler decides which jobs are admitted into memory, so it controls the degree of multiprogramming.
The medium-term scheduler swaps processes out of memory and back in, to reduce the load.

quiz.q: Fastest IPC for large data on one machine after setup:
quiz.why: Once set up, processes read and write the shared region directly, with no system call or kernel copy per access. So it is the fastest.

quiz.q: Blocking send with blocking receive is called
quiz.why: When both send and receive block until the other side is ready, the processes meet at a point, called a rendezvous.
During a context switch, no user process makes progress. So that time is pure overhead.

scenes.text: A browser tab downloads images, runs JavaScript and responds to scrolling at the same time.
Threads in one process share memory and files but each has its own stack and registers.

steps.title: What a thread shares
steps.body:
Threads of one process **share**: code, data (globals), heap, open files, signals.
Each thread **owns**: thread ID, program counter, register set, stack.

Benefits: responsiveness, resource sharing, economy (creation and switching are cheaper than processes), scalability on multicore.

steps.title: User vs kernel threads and models
steps.body:
- **Many-to-one:** many user threads → one kernel thread. Cheap, but one blocking call blocks all, and no true parallelism.
- **One-to-one:** each user thread → a kernel thread (Linux, Windows). True parallelism; creating many threads costs kernel resources.
- **Many-to-many / two-level:** multiplexes M user threads onto N kernel threads.

**Concurrency** = making progress on several tasks (possibly interleaved on one core). **Parallelism** = literally executing at the same time on multiple cores.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Amdahl's law
steps.body:
Speedup ≤ 1 / (S + (1 − S)/N), where S = serial fraction, N = cores.
A program is 25% serial, N = 4:
- (1 − S)/N = 0.75/4 = 0.1875
- Denominator = 0.25 + 0.1875 = 0.4375
- Speedup = 1/0.4375 ≈ **2.29**
Even with infinitely many cores: 1/S = **4** — the serial part caps the speedup.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Which model blocks?
steps.body: Under many-to-one, thread T1 calls a blocking read(). Since all user threads map to one kernel thread, the kernel blocks that kernel thread → **every thread in the process stops**. Under one-to-one only T1 blocks.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying threads share stacks — each has its own stack.
- Treating concurrency and parallelism as synonyms.
- Applying Amdahl's law with the parallel fraction in place of the serial fraction.

activity.prompt: Amdahl's law: read the serial fraction S and number of cores N (one per line) and print the maximum speedup rounded to 2 decimals.
activity.starter:
S = float(input())
N = int(input())
# speedup = 1 / (S + (1 - S) / N)
activity.solution:
S = float(input())
N = int(input())
print(f"{1 / (S + (1 - S) / N):.2f}")
activity.hint: Use an f-string with :.2f for rounding.

quiz.q: Which is private to each thread?
quiz.why: Each thread has its own stack and registers. Global variables, heap and open files are shared by the process's threads.

quiz.q: Linux maps user threads using the
quiz.why: Linux uses the one-to-one model, where every user thread maps to its own kernel schedulable entity (task).

quiz.q: Serial fraction 0.5, infinite cores: max speedup =
quiz.why: By Amdahl's law, with serial fraction S = 0.5 the speedup limit is 1/S = 2, no matter how many cores.

quiz.q: In many-to-one, a blocking system call by one thread
quiz.why: In many-to-one, all user threads share one kernel thread. A blocking system call by one blocks the whole process.

quiz.q: Running two tasks interleaved on a single core is
quiz.why: On one core, tasks take turns, so both make progress. That is concurrency. Parallelism needs tasks running at the same instant.

questions.q: A program in execution is a
questions.why: A process is a program in execution. A program is only a passive file.

questions.q: Which data structure stores a process's saved registers?
questions.why: The Process Control Block (PCB) holds a process's saved registers and other state.

questions.q: fork() returns −1 when
questions.why: fork() returns −1 to the parent when the new process cannot be created (for example, no resources).

questions.q: Number of processes after 4 sequential forks:
questions.why: Each sequential fork doubles the process count. After 4 forks, there are 2⁴ = 16 processes.

questions.q: Which state transition is triggered by a timer interrupt?
questions.why: When the timer interrupt fires, the OS preempts the running process and moves it to Ready.

questions.q: Threads of one process share all EXCEPT
questions.why: Threads of one process share code, heap and open files. Each has its own registers and stack.

questions.q: The dispatcher is responsible for
options: choosing the next job to admit
the actual context switch to the chosen process
questions.why: The dispatcher performs the actual context switch, giving the CPU to the process chosen by the scheduler.

questions.q: Assertion (A): A zombie occupies an entry in the process table. Reason (R): Its parent has not yet collected its exit status. Choose:
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A zombie has terminated but its parent has not read its exit status, so its entry stays in the process table. wait() frees it. Both are true and the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: for(i=0;i<2;i++){fork(); printf("*\n");} prints how many stars?
questions.why: In iteration i = 0, 2 processes each print a star (2). In iteration i = 1, 4 processes print one each (4). So 2 + 4 = 6.

questions.q: Quantum 9 ms, switch 1 ms: overhead fraction =
questions.why: Each 9 ms slice is followed by a 1 ms switch. Overhead = 1/(9 + 1) = 10%.

questions.q: Case: a server creates a new process per request and is slow under load. Best fix?
questions.why: Creating a process per request is expensive. A thread pool reuses cheap threads, so the server handles load better.

questions.q: Amdahl: 20% serial, 8 cores — speedup ≈
What does `if(fork() && fork()) fork();` create in total (including original)?
questions.why: Original forks A (child returns 0 → stops). Parent forks B (child 0 → stops). Parent (both nonzero) forks C. Processes: original, A, B, C = 4.

questions.q: Many-to-many threading is preferred over many-to-one because
options: a blocking call need not block all user threads and parallelism is possible
questions.why: Many-to-many uses several kernel threads for many user threads. So one blocking call does not block all user threads, and they can run in parallel.

questions.q: Amdahl: to reach speedup 4 on 8 cores, the serial fraction must be at most about
questions.why: Setting S + (1 − S)/8 = 1/4 gives 7S/8 = 1/8, so S = 1/7. So the serial fraction can be at most about 1/7.

questions.q: An orphan process is adopted by
questions.why: When a parent exits, its children become orphans. They are adopted by init/systemd (or a subreaper), which later reaps them.

scenes.text: At the college canteen, one student orders 24 plates for a party. Two others just want one chai each.
If the big order goes first, the chai buyers wait ages — the convoy effect.

steps.title: Definitions you must know
steps.body:
- **Arrival time (AT)**, **burst time (BT)**, **completion time (CT)**.
- **Turnaround time** TAT = CT − AT.
- **Waiting time** WT = TAT − BT (time spent in the ready queue).
- **Response time** = first time on CPU − AT.
- Goals: maximise CPU utilisation and throughput; minimise TAT, WT and response time.
- **Non-preemptive:** once running, a process keeps the CPU until it blocks or ends. **Preemptive:** the OS may take the CPU away.

steps.title: FCFS (first come, first served)
steps.body: Run processes in order of arrival; non-preemptive; simple FIFO queue. Suffers from the **convoy effect**: short jobs stuck behind a long CPU-bound one. Never starves anybody.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · FCFS order matters
steps.body:
P1 = 24, P2 = 3, P3 = 3 ms, all arrive at 0, order P1, P2, P3.
- Gantt: P1 0–24, P2 24–27, P3 27–30.
- WT: P1 0, P2 24, P3 27 → average **17 ms**.
Order P2, P3, P1: Gantt P2 0–3, P3 3–6, P1 6–30 → WT 0, 3, 6 → average **3 ms**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · FCFS with arrivals
steps.body:
P1 (AT 0, BT 5), P2 (AT 1, BT 3), P3 (AT 6, BT 2).
- Gantt: P1 0–5, P2 5–8, P3 8–10.
- TAT: P1 5, P2 7, P3 4 → avg 16/3 ≈ 5.33.
- WT = TAT − BT: P1 0, P2 4, P3 2 → avg 2.
If a gap appears (no process has arrived), the CPU idles — include idle time in the chart.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Computing waiting time as start time without subtracting arrival.
- Forgetting CPU idle gaps when the next arrival is later than the current completion.
- Averaging over the wrong number of processes.

activity.prompt: FCFS (all processes arrive at time 0): first line n, second line the n burst times in queue order. Print the average waiting time with 2 decimals.
activity.starter:
n = int(input())
b = list(map(int, input().split()))
# each process waits for the sum of bursts before it
activity.solution:
n = int(input())
b = list(map(int, input().split()))
t = 0
total = 0
for x in b:
    total += t
    t += x
print(f"{total / n:.2f}")
activity.hint: Keep a running clock t; add t to the total before adding the burst.

quiz.why: Waiting time is the time spent in the ready queue: turnaround time minus burst time (TAT − BT).
With FCFS, a long job at the front makes the short jobs behind it wait. This is the convoy effect.
FCFS is non-preemptive: a process runs until it finishes or blocks.

quiz.q: P1=10, P2=2 both at 0 in order P1, P2 under FCFS: average WT =
quiz.why: P1 waits 0 and P2 waits 10, so the average is (0 + 10)/2 = 5.
Response time is the time from arrival until the process first gets the CPU.

scenes.text: A courier with five parcels delivers the quickest ones first so the average customer waits least.
The catch: the OS cannot know the future burst length — it must predict it.

steps.title: SJF and SRTF
steps.body:
**SJF (non-preemptive):** when the CPU is free, pick the ready process with the smallest next burst. Gives the **minimum average waiting time** among non-preemptive algorithms for a given set.
**SRTF (preemptive SJF):** on every arrival, if the new process's burst is smaller than the running process's *remaining* time, preempt. Minimum average WT overall.
Both can **starve** long jobs. Burst length is predicted by exponential averaging: τₙ₊₁ = α·tₙ + (1 − α)·τₙ.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Non-preemptive SJF on the same data
Common mistakes
steps.body:
- In SRTF comparing the new burst with the running process's *original* burst instead of its *remaining* time.
- Choosing among processes that have not yet arrived.
- Breaking ties arbitrarily without stating the rule (usual rule: FCFS among ties).

activity.prompt: SRTF: P1(AT 0, BT 7), P2(AT 2, BT 4), P3(AT 4, BT 1), P4(AT 5, BT 4). Average waiting time?

quiz.why: Shortest Job First gives the minimum average waiting time among scheduling algorithms. It is a proven result.

quiz.q: SRTF preempts when a new arrival's burst is less than the
quiz.why: SRTF preempts the running process if a new arrival's burst is shorter than the running process's remaining time, not its original burst.

quiz.q: A major drawback of SJF is
quiz.why: If short jobs keep arriving, a long job may never be selected, so SJF can starve long jobs.
The prediction is τ(n+1) = α·t(n) + (1 − α)·τ(n). With α = 1, it equals t(n), the last actual burst.

quiz.q: SRTF is the preemptive version of
quiz.why: SRTF (Shortest Remaining Time First) is the preemptive version of SJF.

scenes.text: An ambulance gets priority at every signal — but if ambulances never stop coming, ordinary cars never move.
A fair alternative: every car gets a short green light in turn — round robin.

steps.title: Priority scheduling
steps.body: Each process has a priority (in many textbooks a **smaller number = higher priority**; always check the question). Can be preemptive or not. Problem: **starvation** (indefinite blocking). Fix: **aging** — gradually raise the priority of processes that wait long. SJF is priority scheduling where priority = predicted burst.

steps.title: Round Robin (RR)
steps.body:
Preemptive FCFS with a **time quantum q**. A process runs for at most q, then goes to the tail of the ready queue.
- Large q → behaves like FCFS. Very small q → huge context-switch overhead.
- Rule of thumb: about 80% of CPU bursts should be shorter than q.
- Excellent response time; average turnaround usually worse than SJF.
- Convention when a new process arrives at the same instant a quantum expires: the **new arrival is queued before** the preempted process (state the convention you use).

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Preemptive priority
steps.body:
(lower number = higher) P1 (AT 0, BT 4, pr 3), P2 (AT 1, BT 2, pr 1), P3 (AT 2, BT 3, pr 2).
- 0–1 P1; t=1 P2 (pr 1) preempts → 1–3 P2; t=3 P3 (pr 2) beats P1 → 3–6 P3; 6–9 P1.
- CT: P1 9, P2 3, P3 6. TAT: 9, 2, 4. WT: 5, 0, 1 → average **2 ms**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming larger number = higher priority when the question says otherwise.
- In RR, forgetting that a process finishing before its quantum releases the CPU immediately.
- Ignoring the arrival-vs-preempted ordering convention.

activity.prompt: RR with q = 2: P1(0,5), P2(0,3), P3(0,1), all queued in order P1, P2, P3. Average waiting time?

quiz.why: Aging gradually raises the priority of waiting processes, so they eventually run. It prevents starvation.

quiz.q: RR with a very large quantum behaves like
quiz.why: With a quantum larger than every burst, each process finishes within its first slice. So RR behaves like FCFS.
Round Robin gives every process the CPU regularly, so each starts soon. It improves response time rather than turnaround.

quiz.q: SJF can be seen as priority scheduling where priority is
quiz.why: SJF is priority scheduling where priority is the inverse of the predicted next CPU burst. A shorter burst means higher priority.

quiz.q: RR q = 5: P1 = 3 ms. P1's first slice ends at
quiz.why: P1 needs only 3 ms, less than the quantum of 5. So it finishes at 3 ms and releases the CPU early.

lessons.title: Multilevel queues, multiprocessor and real-time scheduling

scenes.text: Patients are sorted into emergency, urgent and routine queues, each served differently.
A patient who waits too long in routine is moved up — like a multilevel feedback queue.

steps.title: Multilevel queue and MLFQ
steps.body:
**Multilevel queue:** permanent queues (e.g. system, interactive, batch) each with its own algorithm; between queues, fixed priority or time-slicing.
**Multilevel feedback queue (MLFQ):** processes move between queues. Typical: Q0 RR q=8, Q1 RR q=16, Q2 FCFS. A new process enters Q0; if it uses its whole quantum it is demoted; long waiters can be promoted (aging). Favours short/interactive jobs automatically. Most general — and most complex to configure.

steps.title: Multiprocessor scheduling
steps.body:
- **Asymmetric:** one master CPU schedules; **symmetric (SMP):** each CPU self-schedules (common queue or per-CPU queues).
- **Processor affinity:** keep a process on the same CPU to reuse warm caches (soft vs hard affinity).
- **Load balancing:** push migration and pull migration.
- **Multicore/hardware threads:** while one thread stalls on memory, the core runs another.

steps.title: Real-time scheduling
steps.body:
- **Rate-monotonic (RM):** static priority, shorter period = higher priority. Sufficient schedulability test: U = Σ Cᵢ/Tᵢ ≤ n(2^(1/n) − 1) (≈ 0.828 for n = 2, ≈ 0.780 for n = 3, → ln 2 ≈ 0.693).
- **Earliest deadline first (EDF):** dynamic priority, nearest deadline first. Schedulable (periodic, deadline = period) iff U ≤ 1.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · When RM fails but EDF works
steps.body:
T1: C = 25, T = 50; T2: C = 35, T = 80.
- U = 0.5 + 0.4375 = 0.9375 > 0.828 → the RM test is inconclusive; simulating: T1 runs 0–25, T2 runs 25–50, T1 preempts at 50 and runs 50–75, T2 needs 10 more and gets 75–85 → misses its deadline at 80. **RM fails.**
- EDF: U ≤ 1 → **schedulable**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating the RM bound as necessary: U above the bound does not prove failure, you must check (e.g. by simulation).
- Forgetting that in MLFQ a process is demoted only when it uses the full quantum.

activity.prompt: Match the scheduling idea
pairs: Demotes jobs that use their full quantum
Keeps a process on the CPU with its warm cache
Shorter period gets higher static priority
Idle CPU takes work from a busy one

quiz.q: RM bound for 2 tasks is about
quiz.why: The rate-monotonic bound is n(2^(1/n) − 1). For n = 2 that is 2(√2 − 1) ≈ 0.828.
On one CPU, EDF can schedule any task set (deadline = period) with total utilisation U ≤ 1. It is optimal.

quiz.q: In MLFQ, a CPU-bound process tends to
quiz.why: A CPU-bound process uses its full quantum, so MLFQ lowers its priority again and again. It sinks to lower queues.

options: tries but does not guarantee keeping a process on one CPU
quiz.why: With soft affinity, the OS tries to keep a process on the same CPU for cache reasons, but may migrate it. Hard affinity forbids migration.

quiz.q: Tasks with U = 0.6 total (3 tasks) under RM are
quiz.why: For 3 tasks the RM bound is about 0.780. Total utilisation 0.6 is below it, so the tasks are schedulable.

questions.q: Turnaround time =
questions.why: Turnaround time is the total time from arrival to completion: CT − AT.

questions.q: Which algorithm can cause the convoy effect?
questions.why: In FCFS, short processes wait behind a long one, the convoy effect. SRTF, RR and MLFQ avoid it.

questions.q: Which never starves a process?
questions.why: In FCFS every process waits only for those ahead of it, so it eventually runs. SJF, SRTF and unaged priority can starve long or low-priority jobs.

questions.q: RR with tiny quantum causes
questions.why: With a very small quantum, the CPU spends a large share of time switching rather than running processes. So context-switch overhead is high.

questions.q: Optimal average waiting time (preemptive) is given by
questions.why: SRTF is the preemptive version of SJF, which gives the best average waiting time.

questions.q: Assertion (A): SJF is hard to implement exactly. Reason (R): The length of the next CPU burst is not known in advance. Choose:
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: SJF needs the length of each process's next CPU burst, which is not known in advance. So it cannot be done exactly and is approximated by predicting bursts. Both statements are true and the reason explains the assertion.

Case: an interactive editor feels sluggish behind a long compile on the same CPU. Which scheduler change helps most?
questions.why: Round Robin or MLFQ with a reasonable quantum gives the interactive editor the CPU soon after each key press. A long compile then cannot hog the CPU, unlike under FCFS.

questions.why: Timeline with q = 3: P1 0–3, P2 3–6, P3 6–8 (finishes), P1 8–10 (finishes), P2 10–11. So P2 completes at 11.

questions.why: U = 1/4 + 2/6 + 3/12 ≈ 0.833, and the Liu–Layland bound for 3 tasks is 3(2^(1/3) − 1) ≈ 0.780. Since U exceeds the bound, this sufficient test cannot decide; response-time analysis (R₃ = 10 ≤ 12) shows the set is in fact schedulable.

options: Response time is bounded by (n − 1)·q for n processes ignoring switch time
Average WT is always less than SJF

courses.title: Unit 4 · Process Synchronization
courses.summary: Race conditions, the critical-section problem, Peterson's solution, hardware instructions, mutex locks, semaphores, monitors and the classical problems (bounded buffer, readers–writers, dining philosophers).
outcomes: Learners can state the three requirements of a critical-section solution
Learners can verify Peterson's algorithm and spot flawed variants
Learners can solve semaphore value and output-ordering problems
Learners can write semaphore solutions to the classical problems

lessons.title: Race conditions and the critical-section problem

scenes.text: Two bank tellers read the same balance of ₹5,000 at the same moment.
One adds a ₹1,000 deposit, the other subtracts a ₹1,000 withdrawal, and each writes its own result.
Final balance: ₹6,000 or ₹4,000 instead of ₹5,000. That is a race condition.

steps.title: Why count++ is not atomic
steps.body: `count++` compiles to three machine steps: `r = count; r = r + 1; count = r`. If two threads interleave these steps, an update can be lost. A **race condition** occurs when the outcome depends on the order of interleaving of accesses to shared data.

steps.title: Critical-section requirements
steps.body:
Code that touches shared data is the **critical section (CS)**. Structure: entry section → CS → exit section → remainder. A correct solution must provide:
- **Mutual exclusion:** at most one process in the CS at a time.
- **Progress:** if no one is in the CS, the choice of who enters next cannot be postponed indefinitely, and only processes wanting to enter take part in the decision.
- **Bounded waiting:** there is a bound on how many times others may enter before a waiting process gets its turn.
(Assume no speed assumptions about processes.)

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Possible final values
steps.body:
count = 5. Thread A does count++, thread B does count−− concurrently, each as load–modify–store.
- Serial runs: 5.
- A loads 5, B loads 5, A stores 6, B stores 4 → **4**.
- A loads 5, B loads 5, B stores 4, A stores 6 → **6**.
Possible results: {4, 5, 6}.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Minimum value puzzle
steps.body: Two threads each execute `for i in 1..3: x = x + 1` (load, add, store), x starts at 0. The smallest possible final value is **2**, not 3: T1 loads 0 and stalls; T2 does two full iterations (x = 2); T1 stores 1; T2 loads 1 and stalls; T1 finishes its other two iterations (x = 3); T2 stores 2. Puzzles like this test whether you consider worst-case interleavings.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking a single C statement is atomic.
- Confusing progress with bounded waiting: strict alternation satisfies mutual exclusion and bounded waiting but violates progress.
- Assuming disabling interrupts works on multiprocessors — it only stops preemption on the local CPU.

activity.prompt: Match the requirement to its meaning
pairs: At most one process inside the critical section
A free CS cannot be held up by processes not wanting it
A limit on how often others can overtake a waiting process
Result depends on interleaving of shared accesses

quiz.why: count++ is compiled as load, add and store. A switch between these steps can lose an update, so it is not atomic in general.
With a turn variable only, processes must alternate. A process that wants in can be blocked by one that does not want the critical section, so the progress requirement is violated.

quiz.q: Disabling interrupts for mutual exclusion fails on
quiz.why: Disabling interrupts stops preemption only on that CPU. On a multiprocessor, other CPUs keep running and can still enter the critical section.

quiz.q: x = 10. T1 does x = x + 2 and T2 does x = x * 2, each as load–compute–store with no lock. How many distinct final values are possible?
quiz.why: Serial orders give 24 and 22; if both load 10, the last store wins giving 12 or 20 — four values.

quiz.q: The part of code accessing shared data is the
quiz.why: The critical section is the code that accesses shared data, which must not be run by more than one process at a time.

scenes.text: Two villagers approach a one-lane bridge. Each raises a flag to show interest and politely says 'you go first'.
The last one to say 'you go first' waits. This is Peterson's algorithm.

steps.title: Peterson's algorithm (2 processes)
steps.body:
Shared: `bool flag[2] = {false, false}; int turn;`
For process i (j = 1 − i):
`flag[i] = true; turn = j;`
`while (flag[j] && turn == j) ; // busy wait`
`/* critical section */`
`flag[i] = false;`

It satisfies **mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting** (each waits at most one entry of the other). It assumes loads/stores are not reordered — modern CPUs may reorder, so real code needs memory barriers.

steps.title: Hardware instructions
steps.body:
- **test_and_set(&lock):** atomically returns old value and sets lock = true. Spin: `while (test_and_set(&lock));`
- **compare_and_swap(&v, expected, new):** atomically sets v = new only if v == expected; returns old value.
- Simple spin locks with these give mutual exclusion but **not bounded waiting**; a bounded-waiting version scans the waiting[] array in cyclic order.
- **Atomic variables** (e.g. atomic increment) are built on CAS.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Why both variables are needed
steps.body:
Variant using only flags: `flag[i] = true; while (flag[j]);` — if both set their flag simultaneously, both spin forever → **deadlock, progress violated**.
Variant using only turn (strict alternation): mutual exclusion holds, but if P0 wants to enter twice in a row while P1 stays in its remainder section, P0 is blocked → **progress violated**.
Peterson combines both to fix each flaw.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Wrong order
steps.body: Suppose a student writes `turn = j; flag[i] = true;` (swapped). Interleaving: P0 sets turn = 1; P1 sets turn = 0, flag[1] = true, checks flag[0] (false) → enters CS. P0 sets flag[0] = true, checks flag[1] && turn == 1 → turn is 0 → enters. **Both in CS → mutual exclusion broken.** The order matters.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Claiming test_and_set spin locks guarantee bounded waiting.
- Forgetting that Peterson's solution is for exactly two processes (the bakery algorithm generalises to n).
- Ignoring that busy waiting wastes CPU — acceptable only for very short critical sections (spinlocks).

statements.s: Peterson's algorithm satisfies bounded waiting.
statements.why: A waiting process enters after at most one entry by the other.

statements.s: A plain test_and_set spin lock guarantees bounded waiting.
statements.why: Unlucky processes can lose the race repeatedly.

statements.s: Swapping the two lines `flag[i]=true; turn=j;` keeps Peterson correct.
compare_and_swap executes atomically.
Peterson's algorithm works unchanged for 5 processes.

quiz.q: In Peterson's algorithm, process i sets turn to
quiz.why: In Peterson's algorithm, process i sets turn = j (the other process) to politely give way. Then it waits while the other process wants in and it is the other's turn.

quiz.q: Using only flag[] variables may lead to
quiz.why: If both set their flags first and each waits for the other's flag to clear, both spin forever. That is a deadlock.
test_and_set atomically sets the lock and returns its old value. If the old value was false, the caller got the lock.

options: critical sections are very short on multiprocessors
quiz.why: A spin lock wastes CPU while waiting. It pays off only when the critical section is very short on a multiprocessor, cheaper than sleeping and waking.

quiz.q: Peterson can fail on modern CPUs without
quiz.why: Modern CPUs and compilers may reorder memory operations, which can break Peterson's algorithm. Memory barriers prevent the reordering.

scenes.text: The library has 3 study rooms and a token counter showing free rooms.
Each student takes a token (wait); if none left, they queue. Leaving returns a token (signal). That counter is a counting semaphore.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
A **semaphore** S is an integer accessed only via two atomic operations:
- `wait(S)` (P, down): `S--; if (S < 0) block this process;`
- `signal(S)` (V, up): `S++; if (S <= 0) wake one blocked process;`
(This blocking version lets S go negative: |S| = number of waiting processes. The busy-wait textbook version keeps S ≥ 0.)
- **Binary semaphore** (0/1) ≈ mutex lock; **counting semaphore** controls access to n identical resources.
- A **mutex** has an owner — only the locker should unlock; a semaphore has no owner and can be used for signalling between processes.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Final value
steps.body:
A counting semaphore initialised to 10. 6 P (wait) and 4 V (signal) operations are performed.
Final value = 10 − 6 + 4 = **8**.
Another: S = 7, then 20 P and 15 V → 7 − 20 + 15 = **2**. (With the blocking definition the result is the same arithmetic; negative values mean waiting processes.)

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Enforcing order
steps.body:
Ensure statement S1 in P1 runs before S2 in P2. Use semaphore `sync = 0`.
- P1: `S1; signal(sync);`
- P2: `wait(sync); S2;`
If P2 runs first, wait blocks (sync becomes −1) until P1 signals. This **signalling** pattern is why semaphores (not just mutexes) exist.

steps.title: Solved example 3 · Maximum in CS
steps.body: Semaphore `mutex` initialised to 3 guards a section; 10 processes run `wait(mutex); CS; signal(mutex);`. At most **3** processes are inside at once. If one process by mistake does `signal(mutex); CS; wait(mutex);` it can let extra processes in — mutual exclusion breaks.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Swapping wait and signal, or forgetting signal on an error path (leaks a permit → eventual deadlock).
- Calling wait on two semaphores in different orders in two processes → deadlock (P0: wait(S), wait(Q); P1: wait(Q), wait(S)).
- Treating a binary semaphore and a mutex as identical in ownership semantics.

activity.prompt: A counting semaphore starts at 4. Then 9 wait() and 3 signal() operations happen. What is its final value? (blocking definition, may be negative)

quiz.q: wait() on a semaphore with value 0 (blocking version)
quiz.why: A semaphore value 0 means no permit is available. wait() (P) therefore blocks the caller until another process signals.

quiz.q: A semaphore initialised to 0 is typically used for
quiz.why: A semaphore starting at 0 makes the first wait() block until another process does signal(). This is used to order events. A mutex starts at 1.
Each P (wait) decrements and each V (signal) increments: 5 − 3 + 1 = 3.

quiz.q: Two processes take S then Q, and Q then S respectively. Risk:
quiz.why: If each process holds one semaphore and waits for the other's, there is a circular wait. That is a deadlock.

quiz.q: Which may only be released by the thread that acquired it?
quiz.why: A mutex has an owner. Only the thread that locked it may unlock it. Semaphores can be signalled by any thread.

scenes.text: A chai maker fills a rack of 10 cups; customers take cups. If the rack is full the maker waits; if empty, customers wait.
Five philosophers at a round table need two chopsticks each — grabbing left then right can freeze everybody.

steps.title: Bounded buffer (producer–consumer)
steps.body:
Semaphores: `mutex = 1`, `empty = n`, `full = 0`.
Producer: `wait(empty); wait(mutex); add item; signal(mutex); signal(full);`
Consumer: `wait(full); wait(mutex); remove item; signal(mutex); signal(empty);`
If the producer did `wait(mutex)` before `wait(empty)` and the buffer was full, it would hold mutex while sleeping → consumer can never enter → **deadlock**.

steps.title: Readers–writers
steps.body:
Many readers may read together; a writer needs exclusive access. First readers–writers solution (readers preferred): `rw_mutex = 1, mutex = 1, read_count = 0`.
Reader: `wait(mutex); read_count++; if (read_count == 1) wait(rw_mutex); signal(mutex); read; wait(mutex); read_count--; if (read_count == 0) signal(rw_mutex); signal(mutex);`
Writer: `wait(rw_mutex); write; signal(rw_mutex);`
Writers may **starve**; the second variant prefers writers (then readers may starve).

steps.title: Dining philosophers and monitors
steps.body:
Naive solution (each picks left then right chopstick semaphore) can **deadlock** if all pick left together. Remedies: allow at most 4 philosophers at the table; pick both only if both are free (inside a critical section); asymmetric — odd picks left first, even picks right first.

**Monitor:** a language construct where only one process is active inside at a time; **condition variables** with `x.wait()` (always suspends) and `x.signal()` (resumes one waiter; no effect if none — unlike a semaphore's signal, which is remembered).

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Trace the buffer
steps.body: n = 3, buffer empty: empty = 3, full = 0. Producer produces 2 items → empty = 1, full = 2. Consumer consumes 1 → empty = 2, full = 1. Consumer tries 2 more: first succeeds (full = 0, empty = 3), second **blocks** on wait(full).

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Breaking circular wait
steps.body: With 5 philosophers and 5 chopsticks, allowing only 4 to sit (a counting semaphore `room = 4`): by pigeonhole, 4 philosophers holding at most 4 chopsticks leaves one free, so at least one philosopher can get both → **no deadlock**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reversing wait(empty)/wait(mutex) order in the producer.
- Thinking condition-variable signal is remembered like a semaphore's signal.
- Claiming the first readers–writers solution is starvation-free.

activity.prompt: Put the producer's operations in the correct order

quiz.q: Initial value of 'full' in bounded buffer:
quiz.why: 'full' counts filled slots and the buffer starts empty, so full = 0 (while empty = n and mutex = 1).

quiz.q: In the first readers–writers solution, who may starve?
quiz.why: In the first readers–writers solution, readers have priority. A steady stream of readers keeps the lock held, so a writer can starve.

quiz.q: Naive dining philosophers can lead to
quiz.why: If every philosopher picks up the left chopstick, each waits for the right one forever. That is a deadlock.

quiz.q: x.signal() in a monitor with no waiting process
quiz.why: In a monitor, x.signal() with no waiting process does nothing and is forgotten. A semaphore's signal would still increment the count.

quiz.q: Allowing only 4 philosophers at a table of 5 prevents deadlock because
options: at least one can get two chopsticks
quiz.why: With 5 chopsticks and only 4 philosophers seated, by the pigeonhole principle at least one can get two chopsticks. That philosopher eats and then releases them.

questions.q: A race condition occurs when
options: results depend on interleaving of shared accesses
questions.why: A race condition is when the result depends on the timing or interleaving of accesses to shared data.

questions.q: Which is NOT a CS requirement?
questions.why: The three requirements are mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting. Maximum throughput is not one of them.

questions.q: wait() is also called
questions.why: wait() is also called P, from the Dutch proberen (to try). signal() is V.

questions.q: Semaphore initialised to 1 used for mutual exclusion is a
questions.why: A semaphore starting at 1 takes only the values 0 and 1 in mutual exclusion use. That is a binary semaphore.

questions.q: S = 8; 5 P and 2 V → S =
questions.why: Each P decrements and each V increments: 8 − 5 + 2 = 5.

questions.q: Peterson's solution is for how many processes?
questions.why: Peterson's classic solution is for exactly two processes. For n processes you need other algorithms.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Strict alternation is not a valid CS solution. Reason (R): It violates mutual exclusion. Choose:
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Strict alternation does give mutual exclusion, so R is false. Its flaw is that it violates progress, so A is true but R is false.

questions.q: In producer–consumer, swapping the producer's wait(empty) and wait(mutex) can cause
questions.why: If the producer takes the mutex first and then waits on empty while the buffer is full, it sleeps holding the mutex. The consumer cannot get the mutex to free a slot, causing deadlock.

questions.q: Which hardware primitive underlies most lock-free code?
questions.why: Compare-and-swap atomically updates a value only if it still equals an expected value. Most lock-free algorithms are built on it.

questions.q: Case: a logging library uses a binary semaphore; a thread that never locked it calls signal on it. With a mutex instead, this would
options: be an error because mutexes have owners
questions.why: A mutex has an owner and usually only the locking thread may unlock it. So a thread that never locked it calling unlock would be an error, while a semaphore allows it silently.

questions.q: Counting semaphore initial value x; after 15 P and 7 V the value is −2. x =
questions.why: The value is x − 15 + 7 = −2, so x = −2 + 8 = 6.

questions.q: Two processes: P1 executes `wait(S); wait(T); …`; P2 executes `wait(T); wait(S); …`. S = T = 1. Which is TRUE?
questions.why: If P1 takes S and P2 takes T before either takes its second semaphore, each waits for the other and they deadlock. In other interleavings it works, so deadlock is possible but not certain.

questions.q: Readers–writers (reader priority): 3 readers inside, a writer arrives, then a 4th reader. The 4th reader
questions.why: Under reader priority, readers already inside keep rw_mutex held. A new reader just increments read_count and enters, even though a writer is waiting.

questions.q: Threads increment shared x (initially 0) 5 times each with load/add/store, 2 threads, no locks. Minimum possible final x:
questions.why: With the classic worst-case interleaving, each thread's load and store can overwrite the other's progress. The minimum possible final value is 2, not 5.

questions.q: Which monitor signalling discipline lets the signalled thread run immediately while the signaller waits?
questions.why: In Hoare-style monitors (signal-and-wait), the signalled thread runs immediately and the signaller waits. In Mesa style the signaller continues.

questions.q: Bounded buffer n = 5: producer has produced 7 items and consumer consumed 4. Values of empty and full:
questions.why: The buffer holds 7 − 4 = 3 items, so full = 3 and empty = 5 − 3 = 2.
